paragraphs.text: FIRST DISCOURSE. 1. I see that many do not know where this abominable and newly appeared body of the Paulicians got its name, and that a great deal of scattered, inconsistent and conflicting conjecture about it is circulating among everyone. So I thought it not out of place to treat this subject briefly, in plain and concise language, setting out some things I learned from people who came to loathe this heresy and washed away the defilement of their apostasy with tears of repentance. I will also note whether those who came later invented and devised anything beyond what the followers of Mani held in earlier times. 2. Samosata is a city of Syria, in which long ago [?] …of the most holy archbishop of Constantinople, in a synopsis narrating the new resurgence of the Manichaeans [?] … I who made the selection have set down both what has already been said and the chapters that follow in order in the present [?], some in full and some in summary, to avoid length. Some things in the writings of the patriarch mentioned above I passed over: those which, because of the depth of their thought or because of their excessive elaboration and artifice, were accessible and pleasing to few, while presenting almost the same ideas as the passages selected, even if they reached their conclusions in other words and by different kinds of argument. [?]

the God-hated thinking of the Manichaeans burst in like a band of revellers. In this city a woman named Callinice, who had gathered into herself all the filth of this heresy, bore two sons. Would that she had not! One they named Paul, the other John. These boys, born no less of that wretched heresy than of the womb, drank in the undiluted poison of apostasy. Since they surpassed the others in impiety and were energetic in doing evil, the initiates and mystagogues of this abomination sent them out as heralds of lawlessness to the region now called that of the Armeniacs. A village called Phanaroea in the local tongue received them before any other place and conceived the seeds of impiety. From this, one of the hamlets within it also got the name Episparis. From the second of the two, then, the one named Paul, the lovers of the apostasy took the name of Paulicians in place of being known by a name derived from Christ. Others, however, say it came not from one of them but from both, the two names joined together into a barbarized compound title: instead of being called Paulioannae, they are called what they are named now. 3. When time had passed, the council of the apostasy appointed another teacher for them. He bore from his parents the name Constantine but renamed himself Silvanus. And indeed [?] in the same sense, 'revelled in'. (12) Episparis: from episperō, 'to sow over'. [?] p. 758 b, namely the Paulicians. Paulikianoi and Paulik[?] … not only called so, but having become so in truth

19 PHOTIUS PATRIARCH. The shield-bearers of the apostasy rank this man far above the sons of Callinice. This man, this most formidable perpetrator of unheard-of evils, did not venture to commit his heretical doctrines to writing. Instead he sealed them firmly in his initiates by custom and constant teaching, and entrusted the rites of impiety to them to keep unbreached. The Gospel and the Apostle, however, which the divine body of Christians also embraces and honors, he handed on to them in writing. He did not greatly alter the words and names, nor did he adulterate the form of the text, as Valentinus and others did; but he perverted and corrupted the whole sense of piety, and twisted and dragged everything toward the outlook of his own apostasy. He gave them the literal words to hold, as has been said, without openly corrupting the Gospel by interpolations or additions. But to these words he attached and slipped in meanings which none of the sacred words fit and in which no coherence can be seen; meanings that conflict with one another, and are expressed by anything at all rather than by the apostolic and evangelical sayings. Having entrusted these to them, he laid down the rule that they should read nothing besides the Gospel and the Apostle. But in time he was destroyed, in soul even more than in body. [?] rightly the Coislin manuscript [?] … (from enairō, p. 655) [?] … the name [?] … because the heretics, by keeping silent and concealing their own mysteries, were thought by many to worship God.

4. After Silvanus, Symeon presides over their impious school; he too renamed himself, as Titus. Next came an Armenian by race named Gegnaesius, renamed Timothy. Fourth was Joseph, who changed his proper name to Epaphroditus. Then Zacharias, whom no small part of the heresy regards as a hireling and unworthy of their teaching office. Sixth came Baanes the filthy, after whom the seventh and last evil sprang up, Sergius, who also renamed himself, as Tychicus. These, then, are the teachers of their apostasy, and this is how far they have advanced, from the time this apostate and Christ-hating body took its name from Paul down to our own day. But one must carefully note and understand this: when someone demands that the present-day children of this apostasy repudiate the founders of this abomination, they readily anathematize Mani, Paul, John and the rest. But Constantine, whom they call Silvanus, Symeon called Titus, Gegnaesius called Timothy, Joseph Epaphroditus, the filthy Baanes, and Sergius Tychicus, they by no means agree to anathematize. Instead they embrace and accept them as apostles of Christ and teachers of true religion. Not all of them, however, honor all those named in the same way. Those down to Baanes and Sergius they deify equally; but from there they split into two opposing parties, some deifying Baanes and others Sergius, and they press their strife and faction against one another so hard that their rivalry goes as far as bloodshed. 5. They acknowledge six churches. The first they call Macedonia, the second Achaea, the third that of the Philippians, then that of the Laodiceans, fifth that of the Ephesians, and last that of the Colossians. These are names of cities known to ancient history and mentioned by the divine Paul. But they strive to leave nothing unadulterated or unfalsified, and are not ashamed even of things refuted by plain sight. They call Macedonia a small town of Colonea named Cibossa, where Constantine Silvanus taught the apostasy. And a village of Sa- (29) 'An Armenian by race, Gegnaesius': so our manuscript. (31) 'When someone demands of them': so the Colbert manuscript; 'when someone demands of them' with the dative, less correctly.

23 PHOTIUS PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE 24. -mosata is Mananalis, which was the seat of the teaching of Gegnaesius, also called Timothy; to it they give the name Achaea. Those who became disciples of Joseph Epaphroditus and of Zacharias the hireling shepherd they label the church of the Philippians. Those in the small town of Argaoun they call the church of the Laodiceans. Those in Mopsuestia they refashion into the church of the Ephesians, just as they assign the people called the Cynochorites to that of the Colossians. The organization and teaching of these last three churches they trace back and ascribe to Sergius, also called Tychicus. Such, then, are their teachers and so-called churches. This intricate mindset of apostasy, however, is not made up of one single error but of many and varied ones. 6. They confess two principles, as the Manichaeans do. They say that one is God, the heavenly Father, whom they exclude even from authority over this universe, entrusting to him only dominion over the world to come; and that the other is the Creator of the world, to whom they grant sovereignty over the present age. Those who are truly Christians these thrice-accursed men call 'Romans', while they attach to themselves the name of Christians, from which they are utterly estranged. They speak of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, which are pious words, but they put the utmost impiety beneath them. For when they say them, they do not mean what the catholic and apostolic Church of God means; they tear the words away from there and apply them to the most impious ideas. They eagerly declare, 'Let all who do not believe in Father and Son and Holy Spirit be anathema!' But they at once proclaim as Father not the Almighty, the maker of [?] (37) 'Gegnaesius': Euthymius again has 'Genesius'.

heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible. Rather, when they say 'Father', they add 'heavenly', and to him they in no way whatever entrust authority over heaven and what is in it. Some, however, assign him the governance of heaven, but not of the things it contains. Such, then, is the first of their impieties. 7. They also blaspheme our all-holy Lady the Theotokos with things it is not lawful to commit to writing or to hearing. These men, who deserve to perish three times over rather than once, do not shudder to say: 'We believe in the all-holy Theotokos, into whom the Lord entered and from whom he came forth.' By these words they mean the Jerusalem above, and they say that Christ entered it as forerunner on our behalf, as the divine Apostle also said. Sometimes, when they are pressed to confess that Christ came forth from the Virgin and are left with no way out, they spin the fable that he brought his body down with him from above and passed through her as through a pipe, and that this spotless and pure Virgin bore other sons to Joseph after the saving birth. In the same way they heap countless insults on the communion of the precious body and blood of Christ our God. They say they receive the body and blood, but they tell fables about the Lord's words, which they say he spoke as he gave to the apostles: 'Take, eat and drink', without, they claim, offering any bread or wine at all. They also blaspheme the life-giving cross. They say they venerate and accept it, but these deceivers and charlatans make Christ himself out to be the cross: for he himself, they say, stretched out his hands in the shape of a cross. The real cross, however, being wood, they say, and an instrument for criminals, and lying under a curse, ought not to be venerated and kissed. 8. Moreover, they turn away from the holy prophets, the whole of the Old Scripture, and the other [?] … the Savior of us all. It reads: 'For Simon and Menander, Cerdo and Marcion deny the incarnation altogether and call the birth from the Virgin a myth. But Valentinus and Basilides and Harmonius, and those of their company, accept the'

27 PHOTIUS PATRIARCH. saints, calling them robbers and thieves. Above all they revile Peter, the chief of the apostles, because, they say, he denied his faith in his Teacher and Christ. And yet their teacher Mani loudly proclaims to them: 'I am not merciless, I, Christ, who said, "Whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him." But I say: whoever denies me before men and secures his own safety by the lie, I will receive with joy as one who has not denied me, and I will count his recantation and his lie as a safeguard and preservation of his confession of me.' Such is their attitude, and they readily deny the confession of their own doctrine whenever they are afraid, declaring themselves answerable for nothing even if they deny it ten thousand times. Yet the man who for a brief moment, beset by so many terrors, suffered a human weakness and slipped into denial they treat as utterly to be rejected and abhorred. Their real reason is not the one they allege but one they keep silent and conceal: that he foretold their apostasy when he said, 'Be eager to be found by him spotless and blameless, in peace, and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, speaking of these things in all his letters. There are some things in them hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.' These words of the chief apostle plainly foretell the audacity and impiety of these men, who twist the Lord's own sayings, the apostolic writings and the other Scriptures (I mean the Acts of the Apostles and the so-called Catholic Epistles), except those attributed to the chief apostle, which they do not accept even in their wording. These are the ones who truly twist and distort the Scriptures to their own destruction. As for the Acts of the Apostles and the Catholic Epistles, not all of them include these with the other books; there are [?] … our [?], the first of the apostles, to whom first the Father revealed the Son, whom Christ rightly called blessed, the called and chosen one, companion at table and fellow traveller, the good and approved disciple.

some, though, who do include them. Such, then, is their madness concerning the prophets and the Old Testament, the other saints who shone under it, and the chief of the apostles. 9. They call their own assemblies the Catholic Church, especially when they enter into discussions and debates with the orthodox; among themselves they call their assemblies 'prayers'. Moreover, although they spit on saving baptism, they pretend to accept it by substituting words of the Gospel for the word 'baptism'. For they say: 'The Lord said, "I am the living water."' Yet when they fall into some rather serious bodily illness, they even place the precious and life-giving cross made of wood on themselves; then, once they have been healed, they break it or trample it and throw it away. What is more, since presbyters of the Church are often held captive among them, they have their children judged worthy of being illuminated by saving baptism. These men, who are unworthy of any benefit, claim that the cross and baptism are good for the body, but that their power does not extend to the cleansing of the soul or to any other benefit for it. Indeed, not a few of them even partake of the communion of the precious body and blood of Christ our God; but they receive it in order to deceive the simpler folk. In addition to all this, they do not accept the presbyters of the catholic Church or the other priests, because, they say, it was the priests and elders of the people who convened the council against Christ. Those among them who hold the rank of priests they call not priests but 'fellow travellers' and 'notaries'. These men show no difference from the multitude in dress, in way of life, or in any other manner of living a more dignified life. Notaries: [?] properly … shorthand writers

10. They do not hesitate to venerate our Gospel book, not, however, where the figure of the precious cross is engraved, but on the rest of the book, where the image of the cross is not marked. They say they venerate the book because it contains the Lord's words. In matters of doctrine, then, they are impious in this way, and wholly at odds both with the truth and with themselves. Their way of life is full of licentiousness, full of unspeakable defilements and unimaginable filth. They practise intercourse of both kinds, shamelessly ready for every unspeakable act. Some of them, however, are said to shun intercourse with their mothers. They have given over their whole life to drunkenness and debauchery, and pursue every other kind of moral corruption. Why go into every detail rather than say this: the life they lead is in no way out of tune with their doctrines. 11. So much for this. But if anyone wishes to [see] their impiety from its origins and where its first seeds were sown, Cyril, who was entrusted with the helm of the holy city, will guide them through the history, as will Epiphanius, great in wonders, and indeed not a few of those who compiled ecclesiastical histories: Titus bishop of Bostra, and Sera- [?] … 'the apostles,' he says, 'in the memoirs they composed, which are called Gospels, handed down that Jesus had commanded them thus.' (68) 'Venerate': on the veneration of Gospel books [?]. (75) Epiphanius, Heresies 66. (74) 'Ecclesiastical histories': see Eusebius,

-pion of Thmuis, and Alexander, who was entrusted with the high-priestly laws of the city of Lycopolis. Besides these there is Heraclian, bishop of Chalcedon, who more than all of them triumphed over this impiety and refuted it by force, setting down his contests against the apostasy in twenty books; and very many others too. Nevertheless, even now this discourse, not thinking it unprofitable, will [relate] in a cursory way

[?] A certain Scythianus, an Egyptian by country but a Saracen by race, lived in Alexandria. He neither agreed with the Christians nor accepted the ways of the Jews. Having become practised in speech from half-understood scraps of Aristotle, he composed four books, of which the (77) 'Alexander': his book Against the [doctrines] of Manichaeus [?] … of the empty and vain heresy of the Manichaeans, also called Paulicians, edited by Matthew Rader. (80) 'A certain Scythianus': [?] drew from Cyril [?] … the [account] of Peter of Sicily: 'He composed four books'

first he named the Gospel, in which certain pernicious and abominable acts of Christ our God are fabricated with a God-opposing mind. The second he gave the title Chapter, and the third he dignified with the name of Mysteries; in it, as he saw fit, he works out certain distortions and slanders of the Law and the Prophets. The fourth, which brings about the death of the soul, is entitled Treasure of Life. This Scythianus had a disciple named Terebinthus. When the teacher perished from among men by a bitter death in Judea (for he had gone there), this disciple of wickedness inherited his money and his books. While he was staying in Palestine and Judea he was condemned by all the pious, and, unable to bear the disgrace, he left for Persia, renaming himself Buddas. For his name was already being noised about and made the impious man hated even before anyone met him. But he gained nothing from the change of name. His deeds and doctrines exposed him to those who had not known him before, and he was refuted and driven out by the learned men among the Persians, who, though not pious themselves, were better than he was in every respect. Having become a fugitive as a result, he worked his way, under the pretext of hospitality, into the house of a woman whose husband had died, and corrupted her. Then he went up on a roof and called upon the demons he was accustomed to summon, the same demons whom the lovers of the Manichaean apostasy still invoke to this day whenever they perform their loathsome ischas rite. While he was performing this accursed ceremony, he became the object of a divine and truly just threat. He was hurled from the roof like a discus in the very midst of his impiety and abominable rites, and was shattered in his whole body, and [?] … the first, called the holy Gospel, containing not the acts of Christ but as of Mani [?] … the third, of the Mysteries, that is, for the overthrow of the Law and the Prophets that they have contrived; the fourth, which they carry about calling it the Treasure of Life, though it is in fact a treasure of death. It seems (86) 'worked his way in and corrupted': [?] expresses the force of the verb

…ended his life. So this second beast of impiety was also cut down. But the widow got no good, after all, from her impious guest. She saw herself left without husband or children or the rest of her family, with a fortune in money that had come to her, and with those abominable books. As a comfort in her loneliness she bought for a sum of silver a boy named Cubricus. She adopted him as her son and had him taught the learning of the Persians, and so sharpened a bitter arrow against human nature. For when the widow died, he became heir both to the money and to the impious books. So that his slavery would not bring reproach on him, he changed the name that recalled his servile condition to Manes. In the Persian tongue this means something like “good at conversation” and “effective in debate.” And that is how he seemed to many, though he deserved to be called Manes in the Greek sense rather than the Persian. For in very truth he proved to be a vessel of madness (mania) if anyone ever was. He took the whole spirit of error into himself and was driven by it, and he even went so mad as to call himself the Paraclete and the Holy Spirit. He inherited this kind of imitation from his predecessors. Of these, Scythianus called himself the Father, and Terebinthus called himself the Son of God, born of a virgin (O godlessness [Editor's notes, partly garbled: “… Then, so that the slavery of Cubricus … (in the unpublished texts) … he [called] himself Manes instead of Cubricus … having devised a … impiety and madly defined this as a second principle …” and p. 65: “the one who went most grievously mad.” Add p. … (98) ἐνεργούμενος (“driven”): so from our manuscript, instead of ἐνθειού-…]

…that knows no limit!) he dared to call himself. Then he also gathered twelve disciples and sent them out as heralds of his error. Manes, that thunderstruck man, became notorious for his wickedness, and his fame reached even the ears of the king of the Persians. The king's son had been struck down by an illness, and when he heard that Manes promised to free the boy from the disease by prayer, he received the impostor to treat the boy. Manes sent away the physicians who were there, though they promised that the boy would easily be cured, and as he performed his prayer he drove out of life a child who would not have suffered this if he himself had not undertaken the cure. The impiety and imposture of the wretch were exposed quickly and publicly, and the deceiver was condemned to live in the prison for criminals. But he was a slave and practised in slavish tricks, and he knew very well that before long he would be judged to pay the penalty for murder, since by his own apostasy he had killed the royal child. So he escaped from the building and caused the death of his jailers: because they had not guarded the scoundrel securely, they were all punished by beheading. 13. This slave, deceiver, murderer and runaway prisoner made his way to Mesopotamia and began once more to sow the tares of apostasy. But the bishop of Carchar, whose name was Archelaus, a holy man and highly skilled in learning both divine and human, gathered an audience of pagans, so that the truth might not seem to win the prize through the partiality of Christian judges. He took up the cause of piety against the man named after madness, and he shamed and refuted the thrice-accursed man so thoroughly that Manes fled from there at once, and the seeds of his apostasy did not even take root. Escaping from there, he reached a village of the meanest sort, and there again he schemed to nurse and display his own impiety. But Archelaus, the ardent champion of piety and a true shepherd, who took no ordinary care of his sheep, did not slacken in pursuing the one who had risen up to tear the flock more savagely than a wolf. So the man named after madness, unable to bear even his presence without great anguish, ran away from there too and moved from place to place. In these places,

as he wandered, the bodyguards of the king of the Persians, who were searching everywhere for the scoundrel, found him and brought him in chains to the king who had sent them. The king mocked and reviled him at length for his lies and his flight, and exacted a single penalty for all of them: the death that befits a deceiver, and him alone. For even if it was in no way whatever fit for human nature either to suffer or to inflict such a thing, it was certainly not unfit for the unsurpassed impieties of Manes. While the wretch was still alive they flayed his body into a sack, and so they tore him out of life and ripped him apart. They threw the rest of his body to the beasts as food, but they filled the skin itself with air like a bag and hung it up before the gates. Such was the end of life that this apostate received. 14. Another man, slightly earlier than him in time but his equal in impiety, named Zaranes, also did no small harm to the human race by his impieties. The disciples of the ill-named Manes were twelve. There was Sisinnius, who also inherited his rank in the impious teaching, and Thomas, who composed the Gospel named after him. There were Buddas and Hermas, Adamantus and Adimantus, whom he sent to various regions as heralds of their error and apostasy. His interpreters and, as it were, commentators were Hierax, Heraclides and Aphthonius. Also counted in the band of his disciples were Agapius, who composed the so-called Heptalogue, and Zaruas and Gabriabius. The band of impiety that flourished together at that time numbered this many. How could anyone tell their deeds, or recount their doctrines? They went so far in every uncleanness, every filth and every most godless opinion, and their books are full of so many defilements and absurdities, that not even those who came from among them, and who kept most

of their impiety, can bear to go on cherishing and accepting those books. In part they cannot endure the unsurpassed loathsomeness. In part they cannot make the irrationality of the precepts submit to reason. In part they shrink from and avoid, as it were, the reproach, mockery, ridicule and hatred of everyone. For this reason this newly sprung offshoot of those old seeds of loathsomeness, as we said before, does not love or cherish the writings those teachers composed for them. Instead, maliciously and wickedly, they pretend to give their attention only to the books in which the sayings of the Lord are recorded, and to the Epistles of the great apostle Paul, and in some cases to the Acts of the Apostles, and to those of the Catholic Epistles that are not by the chief of the apostles. They make a show of laying claim to these sacred oracles so that they can easily deceive those who are slower in piety and more ignorant, as if they had received from Christ himself and his disciples what the madness of their apostasy bore for them. 15. So this Manes, the leader of so great an apostasy, escaped from his prison in Persia in the ninth year of the reign of Valerian and Gallienus, who held imperial power at Rome (for nothing prevents us from going over what the course of the history passed over above). He came to Mesopotamia, and there the divinely inspired Archelaus, this holy man who was overseer of Carchar in that same country, called him to account with many great refutations of his impiety. Fleeing from there because of this unexpected shame, he slipped away to Dioris, a village of Carchar. There he met a certain Trypho, an earnest and holy man who held the rank of presbyter, and suffered the same fate. Archelaus himself also learned that the deceiver had slipped in there, for he was sharp and fervent in godly zeal. He arrived at the place and filled the deceiver with great perplexity and with the very shame he was fleeing, by overturning and demolishing his abominable doctrines and holding them up to everyone as an object of laughter and loathing. So he made him a fugitive once again [Editor's notes: (16) ἀποστασίας ἐξάρχων (“leader of the apostasy”): I have preferred this reading with … [?] … from his own [manuscript] has ἀποστασίας ἔξαρχος. (20) Διωρίδα (“Dioris”): so the Coislin manuscript, but ours has Δωρίδα.]

and during that flight, as we said before, he was caught by those who were searching and hunting for him, and paid that bitter penalty to the king of the Persians. 16. After he had ended his life so pitifully and miserably, some time later certain of his disciples in impiety sowed the tares of the Evil One as far as Samosata in Armenia. Not long afterward that destructive crop was seen to have spread and to be growing as far as Phanaroea. From it the wicked Callinice too was filled with the filth and, as I said earlier, bore Paul and John, a brood of vipers, for the destruction of the human race. From there, through a succession of heirs to the impiety, down to the times of the emperor Constantine (he was a descendant of Heraclius) [?] this war against God continued without alteration. Many exhortations and teachings were offered, even if they came to no profitable end, and many pious emperors exacted punishment from the apostates by the sword, but not even so was the impious tide halted. Then there arose among the apostates an Armenian named Constantine. His homeland is recorded as Mananalis, a village of Samosata, which even to this day is a nurse and home of Manichaeans. This Constantine gave lodging for a good many days to a deacon of the church who was returning to his own homeland from captivity in Syria. The captive had brought with him from Syria two books, one of the holy Gospel and the other of the great apostle Paul. As if to repay the hospitality, the guest, who did not know that his host's religion was impious, gave him the sacred books in return. The Armenian Constantine saw that his own blasphemy and apostasy were loathed, shunned and abhorred by all, and on the devil's advice he devised the following scheme. He cast away and spurned all the books that his religion loved and embraced. But he kept the doctrines, stripped of their writings, and tried to fit the words of the Gospel and the Apostle to them and attach the words to them. So he condemned every book of his impieties and made it a command and a law [?] to attend only to the Gospel and the Apostle. In this way, by such a trick, he could cover over the filth of his apostasy and mix into many people the deadly

poison of his noxious opinions. He did dismiss the books of the Manichaeans, as was said, but only in appearance and pretense, since he saw that the laws of the Christians hand over to the sword all who use the books of the apostasy, and consign the books themselves to the fire. But the most essential and complete of their opinions he cherished and embraced for the sake of impiety, and he made every effort and used every device to slip them under the words of the Lord and of the apostles and to read them into those words. As for the monstrous tales of Valentinus about the thirty aeons and gods, the loathsome fable of Cubricus about the rain, the defilements and lewdness of Basilides, and the stinking filth of others like them, he neither embraced them openly nor turned away from them in his own mind and in his secret teaching. Instead, like some fresh and new lawgiver, [?] of doctrines born of a harlot-like and many-tangled impiety, he shows himself to be the guide of apostasy and, for those who obey him, the patron of utter destruction. Hence the present-day children of the Manichaeans, as I said before, readily consign Scythianus, Buddas and Manes to anathema, but Constantine they deify and honor above all. And indeed his successors who appeared after him they honor equally with the apostles of Christ, not to say more. 17. This Silvanus, who had been Constantine, moved from Mananalis to Cibossa. (O godless soul and mind, that counts all shamelessness and falsehood as nothing!) He said that he was himself the Silvanus whom the Epistles of the divinely inspired Paul mention. What could anyone say to such stupefaction? To what absurdity could one show him to have been carried, so as to make him ashamed, when from the very start he did not blush to come forward through such manifest theft and derangement? Yet by working such conspicuous marvels and lies he found people whom he drew into obeying him. He called the disciples of his deceit Macedonians, and himself, as was said, Silvanus, and he claimed that he had been sent to them by the divinely inspired Paul, and he stitched together and fabricated many other such tales. That people-deceiving and mischievous monster spent twenty-seven whole years in the places mentioned and made many of the local people share in the same pollution, and [Editor's note: (31) παραδιδόντας (“hand over”): so from the edict of Constan[tine] …]

when he was caught in his war against God, he paid the penalty by stoning and went down to Hades. For the emperor Constantine learned about him and sent a man named Symeon to bring the people-deceiver to justice. As for those who had shared in his error but then renounced it and wholeheartedly took their place among the penitents, Symeon was to hand them over to the churches of God, to stay with them for instruction in the right doctrines and a fuller condemnation of the apostasy. The envoy reached the region where the workshop of error had been opened. He took with him one of the local governors, a man named Tryphon, and arrested those who had been deceived, and arrested the teacher of perdition as well. Those who looked wholeheartedly to repentance, or seemed to, he handed over to the overseers of the churches of God. But he gathered together those who were still breathing apostasy, and after telling them what such people deserved to hear, he set the leader of the error before them as a target and ordered them to stone him. The others set about the task rather reluctantly. But there was a man named Justus, Constantine's adopted son, under whom he had been trained in the Manichaean heresy. Realizing, it seems, into what a pit his teacher had thrown him, Justus took a stone that filled his hand and dealt the wicked teacher a fatal blow, driving the wretch wretchedly out of life. After him the rest of the crowd joined in the deed and turned the corpse into a heap of stones, so that even to this day the place has received from this the name Soros, “the Heap.” 18. Those who had been entrusted to the churches of God, however, for the most part showed themselves incorrigible instead of being converted. And the wretched Symeon, who knew nothing of saving teaching and was in any case light-minded and easily led astray, examined and inquired into the affairs of the apostates, and instead of calling some of them back to a pious way of thinking, went over himself to their ruinous religion. Having done this, he returned to the emperor who had sent him, and for three years he hid the beast within him and nursed it. But since it had spread through him and was now forcing its way to break out completely, he slipped away secretly from the capital and came to Cibossa, mentioned above. There he gathered the followers of Constantine, whom he himself had killed on the emperor's order, and set himself up as their teacher and successor, leading the apostasy, and he changed his name to Titus. He continued in this error for three years and carried off many from piety as plunder. Then he was caught doing these things and paid the penalty of death by fire [Editor's notes: “… changed.” (45) Τρεῖς (“three”): Montfaucon has πρός, wrongly. (42) τοῦ μετακαλεῖν (“calling back”): ours has μεταβαλεῖν, but …]

he himself and all those he had initiated whom their impenitence destroyed. For the Justus mentioned above, by whose hand the apostate's death had come about, after many other conversations and discussions, as one would expect, put forward the apostolic saying that runs: “For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him, and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.” Putting forward this text, he stood up against Symeon. He said that perhaps they themselves had been deceived and were deceiving their followers along with them. For they did not ascribe these things to the God who made heaven and earth, who is truly the Father of our Lord Christ, but to some other besides him, whom the apostolic oracles do not know. From this disturbance strife and implacable conflict arose between them, and Justus went to the bishop of Colonea to grasp the meaning of the apostolic text more clearly, and he revealed everything that he and his companions had been doing. The bishop reported this to the emperor, who was Justinian, the one who succeeded to the throne after Heraclius. The emperor ordered that their affairs be subjected to inquiry and just judgment. He commanded that those who were impenitent, and those who had long ago promised repentance but were still cherishing their apostasy, should suffer death by fire. And so the rest of the multitude, together with Symeon, also called Titus, were bitterly deprived of life. 19. But a certain Paul, an Armenian by birth and the father of two sons, one named Gegnaesius and the other Theodore, escaped the death that had been decreed against the whole apostate party. He came to Episparis, which we named above, and was eager to sow impiety. The abominable nation of the Manichaeans think that no small part of the apostasy takes its name from this Paul rather than from the sons of Callinice. He installed his son Gegnaesius as head of the school of godlessness and renamed him Timothy. From this, envy [Editor's notes: (48) ἀμεταμελήτως (“impenitent”): so in our manuscript, instead of ἀμετα-… (51) ὧν (“of whom”): so ours, instead of ὢν in the Coislin manuscript. Previously …]

sprang up in his brother, and envy gave birth to faction. Impiety, divided against itself, was shared out among the brothers, both [?] the womb and the impiety. One brother said that the grace sent from above to their father had passed to him from the one who had received it, and he would not yield the privilege of impiety to the younger. Theodore drew it to himself instead, saying that he had not received a share of it from his father, from the one who had received it, by a second giving, but from the first gift, from the very source from which his father had drawn it. This faction and rivalry lasted until the loathsome end of their most impious lives. At that time Leo, from Germanicea in Syria, held the scepter of Roman rule. He learned about these most impious men and summoned Gegnaesius. But he lacked the judgment to investigate such matters and knew this well, so he did not examine the accused himself. Instead, he sent him to the one who then held the presidency of the priestly thrones, to be examined about his religion. Many words were addressed to the apostate. Some of his impieties he shed by denial, as is their custom. Others he colored with orthodox phrases, and through the many-tangled shifts of the apostasy he was guilty of, he slipped through and wriggled free. So the verdict of the hearers inclined toward acquittal, and the man who was full of every impiety was thought to be innocent of the charges. The exchanges, as a re-enactment might put it, took this form. “Why, sir,” says the patriarch, “have you denied the orthodox faith?” The apostate replied that whoever denies the orthodox faith is anathema, by “orthodox” meaning his own impiety. When a second question followed, “Why do you not venerate and embrace the cross of Christ?”, the apostate again consigned to the same curse whoever does not venerate the life-giving cross. He who deserved every curse turned everything upside down, calling Christ himself the cross, for, he says, by stretching out his hands he himself traced the cross. His words were for public show and common to all, but what the words signified belonged to the apostasy and its secret teaching. Next he was asked, “Why do you not count the all-holy Theotokos worthy of due honor and veneration?” He hurled his usual anathema, from which he never departed, against those who do not venerate the holy Theotokos, adding that he embraced and revered her in whom [?] he came out [Editor's notes: (56) διαιρεθεῖσα (“divided”): so I write instead of διερεθεῖσα, as … “from the one who received” … wished for himself [?] … (57) ἐφ’ ἑαυτὸν, καὶ μὴ πατρόθεν (“to himself, and not from his father”): so from our …]

…and into whom our Lord Jesus Christ entered, the mother of us all.” In saying this, the man of deceitful tongue was following his abominable rite and way of thinking: he was making a tabernacle of the Jerusalem above and turning it into the Theotokos, the Jerusalem into which, as he preaches from the Apostle's teachings, Christ entered as forerunner on our behalf. The fourth question put to him was why on earth he insults and spurns the immaculate and awesome body and blood of Christ our God and will not bring himself to partake of them. Once again the thrice-accursed man consigned to anathema whoever subjects the body and blood of Christ our God to dishonour and stays outside communion in them. But by “body and blood” the accursed one again meant not what our common Master taught us to call his body and blood, but the words of the Lord in their place. When he was questioned about the catholic Church in the same way and gave his declaration, he meant the assemblies of the Manichaeans and exalted them as the catholic Church. After these, the sixth question asked him about baptism: did he not regard it as a cleansing of souls and of the soul's defilements, and as a bath for the forgiveness of sins? Again he used the same device and readily gave an answer that honoured and accepted baptism. This man, who muddles and confuses everything, slipped in our Lord Jesus Christ under the word “baptism,” since it is written that he is the living water. So, then, that deceitful and evil-scheming monster held no part at all of what the apostolic and catholic Church believes. Instead, he cherished, fostered and honoured everything opposed to it. Yet those present thought he was not fighting against the Church's terms, under which he hid the deadly poison of apostasy. And so, as we said at the beginning, that thrice-accursed man seemed not to be guilty of impiety but to share the Church's mind. For this reason he was released from the examination as innocent. Yet he deserved a double punishment: one for the impiety he had inherited from his fathers, and one for the deceit by which he perverted the judges' right judgment and, though he was utterly impious, went about with a reputation for our piety. However that may be, once he had been released from the tribunal by such devices, he asked for and received from the emperor a written decree. It gave him full licence to live at home, to conduct his affairs without being molested, and no longer to fear the tongues of slanderers. So he set out from the imperial city and reached Episparis, where he gathered the disciples of the apostasy. From there he went to Mananalis, from which [?]

the aforementioned Constantine had set out, and he came there with his followers. He spent a good many years there and corrupted many human souls. Then the wretch was himself seized by a pestilential death (for in those times it was ravaging humankind without mercy) and ended his life, after being the champion of impiety for about thirty years. This thrice-accursed man had a son, Zacharias, from a clandestine union. As we have said, some of those who honour the Manichaean teachings regard him as a hireling, unworthy of the shepherd and banished from the company of teachers. [?] After Gegnaesius perished, however, the body of disciples split in two. Some followed Zacharias; others followed Joseph, whom some also called a bastard. Each contended that the whole working of the Spirit dwelt in himself. One claimed it for himself, while the other drew it away to himself and insisted that his rival was left empty. What spirit would visit these men if not the evil and unclean one, worthy of such vessels? Since the strife had prevailed for the reasons just given, and was already being settled with fists and blows, Zacharias was deeply aggrieved, as a man being driven from his father's inheritance. He struck Joseph a blow that brought him near death. With one of the generals of the apostasy brought to his knees, each party rose up all the more fiercely against the other. Yet they kept watching for the right moment to fight, reckoning the outcome of the battle doubtful. After a short time they decided instead that one party should separate from the other. That way they would not entrust themselves to the uncertainty of battle and be utterly destroyed. After this most public split, each faction was reproached and ridiculed, not only by the other but also by everyone round about, and was held up to all as a subject for songs and laughter. So each party made plans to leave that whole region in secret flight. Meanwhile the Saracens were overrunning the Roman borders and making their sortie by the law of war. Zacharias saw the attack coming from afar and fled as fast as he could. He left his disciples to the enemy and their swords, and he alone escaped the general slaughter. For the whole multitude with him was cut off from life by the sword. This act earned him, among most people, the name of “hireling” instead of [?]

“shepherd.” Joseph, on the other hand, did not trust to his feet as Zacharias had. He was quicker at stitching together a trick and a scheme, and he did not care to acknowledge any difference of faith (for he happened to be fleeing at the very moment of the enemy's attack). Emboldened by these things, and seeing the enemy bearing down from afar, he himself turned back from flight and ordered his followers to turn back the pack animals and the wagons. Then he disguised himself and those with him as deserters and drove straight toward the enemy, as if going over to them as they advanced, together with his followers. His pretence seemed convincing, and he swore that he favoured their ways. So he and his followers were spared death, and he suffered no other loss. Watching for a chance to escape, he found the opportune moment he had been planning and fled with his followers. He arrived at the often-mentioned village of Episparis and received a splendid welcome from its inhabitants (for the place was a workshop of the lovers of apostasy). They even lit lamps for him at his entry and paid him all the other service and honour that is owed to disciples of Christ. Welcomed in this way, he spent some time deceiving and being deceived, and dragging those who believed him down into the pit of perdition. But there was a man surnamed Crikoraches, who was counted among the ranks of the local magistrates. He was devout in doctrine, steady in character, admirable in zeal, and he loathed those hateful to God. He learned that the deceiver had settled in the district and that the apostasy was spreading still further. So he took a band of soldiers and seized the place where the mysteries of the apostasy were performed. He surrounded the house. But the ringleader of the impiety himself, as tends to happen when people scatter in all directions during sud- [?]

-den raids and assaults, he did not catch, for the man slipped away unnoticed. He did, however, seize the deceiver's disciples, and he checked and reined in the spread of so great an evil, which until then had been advancing. This hot-headed teacher of apostasy, Joseph (he also bore the name Epaphroditus), was forcibly driven from the place mentioned and fled toward Phrygia. A short time later he reached Antioch [?]. He settled there, free from those who had been biting at him, since he had moved far away from them. He made many of the locals the work of his ruin and was warmly received by them. After preaching impiety for thirty whole years, he at last ended his execrable and abominable life in a suburb not far from that city, named Chortocopium. [?] While the thrice-accursed man was still alive and flourishing in impiety, a certain woman of his acquaintance, who was joined to a husband in marriage, defiled the undefiled marriage bed and gave herself up to adultery. The man who broke up another's marriage, they say, was one of the deceiver's disciples, who had come over from the Hebrews to that godless cult. From this unlawful and abominable union the adulteress bore that abomination notorious for shamefulness and foulness, the filthy and unclean Baanes. This Baanes, the worst of men, succeeded the said Epaphroditus at the summit of evils. He cherished all the doctrines of his predecessors that held the impiety together, but he strove to outdo those before him in impurity of life, in unspeakable bodily unions, and in other lawless deeds. And he went on teaching the deadly doctrine to those who obeyed him. At about the same time, alongside this many-formed and abominable beast, there sprang up another like it, full of a dragon's venom. His native village was Ania, near the city of Tabia, and the wretch's name was Dryinus. The name proclaimed the venomous and destructive snake hidden in a human tent. To this beast a son was born. I think he drew the beginnings of his existence from the venomous seed of the serpent who began all evil, rather than from his immediate father. The father gave the newborn the name Sergius, [?]

a vessel later shown to be able to hold all the devil's wickedness. He was persuasive in preaching impiety and effective at hiding his mind when the occasion demanded. He was clever at putting on a show of virtue and quick to stitch together deceits and draw human souls to perdition. In short, of all who have ever belonged to the apostasy, he was the most skilful and convincing at every kind of play-acting. This accursed man initiated those he had deceived into various unlawful things [?]. Little by little he set before them a view of himself as someone exceptional and entrusted it to them. He did not consider it dreadful, or the height of godlessness, to call himself Paraclete and Holy Spirit (O tongue, soul, mind and mouth that fight against God!) and to have them name and regard him so. He handed these things down to be believed and spoken of among themselves in secret. This enemy of God laid it down that outside hearers were unworthy of such a rite and such mysteries. And those thrice-wretched people, truly worthy of his initiation, neither spurned nor loathed this excess of abomination. Instead they accepted an impiety that left no extreme of godlessness unreached, and ratified it by their own votes. [?] Alas, man is a wretched creature! When he departs from his Maker and cuts himself off from his providence, he becomes wholly the prey of the Evil One and is swept under into every wickedness. That execrable man also called himself the lamp-bright star, and many other things that deserve silence rather than proclamation. Yet this Sergius, whose mind was damaged toward God, though born of a most impious father, as I have said, was not initiated into the mysteries of the apostasy by his own father. While still young, he was corrupted by a woman who championed and preached the deadly doctrines of the Manichaeans. She initiated him over a long period and brought him to perfection in impiety, and he became a forerunner of Antichrist. For it was fitting, truly fitting, that of the teachers and heralds of this abominable apostasy that fights against God, some should be offspring of Hagarenes, and some be seen branded with the outrages and sufferings of slavery. Others came forth as shoots of adultery, and still others were known as disciples of a woman's folly and frenzied mind. Be that as it may, Sergius, to put it briefly, began to receive instruction in the apostasy roughly as follows. When the Manichaean woman just mentioned first got into conversation with him, she said, “Tell me, why do you not read the divine Gospels?” He replied (for the venom of the apostasy had not yet sunk deep into his innards) that it was not permitted for one who [?]

belongs to the rank of the laity to read the awesome words so freely, since that task was reserved for the priests. From the maenad he heard that he was showing so much reverence for these things in vain. “For there is no partiality with God,” she said, “since he wants all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Your being so reverently disposed toward the Lord's words does not come from honour for them. It is a device and a trick of your so-called priests. They want to peddle the word of God, and they are eager to keep you from any share in the mysteries in the Gospels. That is why they forbid you to read these things as they do. Even what they read in your hearing they cut out and tear away from the whole body, and only in this way do they admit you to hear what is said.” This is how the harlot and maenad made her first attempt on a man ready to fall, undermining the wretch's mind and prying it loose. Next she asked, “What does that saying of the Lord mean, which goes: ‘Many will say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?” And then I will declare to them, “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.”’ Who, then, are these people to whom the Lord says, ‘I do not know you’?” She asked these questions. He was still one of the herd and the country folk, wholly ignorant of the divine words, so he kept silent, at a loss, and tried to learn from the questioner herself the meaning of what she had asked. She did not tell him at once. For a woman is skilled at hunting the man she is after by means of delay. Instead she kindled the deceived man's desire for what he was seeking and fanned it further. She did not give him what he longed to obtain. Instead she put another Gospel saying to him, asking whom he thought the Lord meant when he said, “Many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness.” “Whom do you take the sons of the kingdom to be? And how is it that they are cast out of it and sent off into the outer darkness?” [?]

That woman-shaped instrument of deceit put these and other such questions to the thrice-wretched man and gradually bewitched him. When she had him wholly inclined toward her and saw him attending to her as to a teacher, she took up the matter and said: “The sons of the kingdom who are cast out of it and condemned to the outer darkness are those whom you and people like you call and regard as saints. They drive out demons and heal sufferings, and you have resolved to offer them veneration, abandoning the only living and immortal God. These, yes, these are the ones who will hear from the just Judge there: ‘Depart from me, for I never knew you.’” So from this wicked and deadly sowing she made the willing man her own field for growing tares. She then easily had the rest of the crop of impieties springing up by itself. In this way she made his soul a field fruitful in every ruin and corruption. As a result, all those before him who were notorious for impiety would be thought mere children when measured against his knavery, his thievish habits, and all his other contrivance and ingenuity in deceit. For those before him held first place in the mire of licentiousness, in the unspeakable nature of their other deeds, and in blasphemies against God that none could surpass. Yet nearly all people regarded them as abominable and repellent, because their defilement was plain to see, and everyone hated what they dared to do. Few were seen going over to their deception, since their indecent deeds were laid out openly, without concealment or artifice. The shamelessness of the apostasy itself was enough of a safeguard to keep people from quickly slipping toward it and becoming the Evil One's prey en masse. [?] But this man cut away whatever was obvious in their pollutions and covered up whatever licentiousness he kept. He toned down impieties that are unbearable even to hear about, or mixed them in with more tolerable ones. In short, he hid the wolf in a sheep's fleece. So to many he seemed a teacher of piety and a guide to salvation, but he hurled many who were swallowed up unawares down into the pit of final perdition. For he also contrived, with greater care, something his predecessors had neglected. He did not venture at the outset to initiate those who came to him straight away into the more advanced impieties, nor to [?]

set before them the execrable things of the mysteries. The chief of these is the total denial of God, together with glory, power, creative might, honour and close kinship ascribed to the devil. He entrusted nothing of this kind to the newly initiated. First he tried to regulate their morals by sayings from the Gospels, sayings that laid down nothing about doctrine. With these he tried for a while to charm and enchant those he was initiating and to make them tame. But once he had won their goodwill and saw them devoted to him as a teacher and guide to salvation, he gave them the whole venom of the apostasy to gulp down. Then he declared and proclaimed them perfected in impiety, just like himself. This thrice-accursed man also called himself Tychicus. He did not merely steal the name of the blessed Paul's disciple. He also refashioned and counterfeited that man's very existence and person into his own, and passed himself off as him. For he spun the marvellous tale (O foolish tongue, and more foolish ears of those who accepted it!) that he was none other than the Tychicus who appears in the Apostle's Epistles and is often mentioned there with praise. This invention was ill-made, shameless, silly and godless, and nothing like it is found in any heresy that has ever existed. Having laid it down as a foundation in the souls of the deceived, he built everything else upon it. He claimed that he had been sent to them by Paul as a herald, and that what he announced and said came not from his own wisdom but was the instruction of Paul, who had taught and sent him. To those initiated more deeply into the impiety he often sang his own praises as Spirit and Paraclete. Yet to the rest of the crowd he counted himself among the company of the disciples of the inspired Paul, though he lived nearly seven hundred years after Paul and Tychicus. For this accursed charlatan was known in our own times, a herald of impiety more ardent than any other before him. The deceiver went round many cities and lands, hunting, deceiving and snaring the souls of the simpler folk, alas. As this true son of falsehood himself says in one of his letters: “From east and west, from north and south, I have run, preaching the Gospel of Christ on my knees.” Even if he was boasting here, as he did in everything, he still ran no short course toward his own perdition and that of those who believed him. This man too presided over the impiety for nearly thirty-four years and ran the race of error to its end. At that time Irene, that God-loving [?]

…when the God-blessed lady was at the head of the imperial government, at the time when this fighter against God and blasphemer was at the height of his apostate thinking. From that time until the present, the impiety that now prevails in these parts has depended on his teaching. It surpasses its rival heresies in repute, even though it and the sects that support it lead to the same destruction. The wretches among his disciples deify him to such a degree that they say other absurd things about him that are unbearable to hear. They even seal their own prayers, or rather their barkings, in his name, saying: "May the prayer of the Holy Spirit have mercy on us." This crooked serpent called himself doorkeeper, shepherd and guide. For he writes to those in Colonia: "Knowing beforehand the genuineness of your faith, we remind you that, just as the former churches received shepherds and teachers" (he means Constantine and the others whom our account listed above), "so you too have received a bright lamp, a shining lantern and a guide to salvation, as it is written: If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light." And a little later: "Let no one deceive you in any way; but since you have these promises from God, take courage. For we are persuaded in our hearts, and so we have written to you that I am the doorkeeper and the good shepherd and guide of the body of Christ, and the lamp of the house of God, and I am with you always, to the end of the age." As for this man, then — oh, what could one call him that would do him justice? — the wickedest and most godless of men, carrying himself above all and exalting himself, was brought down to a fall he deserved, as will be shown later. He also writes to a certain Leo, a Montanist: "But you, guard yourself; give up cutting apart the unswerving faith. For what charge do you have against us? Have I defrauded anyone, or been arrogant? You cannot say so. And even if you say it, your testimony is not true. Far be it from me to hate you; rather, I exhort you: as you received [?] apostles

and prophets, who are four, receive also shepherds and teachers, so that you may not become prey to wild beasts." In this way he changed himself into countless shapes, adapting himself to the various characters of those he deceived: now a giant, now an ape, now a lion, now a fox, now taking the form and shape of one thing after another. Elsewhere again he says: "The first fornication, which we have carried with us from Adam, is a benefit; but the second is greater, and of it the Apostle says, He who commits fornication sins against his own body." By "fornication" here the accursed man means withdrawal from his own abominable doctrines, and he called himself the body of Christ. That is why he reviled those who left him and his God-hated commandments as having been caught in the passion of fornication. Many other things belonging to the same blasphemy and fantastic talk can be seen in many of his foul writings. To go through them in order and expose them, together with anything else connected and interwoven with them, would be the task of a second, separate treatise. For what has been said was said only to give a demonstration of this intricate and many-sided war against God.

22. Let no one think that this offshoot of the impious doctrines of Sergius sprang from a different root from the one planted by Mani, the fighter against God. For it is one and the same root, and it bears the same soul-destroying fruit. When Sergius mounted the teacher's throne of the apostasy, wishing to lead many astray from the catholic Church of Christ, the filthy Baanes, who until then had herded together with him, openly split away. Sergius took up an open rivalry and fight with him before the disciples, and their quarrel was played out as if on a public stage. Through it he contrived to entice others and draw them after his own error, as many as he could, including the companions of Baanes. He also had a show of virtues put forward as a great bait for those who approached him: a humble character, a feigned affability, and a gentleness that not only won the assent of his own people but also smoothed over and carried off those who were more harshly disposed. For while he made it his concern, especially in public, to expose and repudiate the filth of the foul deeds of his rival Baanes, he was never seen to oppose or differ from him in anything regarding the impious doctrines. Baanes, then, having no defense for the display of his lawless deeds, took refuge only in those who had gone before him. By the standing of these persons, as he thought, he propped up and lent dignity to the falseness and odiousness of his thinking, boasting that he was a disciple of Epaphroditus and honored his tradition, which held that, regarding abominable and loathsome deeds,

one should feel no hesitation or blush, as though they ought not to be done. He reviled Sergius as a newcomer who had neither seen any of the distinguished teachers nor been their hearer, and who therefore, having drawn no light from that source, was going about in error and deceit. With such words the accursed Baanes attacked his fellow craftsman and rival and magnified himself. But Sergius, that many-colored beast, was not so openly sunk in the mire of such deeds, nor did he reek of impurity as Baanes did; he wrapped it in many veils of words and appearances. In this way he gained, unnoticed, the strength to split the apostasy in two. Those who were seen to belong to Baanes's party he spat upon and called Baanites. Baanes, repaying the insult, treated those whom Sergius's portion held as abominable, and in the same way named them Sergiotes. Their strife and faction grew and strengthened day by day, and set the foul parties in implacable enmity.

23. Some time later, when Sergius had ended his life in death, his disciples broke out into such fighting against the Baanites that the dispute was settled no longer by words and abuse but by hands and swords, and much Baanite blood flowed. For Sergius's party prevailed both in numbers and because the commander of their armed force inclined to Sergius's opinion. And the Baanites would have been utterly destroyed, as they deserved, by the hands of their own kin and tribe [?], had not a certain Theodotus, as impious in religion as anyone and said to have been a fellow traveler of Sergius, checked and halted the swiftly flowing slaughter. With many other wily words he urged what would serve the common good, asserting and insisting, and supporting his proposal with many deeds and words: that each party were shoots of the same sowing, had grown up with the same customs, shared a common way of life and were walled about with concord, not quarreling much over the disputed points; that this had held for many years until Sergius was appointed teacher; and that it was wrong to dissolve into blood and slaughter the harmony and union of so many years, or to send mercilessly to destruction by the sword, as men of another faith and utterly godless, those who were even now united and like-minded on the essentials, on account of certain differences only recently stirred up. With some such words he stopped their mutual slaughter — would that he had not! For then the soul-destroyer would not have fed upon more souls.

24. However, the emperor Michael, who held the Roman scepters and who exchanged the imperial robe for the monastic habit, and Leo who reigned after him, did not treat the search and inquiry into the apostasy carelessly, but took it up with fitting zeal. Certain men of no mean rank were sent throughout the whole Roman realm with orders that any found to be possessed by this war against God should be led to death by the sword. For the admonitions and exhortations of bishops and priests had often been of no help to them, nor persuaded them to give up their impiety; those who remained so unchangeable were to be put to death as a common plague and corruption of the race. The orders came also to the region called the Armeniakon. Thomas was then bishop of Neocaesarea, and another man, surnamed Paracondaces, was at that time exarch of those who held to holiness of life and professed to keep the bonds of the higher way of life [?]. These two men received an imperial decree to sit together with certain other learned men. Whatever apostates the civil authorities found, arrested and sent to them, they examined and scrutinized in detail. Sifting the guilty from the innocent, they released some and subjected others to ecclesiastical penalties, while those who were wholly incurable were handed over to the civil laws and the tribunal of the magistrates under them. As the inquiry, judgment, examination and proceedings went on in this way, the slaughter of the judges named above was divided between those called Cynochorites and those whom they named Astati. These were the picked men among Sergius's disciples. The Astati, needing no one else, themselves slaughtered the exarch by guile and treachery. The Cynochorites, since they lacked a leader for the crime, had one of the Astati set over them, and they too slaughtered Thomas, the bishop of God. When these crimes had been so shamelessly committed, the architects of each murder, as I said, fled in haste with their followers from every land adorned by the law of Christians, and came to the city of Melitene in Second Armenia, which was then a state of the Christ-hating Saracens, ruled by an emir whom they called Monocherares. And this Christ-hater

received the Christ-hating fugitives with kindness in every respect, freed them from all human fear, and allowed them to live in Argaoun, a small town so called in the local tongue. Within a short time a crowd of those who held the apostasy had streamed together, enough for raids and a band of fighters, and the godless repeatedly carried off many of the neighboring Christians as captives. Gaining strength from there, the evil not only allowed its original devotees to practice their impiety without fear, but also gave them ample power to compel some of the captives to fall into the same godlessness with them. Sergius too, whom our account has often mentioned, went there. He spent some time with the fugitives and grounded their impious doctrines still more deeply, but he did not escape the judgment from above. It was the season for woodcutting, and Sergius was not unpracticed in carpentry; indeed he was used to plying the craft and hewing suitable planks from tree trunks. As usual he went to the mountain near Argaoun, went about his business, and hewed the timber into planks. While he was at this work, a man named Tzanion, from Nicopolis by birth, pious in religion, brave in spirit and no less strong in his hands, saw the God-fighter so emboldened by his sorceries, trusting his life to his witchcraft and presuming to cut wood alone. He gave a great, piercing shout at the deceiver, filling him with fear and astonishment by his voice; and though he himself was unarmed, he snatched the axe from the man's hands and struck the deceiver a mortal blow. Bitter death followed upon those very blows for the wretch. Thus, then, the very spirit of deception [?], the destroyer of human souls, the bitter and deep root of the apostasy, the last and worst of all the evils before him, was cut down by the tool of his own hand and craft. He was cut off from his God-fighting and arrogant words, his abominable and unholy deeds, his impossible promises and hopes, and from life itself, and was dispatched, together with his God-fighting mind, to the unquenchable and eternal fire.

25. It was the year 6343 from the beginning of the creation of the world when this God-fighter paid the penalty of a violent death. He left behind three disciples of his foulness and apostasy, who held first place in the mystic sorceries and witchcraft: one was named Michael, another Canacares, and the third John; with them was counted the Theodotus mentioned above. After them came Basil and Zosimus and several others. But these thrice-accursed disciples of that thrice-wicked man, whom the deceived

multitude also call "fellow travelers," went on corrupting and ruining with the same evils the people gathered at Argaoun. They did so although they had seen with their own eyes the bitter, God-sent death of their teacher, and had seen that none of the things for which he fought against God and told his marvels had come to pass. They no longer referred the teaching office of the war against God to one or two, but themselves, holding equal rank with one another, led the multitude of error in great numbers. Even so, they appointed certain others as their subordinates, whom they called notaries, and assigned them to oversee and perform some of the secret and abominable rites.

26. At the same time there also appeared the thrice-wicked Carbeas. He was skilled at worming his way into a crowd, close in hiding what should not be divulged, and most persuasive at uttering with his lips something other than what he pondered in his heart. He was content with no faith whatever, since he even pretended to revere the religion of the Arabs; yet he was a lover of the apostasy and took pride in being called and thought one, and he was not untrained in military experience. Therefore, since that apostate multitude was already growing into a heavy warlike force, he was chosen by the multitude to rule. He increased and strengthened the God-fighting assembly still further. Seeing that those under him were cramped by the burden of the small town, he built another, roomier city, which he named Tephrike, and settled it with his followers, at the same time escaping the tyranny that the people of Melitene were bringing upon them. For although they had received them kindly at first, when they saw them growing rich, and through their daily raids advancing to prosperity beyond what they had expected, they could no longer look on them without envy and greed. So they did not cease to plunder them by many arts and methods. This, then, was one reason why he decided to settle his subjects farther from their former dwelling. Another was his concern that, being unmixed with other people and by themselves, they might proceed without fear and with full freedom to their demonic and outrageous practices. For before, when they had the Saracens as neighbors, they revered their own rites and revered those of the Saracens too — but the Saracens' as a show, and their own as mysteries.

27. Besides this, the city he founded seemed well placed for incursions into the Roman realm, for it lay closer to its borders. Moreover, if any of those who carried the same impiety in their bosom wished to desert from there, he

found refuge and retreat to him readier because of the nearness. As for the wars he waged, no longer as raids but in pitched battle and in alliance with the Saracens, those in which he had the upper hand and those in which he came off worse, they belong to another subject and a separate time. But that he filled the lands of the Roman realm near him with every kind of calamity — the very magnitude of the suffering is enough, in place of an account, to give those who come after us an unforgettable knowledge of it.

28. That bloodstained man, however, after doing irreparable harm for many years, at last, late and with difficulty, ended his life by disease. As successor to his tyranny and his impiety was appointed his son-in-law through his daughter, who was also his nephew by birth, surnamed Chrysocheir. At this point the account, having arranged this composition, ceased from going further, since it neither has nor professes knowledge of the future. Yet if one may grant that our hopes — especially those that depend on divine favor and long for the salvation of our race — are not mistaken or deceptive, perhaps this writing would not be acting rashly in predicting that before long the insolence, the doctrines and the strength of this apostate and godless body will ebb away and be destroyed. The present book, then, has gone through these matters: where the error had its first beginnings; how this root of bitterness put forth shoots of the war against God by a second sowing, and how it advanced even to a third crop of tares; which are the so-called churches of the apostasy and how many; what teachers it had; how they adulterate the sacred words, and by what means they overshadow their impious mind; and whatever else the history has covered in brief. Having gone through these, it reserves for the second book the point-by-point refutations of the impious doctrines, especially those that have not yet been refuted, and anything else that needs to be said — if the benevolent divine favor should grant the writer a respite from his great distress.

Questions and Answers concerning the Manichaeans

1. If the Good One creates the soul and the Evil One the body, how did the Good One tolerate his creature being united with the creature of the Evil One? And how did the Evil One endure the union? For the union will either make the body good — and the Good One ought not to make the work of the Evil One good — or make the soul evil, which is far more absurd: that God's creation should be overcome by the creature of the Evil One. Why did the good God tolerate his work being united with the work of the Evil One and being made evil by it? And again, how did the Evil One submit to having his work made good? Apart from these points, who began the union? If the Good One, how was he not made evil in this, since he took on the evil work? If the Evil One, then clearly he too was made good in this, having conceived a desire for a good creation; and the Good became at once evil and good. For the union, confounding the nature of each by sharing, both damaged what was proper to each and appropriated what was foreign, so that the Good One made his work at once evil and good, and the Evil One made his likewise both evil and good. What could be more senseless or absurd than that? So it is if the union came about together with the creation of the works. But if these things were once separate from one another, and each creature was granted the providence and care of its own maker, kept unmixed with its opposite, what was the reason for the separation at that time? And from what cause were they later changed to union? For either each maker at first kept to what was advantageous for himself and his creature, or [?], finding the unmixed state disadvantageous, they were brought to their senses afterwards and turned to union. And how many other impieties and follies spring from the first premise of this error, so God-fighting, mad and senseless as it is: to invent one creator of the soul and another of the body!

2. As for the claim of those held in error that the Evil One troubles us and drives us toward wickedness, that is the way of truth, not of error. For this very thing — being led astray into dividing God's uncut and indivisible principle and authority into two — is the work of the Evil One's many-sided and violent harassment. But while he is able to harass us, we are not unable to repel his harassment. And we repel it through both body and soul. So if our body can repel the harassment of the Evil One, and not only repel it but also overthrow all his

…device, how is that one their fashioner? That God's creature should disregard the Master's commandment and fall into the enemy's deceit comes from the will, which can incline either way and was given to us when we were fashioned; for the soul is free to choose. "And behold, I have set before your face death and life." But if the body already possesses evil in its fullness, how can it outmaneuver its own first principle? For where would it get the judgment to turn away from the worse, when it has no judgment at all? How did it incline to the better and overcome the power that produced it? So it is impossible to trace the making of body and soul back to opposed first principles.

3. But they go on to say, and say it rightly enough, that not even in this way did the enemy prevail over the souls of those who willingly gave themselves up to him, so completely that the darkened could never turn toward any gleam of truth at all. That is why they say that the good God always was, and is, and will be, and that he is invisible and incomprehensible. This much does come from the ray of truth. But in time the darkness gains great power and immediately pours over their minds. It blinds their reasoning, so that they think senselessly and say that the Evil One came into being from darkness and fire. This deserves loud laughter, or rather ceaseless tears, and is a mindless offspring of the soul. For if they call the darkness and the fire sensible, then whatever proceeded from them is certainly sensible too, and so the Evil One is sensible. But if that darkness and fire are intelligible, then the Evil One and whatever proceeded from them are intelligible as well. And are this darkness and this fire coeternal with God, or did they come into being later? And where was the Evil One at the time when these existed? If they came into being later, who produced them? For an intelligible darkness that existed as darkness from the beginning does not leave the one who produced it guiltless either.
