Nor does the fire, if, being intelligible, it emitted the author of evil. And how is he an author at all, when he received his existence from others? How much could one say in reckoning up this irrational pairing?

4. Why was darkness alone not enough to produce him? Why not fire alone? Who brought these two together instead, and what became of him? And what does it do now that its own offspring has seized the rule? Besides, if the Evil One came from darkness and fire, [?] … God placed the soul in an earthly body, as [?]

how can they turn around and call the Evil One the maker of darkness and fire? And if the Evil One is not the maker of fire, yet fire is sensible, how can they say that the good God made nothing sensible? Their brazen error might be ashamed to grant the Evil One the generation of fire, and so be caught babbling that the same thing is now the fashioner and now the fashioned. If so, let it know that it ends in no less shame. For it will confess, however unwillingly and silently, that fire is the handiwork of the good God, which is the very thing it was trying with all its zeal and every device to take away from him. However darkened they may be, they will certainly not call sensible fire either without beginning or eternal.

5. Then again, some of them, though not all, come up out of the darkness and say that the good God holds the heavenly things, that he is creator of heaven, and that he supplies people with good deeds. But after shaking off the mist for a good while, they blaspheme again. They do not attribute to him the creation of the earth or of the things in between, and they bring in another creator. Some of them, for the error has many branches, have even dared to say that heaven itself and everything in between are the works of the Enemy. But if heaven is the work of the Evil One, as their stupefied minds hold, how does the good God rest in the heavenly places? Heaven contains the air, the earth and the water, for even the things beneath the earth are contained in it. So how can heaven, the house of the heavenly God, contain the works of the Evil One, that is, earth and fire and air, and not only contain them but govern them? For through the rising and setting of the sun and of the stars, which belong to heaven, earth and water and air and fire enjoy a good balance by God's providence. They reap the benefit of changing into one another for the common good of the human race, and they are fitted to the present needs of the other living creatures too. But if heaven belongs to the evil principle, how is it that our Savior, when he taught and handed down that wonderful and awe-inspiring prayer, said, "Our Father who are in heaven," and "Hallowed be your name … as in heaven, so also on earth"? How then does the creator of all creation dwell in a creation not his own, one subject to the Evil One and itself the work of the Evil One? Elsewhere the Savior lays down that we should be compassionate toward one another and says, "If you forgive people their trespasses, your heavenly Father will forgive you too." And again, urging us to follow the will of God, since he himself had first fulfilled that will in a way beyond nature, he says, "Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven,

that one is my brother and sister and mother." In his loving-kindness he bestows on them what he himself had by nature. For he is Son of the Father not by grace but by nature. But by fulfilling the Father's will in his humanity, he leads those who fulfill it in imitation of him into adoption as sons, and grants them the name of brothers. Why should one collect all the passages in which the Savior praises the Father as heavenly and as dwelling in heaven? Why mention the rest? How can these wretches' shamelessness fail to sink out of sight when the Master's voice rings out, "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth"? For here he plainly declares him Lord not only of heaven but also of earth. What could be clearer than this testimony? What could be more powerful, both for presenting the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ as creator and Lord of all, and for triumphing over the apostates' war against God?

6. Again, when Peter, the chief of the apostles, confessed our common Teacher as God, Christ, as if repaying him for this confession of divinity, blesses the one who confessed it in a manner befitting God. He teaches that it was the Father in heaven who gave him this revelation: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah," he says, "for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." One could gather countless other passages from the sacred Oracles to refute their impious thinking. Consider this too: "When Jesus had been baptized, he came up at once from the water." O tongue that makes a practice of impiety! In the creation of the Evil One, the good Son of the good Father is baptized and comes up out of it, and "behold, the heavens were opened to him"! Here again is another creation of an evil hand. Why were they opened, and for what purpose? "He saw the Spirit of God," it says, "descending like a dove." This is the third triumph over impiety in a few words. For how could the Spirit of God take the form of the Evil One's creature, come down out of the Enemy's works, and descend from there upon Jesus? And a fourth monument

(96) "Having": I would gladly read "resounding," from "to resound." (97) "Confessed as God": that "confess as God" here is the same as [?]

to the defeat of impiety: a voice comes from the heavens, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Examine each word with me, beloved, and see how an inescapable refutation of impiety comes along with them. "This is," it says, "my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Who is this? The one being baptized in water, for whom the heavens were opened, and upon whom my Spirit, descending from heaven in the form of a dove, also bears witness to the sonship of the one baptized. All things are mine. Through my creatures my Son, fulfilling my will, accomplishes the salvation of the world. The authority of the Spirit alone is present with the one who shares his nature, and by this very act proclaims that the sonship is genuine. Elsewhere, rebuking those who do everything to please people, he says, "You have no reward from your Father in heaven." And: "How much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him?" And: "You have one Father, who is in heaven." Why did the good Son of the good Father look up to heaven, if it was a creation not his own? And why did he put his fingers into the deaf man's ears, spit, touch his tongue, and free him from his deafness? That man too, as the God-fighters say, was another evil creation. And why, when he said, "Father, glorify your Son," did a voice come from heaven saying, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again"? He himself knew that the Father had glorified him and would glorify him, and that was not why he asked the Father. For he possesses all that is the Father's, and he alone knows the Father, so he was not ignorant even of this. He asked so that the crowd of listeners present might clearly recognize and learn two things: that as a man he shrinks from his passion, and that he seeks it. In this way he teaches everyone that he undergoes it willingly. That is why he also said, "This voice has come not for my sake but for yours." It is as if he said: I knew all the Father's purposes and was ignorant of nothing. I did not raise my voice to him for my own sake, nor did he confirm it for my sake, but for yours. I did it so that you may know that my will agrees with the Father's will and that I call my passion glory. For I take it upon myself for the sake of all of you. That is why the request was made, and why the Father's voice from heaven confirmed what had been asked. But enough about these matters for now.

7. If fire is the work of the Evil One, how does the good God, the Son of the Good, baptize those he initiates with the Holy Spirit and with fire? Would he join the Enemy's creation to the Holy Spirit and sanctify the one being baptized through opposites? What mind could accept this? What reasoning could bear such blasphemy? Who would not condemn the enormity of this impiety? And again, how does the good God make his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire, signing himself as the maker of works that belong to another? For this prophetic

saying Paul also confirms as coming from God, divine, and the proclamation of the truth. And the chaff stands for the worthlessness of sinners. How, then, does he hand it over to the Enemy's creation to be punished? For he says it will be burned up with unquenchable fire. And how could the one who destroys the Enemy come to cast fire on the earth, enlarging and increasing the Enemy's work? And how has the fire been prepared for the devil, if he is its creator? Surely he does not set up a punishment against himself. Otherwise, if, as it seems, it was not the Enemy who brought fire into being, [?] through it he will punish those who keep sinning without turning back, and the sower of the tares himself as well, and so exact a just penalty. How many more such points could one list?

8. But if, as their blasphemous and impious tongue boldly claims, earthly things belong to the Evil One, how can our common Master and Savior call them his own? "He came to his own," it says, "and his own did not receive him." The apostates may say that "his own" means the prophetic words, that Christ came to them, and that they did not receive him. But see how far their folly and shamelessness go. First, how can they say that the prophetic words are Christ's own, when they say that the prophets themselves are a creation of the Evil One and receive their inspiration from him? Second, how did Christ come to the prophetic words? On their own account, he came to what belonged to another. For the prophetic words belong to another, since they were inspired by another and not by the good God. Then again, how can the prophetic words be Christ's own at all, when they did not receive him? For it says, "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." Furthermore, to whom did Christ give power to become children of God? To the prophetic words? How is this not drawn-out nonsense? For if words come from God, they belong to God for that very reason. But if they are evil, how could they become children of God? Furthermore, what prophetic word was born of blood, and of the will of a man, and of the will of the flesh? For it goes on: "who were born not of blood, nor of the will of a man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God." Who then are these words born of blood? And

…world, as he says somewhere else to the disciples: "Behold, the hour is coming, and has now come, when you will be scattered, each to his own." What does "his own" mean here? The prophetic words? Or obviously each one's property and dwelling? Here "his own" does not mean the prophetic words, as their crazed nonsense has it, but each person's property and own house. In the same way, when he says, "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him," by "his own" he means the sensible world, for this is his possession and his creation. The same goes for those in it, some of whom received his teaching, while others did not. And elsewhere Jesus our Savior himself, as he went around his own homeland, gave the reason for his going around and bore witness, saying, "A prophet has no honor in his own country." The gospel words themselves, then, have made it plain that the expression "his own" denotes the world, or one's homeland in the world, or one's property. How then are those who twist such obvious things into myths and nonsense not all the more plainly mad? The Lord's oracles call the world the Lord's own, and those in it his own, whether they received him or not. Those who received him were his own as his creatures, and in addition they were made his children, because they welcomed the one who had come for their salvation. Those who did not receive him are still his own, since they are his creation, but by not welcoming him they estranged themselves from the second, spiritual adoption. Since the oracles interpret "his own things" and "his own people" in this way, how is it not abominable to slip some other meaning, one of error, beneath the words? That he calls the world "his own" can be seen clearly from these words too: "There was," it says, "the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world." Which world? Evidently the sensible one. And when did he enlighten them? When he came into it. And when did he come? The Gospel cries out, "He was in the world." For surely, being in the sensible world, he enlightened whoever was coming into the sensible world. Then whose creation was the world in which he himself was, and in which he enlightened whoever was coming into it? We can learn this from nowhere else than from the gospel words themselves: "The world came into being through him, and the world did not know him." This is the same as "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." Do you see how truth bears witness to itself from every side, and [?]

[?] … you will understand either the whole world or Judea. (5) [?] "coming into it." [?] therefore this [?]

its light shines out all the more for those who seek it? The sacred words call this visible world the Savior's own. They proclaim that it came into being through him, and that no one else but he enlightens those who come into the world. How then do they not shudder, these truly creatures of apostasy and children of the Evil One, when they bring in one creator of the visible world, and another who enlightens whoever comes into the world, leaving him as creator only of intelligible being?

9. One could also show their absurdity laid bare from another direction. If earthly things belong to the Evil One, how could he bring himself to feed many thousands with fruits grown by the Evil One's creation, once from five loaves and once from seven? How much better and more fitting for God it would have been to feed those he was initiating not from fruits belonging to another but from his own creations! Indeed, how could he himself eat or drink anything at all, if it was the fruit of the Evil One's works? Again, when he made eyes for the blind man, he renewed his sight not from some other material but from earth and water, which belonged to the Evil One. Did he then all but share the work with the Enemy, leaving him to do the greater part, while he himself, as if he had no material of his own, completed the part from another's material and filled up another's creation? Yet if nothing else, this very fact ought to have put the wretches to shame and made them understand that the one who fashioned the eye from clay is truly the same one who in the beginning fashioned man from clay. For the part is made of the same material as the whole, and the part has the same creator as the whole. Besides, if the body comes from the Evil One, how could he weep over its destruction in the case of Lazarus? And how could he bring himself to bind together again the dissolving work of the Evil One, give it life, and raise Lazarus, calling on his own Father as he did so? Was it so that he himself might rescue again and bring back to life the Evil One's creation, which was rightly being destroyed? And if the body belongs to the Evil One, how did he raise the widow's dead son? How did he perform the countless other divine signs by which he benefited human bodies? Think of the centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, the woman bent double by her ailment, and the woman worn down by a long-standing flow of blood and stripped of all hope of recovery. Think of the lepers, the paralytics, the deaf, and the countless kinds of ailments and diseases, from all of which he set the body free and clean. Is all this not enough to shame those who say that human bodies are creations of the Evil One? For how could the good God renew the Enemy's creation as it was perishing? Not only did he drive away the ailments of those who came to him, but he also went to them himself and visited them. For Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and healing every disease and every infirmity. Nor did he heal them and then keep the healing quiet. He even ordered it to be

announced. "Go," he says, "and tell John: the blind see again, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, and the dead are raised." To the disciples, too, he gives the laying of hands on the sick and their healing as a sign of his power, strength and grace. In this way Christ our God cared for the body as his own creation. He came to save both soul and body, and he did not confine his benefaction to himself but also gave the disciples authority to do the same things. But if, as the mouths of the Evil One declare in their war against God, the body belongs to the Evil One, how do we accomplish through it the greatest of virtuous deeds: chastity, self-control, keeping vigil, standing at prayer, endurance in hardship, the labors of martyrdom? All these belong to the body more than to the soul, and they redound to the glory of the fashioner and creator. For the soul by itself could neither enter the contest to accomplish these things, nor will it be called to account for any fault in failing to accomplish them. How then can the Evil One's creation do good and help the soul achieve things which, without the body, are not counted as achievements at all? Consider this too. If the body belonged to the Evil One, why was Paul grieved when Epaphroditus was ill, and why did he say, "May God have mercy on him, and not only on him but on me too, so that I may not have sorrow upon sorrow"? Why should Paul have grieved to see the Evil One's creation breaking down? And if it was the Evil One's creation, how could that same exalted man write to Timothy, "Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses"? If, as you claim, the body was the Evil One's creation, then that heavenly teacher, if he cared about Timothy, should have written to him, "Do not use wine at all, so that the Evil One's creation may break down sooner and you may be freed from its burden." And if bodies belong to the Evil One, how can our Lord Jesus Christ say, "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall without my Father who is in heaven." Why should the good God care about the Evil One's creations, for which no prizes are set, neither eternal life nor the kingdom of heaven? But because he is their creator and Lord and ruler, not even these lose their life without him. And how will Christ be magnified in Paul's body, if the body is the Evil One's creation? And again, the interpreter of God's mysteries himself, if the body were not the creation of the one over all…
