For he says: "May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." Apart from this, if the soul were the work of one principle and the body of another, how could our true Fashioner and God, wishing us to be free of distraction, admonish his worshippers and exhort them about both, saying: "Do not be anxious for your soul, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor for your body, what you will put on"? Then, drawing us still further toward his admonition by an example, he says: "Look at the birds of the sky: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns. And where does their [?] come from? Your heavenly Father feeds them." If, then, the fount of truth knows and says that our heavenly Father is the one who feeds the birds of the sky, and says too that the grass of the field, which is thrown into the oven, is clothed by this same God with such beauty as not even Solomon put on in all his glory, how do the unguarded mouths of impiety appoint one creator for the grass, the birds, the body and all things perceived by the senses, and grant another a sovereignty cut in half? 10. That it is the same one who gives both these temporary things and the kingdom of heaven, he confirms the doctrine in greater detail: "For your heavenly Father knows," he says, "that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God,

[?] through the moisture from the rains, for a well-tempered [?]. Where, then, are the outlawed dividers of God's undivided kingdom, who invent one creator of the earth and the air, of the rains and the sun and all things of that order, and another who holds the rank of the intelligible things beyond these? 11. But consider this too, I ask you. If he who knows the Father and the things of the Father better than anyone calls heaven the throne of God, the earth his footstool, and Jerusalem his city, how is it not the height of impiety for some to cut away from him the very things to which the Son bears witness, and to make someone else the maker of what they have cut away? For Christ our God, who does and counsels everything for our salvation, shutting the oath out of human life as the gateway to perjury, says: "But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God, nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King." "Nor by your head," he says, "for you cannot make one hair white or black." By head, Jerusalem, earth and heaven he means things perceived by the senses and judged by sight, by which the Jews were accustomed to swear. So let no madness divert head, Jerusalem, earth and heaven into myths and nonsense again. For the visible heaven, the earth that the senses perceive, and Jerusalem, which had been built long before and which David generations later rebuilt and made a city: these he calls, the first a throne, the second a footstool, the third the city of the great King. Which king? He himself teaches more clearly elsewhere, saying: "Do not make my Father's house a house of trade," honoring the temple in Jerusalem as his Father's house; and it is on account of this temple that he calls Jerusalem the King's city. For the one whom he proclaimed the great King when he forbade oaths, he here declared to be his own Father. That is why, cleansing his Father's house of the drunken excess of trade, he drives out those who sold oxen, sheep and doves, and threatens them with just wrath, since he found them despisers both of his Father's house and of his Father's commandment. Apart from what has been said, David first, inspired by the all-holy Spirit, and later the divine Paul cried out in a clear voice that the God proclaimed by Moses speaks to our Lord Jesus Christ. For Paul, writing to the Jews, applies to our Savior the Father's voice prophesied through David: "You are my Son,

today I have begotten you." And again: "I will be a Father to him, and he shall be a Son to me." And again: "And let all the angels of God worship him." And: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; [?] the scepter of your kingdom." Then he adds (hear, you deaf, and look up, you blind!): "And you, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail." David, the forefather of God, foretold these things in the Spirit, and the initiate and teacher of ineffable mysteries set his seal on them: that the God of the old legislation is himself the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; that he it is who established the throne of his Son by nature for ever and ever, and made all the ranks of the angels worshippers and servants of his Offspring; that he and no other laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of his hands. If so, how do they not outdo all impiety, who say that the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is one, and the maker of heaven and earth another, who take the creatures away from the Creator and assign them to the sower of the tares? For this he will repay them with destruction, and they will be carried off with him into the punishment prepared for him. The divine Luke too records the same things in Acts. Even if most of their apostasy does not accept his words, nevertheless he, using the voice of Isaiah, or rather the tongue of Stephen, plainly stops their mouths by way of the Jews. For Stephen, who was the first to bind on the crown of victory, in his rebuke of the Jews, shaming their shamelessness with other arguments, also brings in the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ crying out and saying: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet; what kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord?" And what the Savior said about the Father in the Gospels, calling heaven his throne, earth his footstool and Jerusalem his city, the protomartyr confirms, bearing joint witness with the Master, by presenting the Father through the voice of Isaiah as saying the same things. Elsewhere again the Savior, exposing and silencing the idle talk of those who swear oaths, reinforces the same teaching. "You fools and blind," he says, "which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the

gold?" So the temple of the old covenant was not only holy but also had power to sanctify. And again: "Which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?" Here too he shows clearly that the altar was holy and made holy whatever was offered on it. And shortly after he says: "And whoever swears by heaven" (open your ear, man, which God fashioned for hearing, but which the Evil One has truly refashioned into deafness; still, listen!), "whoever swears by heaven," he says, "swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it." So the temple is holy, the altar is holy and has divine grace to make holy, and heaven is the throne of the true God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose making and work the whole creation is. Now these people contradict the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ when he cries out these things, and do not obey Christ our true God when he speaks in harmony with the one who begot him. They set aside the testimony of Paul, whose name they falsely bear; they disdain David when he prophesies; they pay no heed to Luke, the disciple and evangelist of the saving word; they sneer at Stephen, the first among the martyrs, and at the prophet he brings in. It follows, then, as indeed they do, that they obey the Evil One alone, to whom they have handed over both their souls and their bodies: their souls by the impiety of their thinking, their bodies through the filth of their deeds. The Master's reproach against the ungrateful Jews, that they called the master of the house Beelzebul, would fit them very well too. For the apostasy truly names the Master of the house of the universe Beelzebul; or rather, they commit each of the two outrages by means of the other. So much lighter does their present war against God make every other impiety and every other audacity. 12. Again, the Savior, calling the Mosaic ordinances commandments and everywhere honoring his Father's legislation, says: "God commanded: Honor your father and your mother; and: Whoever speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death. You have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition." Having said this, he brings in Isaiah as a witness, saying: "Well did Isaiah prophesy about you: This people draws near to me with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Now pay attention: "In vain do they worship me." Why? "Because they teach as doctrines the commandments of men." So the things that were commandments of men did not please God the lawgiver; rather, he made those who introduced them liable to judgment. And these were introduced by the elders of the scribes and Pharisees, who claimed to worship the true God with their lips but stood far from him in their hearts. So the true Child and Son of the true God and Father, whose legislation the senseless in Israel set aside in favor of their own teachings, our Savior himself, silenced the vain blame which the ungrateful Jews laid on his disciples, and cleansed foods, as the Father's creations, of every evil suspicion, as indeed

the evangelist also attests: "It is not what goes into the mouth," he says, "that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth, that is what defiles a person." Elsewhere again, in a few words, he strengthened and laid down as law peace and righteousness among people, saying: "Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them." And to show that this exhortation and law of his is irreproachable and beneficial, he seals it with the authority of the Law and the Prophets: "For this," he says, "is the Law and the Prophets." Yes, and the parable in which the Savior likens the kingdom of heaven to a man sowing good seed in his field shames impiety no less. For how are the present world and those in it not part of the kingdom of God, when he calls the field his in so many words, not once but twice, and says that the field is the world, and that the world, just as it is his field, is also his kingdom? For in explaining the parable he says: "The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is the world; the good seed, these are the sons of the kingdom; the tares are the sons of the Evil One; and the enemy who sows them is the devil." Do you hear how he calls the world his, and those in it his seed, whom he also calls sons of the kingdom, and assigns only the oversowing of the tares to the Enemy? But attend to the argument, if you carry in yourself any remnant of the Fashioner's hand. For in what follows he openly proclaims the world his kingdom. How? "At the end," he says, "of this age" (not of the age to come), "the Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom" (that is, out of the present world) "the stumbling blocks." For in the coming and endless kingdom no tares grow at all, nor does the Evil One sow them, nor do stumbling blocks arise, so that the angels of the Son of Man would have to gather them out of it. Indeed, after they are gathered from here, they are thrown into the furnace of fire. "Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father." What could be clearer or more powerful than these words of the Lord for demolishing the apostasy and for exalting and strengthening true piety? By them they proclaim Christ our Savior Master of the world and all that is in it, and declare him King of all, of the present kingdom just as of the one to come. Why are they so eager to become more insensible than lifeless things? The sun, the earth and the rocks proclaim his lordship by suffering together with the Master's passion, yet these people are not ashamed even when those very things expose their folly. "From the sixth hour," it says, "until the ninth there was darkness, and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split." For what

fellowship or sympathy can there be between an evil creation and the Master's [suffering?]? According to the doctrine of the impious, creation ought rather to have grown bright and put on greater and more splendid adornment, seeing that the one who had come to destroy its fashioner was undergoing so great a suffering. And how, after the resurrection but before he ascended to his Father's bosom (which he never left), does he receive from the Father authority over heaven and earth, if the giver was not their Lord? For that is how the tongue that fights against God blasphemes. Besides this, if fields and houses are the handiwork of the Evil One, how does the good God, our Savior, promise to give fields and houses, together with eternal things, to those who eagerly followed him, when these things are base and the work of a base maker, things he himself is not Lord of, either to have or to give to others? And why should he bring the Enemy's goods as a reward to those who left everything and followed him, include them in the gift, join base things to eternal life and its goods, and by adding what is worse insult what, without the addition, would have been the finest of gifts? And again, when the Savior was asked about the commandments of the Law, how does he say that the first is: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind"; and the second, which the question did not even ask for: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself"? And he did not stop there, but finding the questioner in agreement with him, he declared that he was not far from the kingdom of God. For if the Mosaic laws were the Enemy's, how would they lay down first that one should know and recognize one God and Lord, and then love him alone with all one's heart, and one's neighbor as oneself? If, then, Moses proclaims one God and Lord, and commands that one neither serve nor worship any other besides him, and after this truly first commandment lays down mutual love and love of humankind in the same way as the Savior's command, where is the evil principle of the apostasy? But the scribe understood the Master, who was confirming the Mosaic word that God is one and there is no other besides him; while these people, who were commanded to surpass the scribes and Pharisees, do not preserve in themselves even the least share of piety. And Luke, the recorder of the Master's words: how does he testify that Zechariah and Elizabeth, who lived under the old legislation, were righteous, and that before God, not before men, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of God? And then that Zechariah performed the priestly service before God, and he calls the temple of the Law, which Zechariah entered, the temple of God? And that the angel of the Lord appeared in it, and which angel? The chief commander Gabriel, who also

announced the good news of the Master's birth from the Virgin, to the undefiled Maiden herself and through her to the world. He confirmed through his good tidings that the priest's prayer had been heard, and that the child of these good tidings would be great before the Lord, filled with the Holy Spirit, the bringer of great joy to many, and the cause of the turning of not a few of the sons of Israel to God, endowed with the spirit and power of Elijah. So the evangelist, or rather God, who said these things through the archangel, gives unassailable testimony that not only John, who saw grace beginning to bud, but also Elijah, who came long before grace, turned souls that were straying from the true God and whoring after demons back to the true God. Again, Zechariah is filled with the Holy Spirit and proclaims the prophets of old a choir of saints. "He has raised up," he says, prophesying and moved by the Holy Spirit, "a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David." And what is the proof? "As he spoke," he says, "through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old" (and not of the Enemy). And what did they prophesy? "That God would remember his holy covenant" (and not, you thrice-wretched man, the Enemy's). And bridling the mouths of the impious still further, he adds "the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, to grant us that, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear in holiness and righteousness." Reckon up what has been said. The Holy Spirit fills Zechariah, and, filled from that source, he proclaims the prophets of old to be holy and ministers of God; he foretells our freedom; he proclaims that the one who swore to Abraham is the giver of that freedom; and he proclaims that those who offer him worship worship in holiness and righteousness. If Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, declared these things, how are those who say the opposite not convicted of being filled with the evil spirit? And what would the bitter accusers of the Mosaic covenant, or rather the dividers of God's kingdom, say when they see in the Gospel Jesus brought up to Jerusalem, fulfilling the Mosaic rites and offering sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, and carried as an offering in the arms of righteous Simeon? Simeon, besides his other piety and righteousness, had received an oracle through the Holy Spirit; at once he took the common Redeemer in his arms, blessed him, and, speaking of God, prophesied that salvation had come before the face of all peoples, and a light for revelation to the nations who would afterward believe in him. Yet the divine evangelist was not content to tell only what had then taken place to refute the impious. Foreseeing their shamelessness, it seems, he also [tells of] Anna, whose tribe had Asher as its founder, who was present with the

…to the elder; and the sacred history also tells of Anna giving thanks to the Lord and prophesying things equal and alike about our common Master. What happened later has great power to cut down and humble those who raise their brows against the divine glory. He went up to Jerusalem with the Virgin, his mother according to the flesh, and with the man thought to be Jesus' father, and everything the sacred oracles describe was done. Then, on the journey home, the child stayed behind, so his mother according to the flesh and his supposed father were at a loss and went looking for the one they longed for. And he who is the maker of all things, but out of love for humankind became a virgin's child, says: "Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" He calls his Father's that very temple which the mouth of perdition slanders as the altar of the evil principle. How, then, can the heretics' drunken raving claim that the creator of heaven and earth is someone else? For our Saviour himself, rejoicing in spirit and with an unspeakable and inconceivable thanksgiving, cries out: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to infants." "Father, Lord of heaven and earth," cries the true Son, and the abomination that conceals every impiety contradicts the Saviour and names Beelzebul lord of heaven and earth. And if the law belonged to the Evil One, how does the lawgiver of grace send the lawyer who was testing him, and pretending to seek eternal life, to the law as to a great [?], and suggest that he will find there what he is seeking? When the lawyer recited the first two commandments word for word, the Truth said that he had answered well and that if he lived by them he would inherit eternal life.

13. See from other passages too that the law and grace are equal in honour, so that you may know that the same one is the lawgiver of both the Old and the New Covenant. "Truly, truly I tell you, heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." That is said of grace. Now see what is said of the law: "It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall." Do you see how our Saviour, foreseeing the audacity of the apostasy, gives equal honours and glory to the Old and the New Testament? This is so even though in many respects the things of grace far surpass the law, for the law was a tutor leading people to grace. But to show that he himself legislated both the former things and the present ones, according to a different and ineffable mode of dispensation, he used the same, equal words about each legislation. Moreover, against those who disobey his saving

teachings he brings in no other accuser and exposer than Moses. "Do not think," he says, "that I will accuse you before the Father. No; who is it that accuses you" (meaning Moses, of course) "before the Father?" Moses had been entrusted with the laws and with the prophecy about Christ. So he would be a trustworthy accuser and an unimpeachable witness against those who boast that they honour and love his laws, yet accept nothing he decreed about our common Master and Saviour, which was the chief point, the foundation and the prelude of his whole legislation. Nor do they even become aware of anything that might check their drunken violence and their war against God, directed at the one he prophesied. The error that splits the sovereignty of God's kingdom into opposing principles has been refuted by many sayings of the Lord, and not only by sayings but by deeds, and also by the works and words of the apostles. After so many refutations of their impiety, then, what pardon is left for those who still serve the will of the Evil One by what they think and how they live? They call the Master of the house of the universe Beelzebul, and declare Beelzebul to be a hidden, ineffable God, good, and father. I will not utter the still more godless thing they say. They are not even struck with awe or made to cower by the Lord's public exposure of the Jews who blasphemed him, an exposure aimed through them no less, if not more, at the present apostasy. For warring against God is common to both, even if the apostate is more brazen in his audacity. He said: "Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand." When the ungrateful among the Jews saw the Creator driving out the sufferings of souls and bodies, they ascribed the divine signs to Beelzebul; and the champions of the apostasy attribute the works of his hands to the same one. So both may justly be pilloried for warring against God by the same word of the Lord. For if the one principle of the Almighty has been cut in two, once cut it cannot stand. Rather, the first cut becomes a road to division into ten thousand parts, with no seat or stability ever again to be found. So each is convicted of fighting against God, the Jew and the apostate alike: the one gives God's signs to the Enemy, the other God's creations. The Lord's sentence is therefore common to both and inescapable.

14. But where are you being carried off to, people? Why do you abandon the Master and inscribe as your creator a fellow servant? Or rather, a slave and an apostate, who has plotted against our whole nature from the beginning? Why do you reject the Fashioner and hand yourselves over to one who seeks and strives to destroy us, not only in soul but also in body? Why have you become blind to the light? Why have you exchanged light for darkness? Sober up from your drunkenness; rise from your

soul-destroying stupor; take yourselves back from perdition. And how could this happen? It could happen if you practise turning away from the deeds in which the Enemy holds power. First, turn from fornication, which corrupts the body and corrupts the soul with a worse corruption, since the soul then gives up its self-mastery to serve the passions. Turn from injustice: where it rules, no household, no city, no human life at all is preserved. Turn from perjury, which plunges the soul into contempt of God. Turn from hatred of your brother, which insults our common Fashioner, for whoever hates the creature without cause carries his drunken outrage over to the Creator. Hate lying, understanding that the devil is the father of the lie. Loathe slander, which has caused many unexpected evils to be done. Flee murder, for the Enemy was a murderer from the beginning. Flee love of money, keeping Judas in mind if nothing else. Abhor theft and deceit against your neighbour, and the corruption of other people's marriages. And cleanse your way of life of luxury, licentiousness and drunkenness. For the Enemy comes in with these and delights in them, and in them he gains the strength to enslave your mind and separate you from God who created you, and to persuade you to be his creatures and to be called his. If you depart from his works, those already named and others like them, he too departs from you, since he has nothing in you on which to settle and rest. And then divine grace will shine on you and enlighten you to recognize as your fashioner and creator not the hostile plotter, but the good God who loves humankind. In him were created things visible and invisible, principalities and thrones, authorities and powers, and the whole present, visible world. For all things came to be through him, even if the apostasy has seized the eyes of the soul beforehand and does not allow them to see the creator. But as long as you serve the will of the Evil One, wallow in the mire of shameful pleasures, and choose soul-destroying ease over saving labours, the divine and heavenly radiance will certainly not flash upon you. Nor will the Enemy withdraw from his dominion over your souls and thoughts, since he holds you enslaved by your deeds. Still, we would certainly not let reluctance keep us from continuing to guide you to the light of piety by the testimonies of the Holy Spirit, and from refuting the apostasy.
1. Open your ears to me without bias, carrying nothing taken from the Evil One, and examine with me the anti-God mindset of those who

insult the Old Legislation. For if it belongs to the Evil One, how could he who came to destroy the Evil One consent to take its book and read aloud, in the hearing of many, the passages that proclaimed beforehand what concerned himself? And he did not only read them; he also solemnly declared: "Today this has been fulfilled in your hearing." And he proclaimed the year acceptable to the Lord, the year being a cycle of times, and time the measure of perceptible motion. How, again, in the parable of Lazarus and the rich man, does our loving and good Master call Moses and the prophets teachers of saving conversion and repentance? "They have Moses and the prophets," he says; "let them listen to them." Would he who took on our nature for the common salvation of the race send those he was initiating, those being set free from error, to the servants and ministers of the Enemy, so that they could then obtain salvation? Who that is truly God's creature could tolerate such an excess of madness? Again, if the Evil One was the lawgiver of the Old Testament, how can the fount of goodness say: "Search the Scriptures, for in them you will find eternal life"? Where is eternal life to be found in writings where the sting of sin governs? Where is eternal life in writings where the murderer legislates and gives orders? Yet this is what the God-fighting tongue dares to say. Besides what has been said, if the Old Testament belongs to the Evil One, how can the Truth say: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me"? He did not say, "If you believed Moses in some things"; he proclaimed Moses' trustworthiness without qualification. And again, some gaped eagerly after the dissolution of marriages and put Moses forward as the advocate of their passion. How does he answer them, splendidly championing the lawgiver? He says: "Because of your hardness of heart Moses permitted you to divorce your wives; but from the beginning it was not so." And where does he draw his proof from? "He who made them," he says, "made them male and female." So he showed that what the Saviour laid down in the Gospels about marriage came from him who established the natural laws in his own creatures and works. He also showed that Moses did not despise the laws given through creation, but out of

the pressure of circumstance made a concession [?] in his ordinance. "For my law," he says, "agrees with the law of the original formation. The dissolubility of marriage is a matter of Mosaic condescension and dispensation. 'Because of your hardness of heart,' he says, 'Moses wrote this.' But the indissolubility of the union, which I legislate, was foretold and laid down in advance by his works, in agreement with me, by the one who fashioned humankind in the beginning with different bodily forms." Therefore he adds: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and be joined to his own wife, and the two shall become one flesh." And so that you may learn more clearly who it was that formed bodies in this way, he himself, in naming the one who yoked them together, names also the [?]. For he says: "What therefore God has yoked together, let no one separate." The Saviour thus testifies that the difference in shape between the creatures, man and woman, is the work of God who is over all, and that it ought to preserve its union indissoluble. He also testifies that the Mosaic introduction of divorce had as its occasion the hardness of heart of those receiving the law, which dragged down and diminished the dignity of the law silently contained in creation.

2. Here is another argument. If the Old Testament came from an evil principle, how can Christ our Saviour, who joins grace to the law, say: "Many righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it"? How could those who belong to the Evil One have wished to see the things of the Good? For desire for the Good grows from a good impulse. And again, how can he say: "Abraham saw my day and rejoiced"? How would it be consistent, how would it even be possible, for a man of the Old Testament to be raised to such heights of contemplation and power that he saw the day of the coming of the good God and rejoiced? This is especially so since the divine Paul testifies that the mystery of Christ and the Saviour's coming escaped the notice of the principalities and powers of the world, and of the world-ruler. If, then, the mystery escaped even the world-ruler himself, how did his servants foretell and foresee it? But now hear from me what refutes their impiety still more clearly.

The unbelieving and meddlesome Sadducees once made up a story of seven brothers, gave one and the same wife to each of them in turn, and used their fiction to try to do away with the resurrection of bodies. They questioned the Saviour about the difficulty their fiction seemed to them to raise, and demanded to know which of the seven would have her as his wife. First he rebuked them for their error, saying that they did not know the Scriptures. Yet why rebuke anyone for not knowing the things of the Evil One? And to their ignorance of the Scriptures he adds another, more serious reproach: they did not know the power of God either. Then he unfolds the mystery of the resurrection more clearly: "For in the resurrection," he says, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven." Next he refutes their folly still more vehemently and forcefully. At once he declares plainly the harmonious bond between grace and the law, and strikes them a blow through the Mosaic legislation, and through them the present apostates as well. "Have you not read," he says, "what was spoken by God: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?" By this he shows clearly that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are heirs of eternal life, and that their God is the eternal God, the author of the resurrection, and the giver of the joy that follows it. And he continues directly: "So God is not the God of the dead, but of the living." He said this to cut off every [?] of the impious. [?] he did not leave out where it is written, but through the sacred Mark he cries out that God said these things to Moses in the book of Moses. God, then, is not the God of the dead. Abraham lives with him, Isaac lives, Jacob lives, and so do all who emulated their way of life, and they are like angels of God in heaven. How, then, can those who lived under the old way of life belong to an evil principle, as wickedness claims?

3. The mindset of the apostasy is refuted still further by another passage. The Saviour urges those who wish to gain entrance into heaven to strive to enter through the narrow gate. Those who neglected the commandment he sends away, as workers of sloth, to where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. But those who were zealous for the commandment he gathers from everywhere and brings into his kingdom, and seats them at table there. And (pay attention, reader!) before them he seats Abraham and Isaac and

Jacob and the prophets. For he says: "Whether or not you are willing to hear it: when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, and yourselves thrown out." And who are the ones thrown out, if not plainly all who did not live in imitation of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the prophets? But if all who did not emulate their life and piety are thrown out of God's kingdom and cast into weeping and gnashing of teeth, what punishment could be found to match those who have been driven to such a pitch of madness? O unguarded mouths, so ready to serve the father of lies that they dare to insult those men as robbers and thieves, and as creatures and servants of the Evil One! And they do not stop their rage even there. He who grants us eternal life and the kingdom of heaven is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of the living and not of the dead. Yet they slander him as an evil principle and the creator of evil works, and call [the patriarchs] [?] creatures of the Evil One. Will they not pay a penalty no smaller than their audacity, when the punishment of fire and darkness prepared for the devil is exacted from them for ever? Nor do they shudder at the chasm between the rich man and Lazarus, which walls off those who rejoice with Abraham from those punished in torments. But alas! Even if they are not awed by the Saviour's threat now, because they have no sense of the punishment, then, yes then, when they learn the bitterness of torment by experience, they will condemn themselves at length, without end, though they will gain nothing by it. This will be especially so when, as in the parable of the rich man, they call for help on Abraham, whom they used to mock, and find that he has no pity for them. The man who treated Lazarus with drunken contempt is banished from the bosom of Abraham by a fearful chasm. He pays the penalty of his unloving disposition in unsleeping fire. He longs for that blessed joy and rest but is shut out; his tongue burns and he suffers bitter pains. And his outrage was only that he did not share any compassion with one of his own kind, not that he mocked or was seen blaspheming. How much more, then, will the mouth, the tongue and all the inward parts of those who pour such outrage on Abraham be burned many times over, since through him they carry their war against God on to our common Master and Creator? But follow me in what comes next and consider it with me.

4. In the Gospels the Saviour pillories the boastful, murderous and unbelieving spirit of the Jews and judges them unworthy of descent from Abraham, even though they were born of his line. "If you were Abraham's children," he says, "you would do the works of

…Abraham. And his triumph over them does not stop there: he attacks them still more vehemently, saying, "You are not children of Abraham; you are of the devil." For it is a very strong verdict [?] to put them under the name and lineage of the one whose true likeness they bear in the way they live. If the Old Testament came from the godless utterances of the Evil One, and Abraham belonged to it, then saying "children of Abraham" would be the same as saying "children of the devil." In either case the Jews would be shown to honor alike the things that God hates and the Enemy loves. And how is it that elsewhere the Savior assigns the kingdom of heaven as an inheritance to Abraham and those with him? He ranks with them those who, with wholehearted resolve, have proved to be unhesitating keepers of the commandments and have offered him pure worship. As though he were giving some great and wonderful prize, he promises them fellowship with those men in the kingdom of heaven: "For I tell you that many will come from east and west and will recline at table with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven." Is this, then, the prize for those who have recognized him? Is this the gift for all who suffered slaughter for his sake? Is this the reward of his generosity, this the prize: to be with the servants of the Evil One, to be counted among them, to herd together with them? What ear that has any hearing at all will put up with such words?

5. And if the Old Testament belonged to the devil, how is it that Matthew and Luke, in setting out the Savior's genealogy, list as his ancestors and forefathers the very men whom the Old Testament held in renown? For how could the good God be born in mere appearance and pretense? There is, indeed there is, no small faction of this apostasy that brings this madness forward as well, against the incarnate coming of the Word. But how could the Good One, whether by appearance and pretense or in truth and reality, consent that men distinguished in the evil covenant should become his forefathers and ancestors? How could he take hold of such a seed, when he knew perfectly well that its fashioner was the Enemy? And why did he not come forth from some other nation, one that bore no second working of the Evil One? Instead he comes forth from the very nation that the laws of the Old Testament shaped and ordered, the nation which, after its evil fashioning at the beginning, those laws trained and molded by other works and customs more evil still. And if the Old Testament was not from God, how is it that he punishes with fire those who set aside the Creator's laws in nature, who ran aground in licentiousness and were wholly enslaved to the will of the Enemy, and exacts from them the penalty for their outrages? That the Evil One should exact a penalty for wicked deeds that delight him and proceed from him: how could this be conceived [or said] at all without madness? Yet the apostate claims that the wicked are made to pay for their wicked works by fire, by another wicked

creation [?]. He says that the one who [?]… punishes with a flood those who, in [?] years, were swept away by the passions of the flesh. For it belongs to one who hates evil, who is good and just, both to check evil and to exact an equal punishment from those who have grown shameless in sin. It does not belong to one who is evil, nor to one who loves and legislates the

6. So that you may learn more precisely that one and the same good and benevolent God is the avenger of justice both in the Old Testament and under grace: he withers the fig tree that bore him no fruit; he subjects to countless threats those who do not obey him; and he condemns those who have transgressed his laws to the outer fire prepared for the devil and his angels, which is the severest punishment and has no equal. At the beginning he punishes with fire and water that last only for a time, but at the end with fire that is everlasting and unending. Do you see how hatred of evil, just like benevolence, is everywhere a mark and testimony of God's goodness? Nor does he do these things himself while keeping his disciples from such action [?]. Under Peter, illustrious in grace, Ananias and Sapphira received death as the penalty for their lying. Paul, the fervent herald of grace and teacher of the whole world, at once makes Elymas blind, having learned from his own experience how much good punishment brings. He hands over the Corinthian who had committed fornication to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and he sends Alexander on to the torment and judgment of the next world. And Paul solemnly testifies that wrath and tribulation and distress come upon every human soul that does evil, just as glory and honor and peace come to everyone who does good. If that is so, how could it be true that God shows no partiality? Were not those condemned in the Old Testament condemned by the same good God who also legislates grace, and who confirmed his impartiality by what he established? And in how many cases could one show that justice, which hates evil, holds unassailable power in the laws of grace? 7. Besides what has been said: if the Old Testament came from an evil principle, how is it that Paul, that lofty and heavenly man, says at the very beginning of his Epistles that God promised beforehand, through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, the gospel concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh? If the prophets and the holy Scriptures through which God promised beforehand concerning his Son belong to God, where will the Evil One find any foothold? And if his invisible attributes, that is, those of the [(28) "Punishes": I read "to punish" … [?]]

God and [of] our Lord Jesus Christ, have been understood from the creation of the world through the things he has made, and are clearly seen [?]… The invisible and intelligible attributes of God [?] are clearly seen from the perceptible and visible creation. For if the invisible attributes of God were not clearly seen through the visible creation, he would not have distinguished the invisible things from it, nor taught that they are clearly seen through it. How, then, could the invisible attributes of God, and with them his eternal power and divinity, be clearly seen in perceptible things made by the Evil One? On the contrary, in the works of the Enemy, if he made any at all, it would be his wickedness and [?] that would be seen. That the law is from the good God could be shown still more easily from the following. Paul, the mouth of Christ, says that it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. How then is the law not from the good God, who, instead of punishing those who keep it, honors them as righteous [?]? And if the transgressor of the law, though circumcised in the flesh, is reckoned as uncircumcised and judged unworthy of God, while the uncircumcised man who keeps the law's requirements bears in his soul the circumcision of the all-holy Spirit, how is the law not from the good God? And Paul has cried out that Christ Jesus became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and Christ did confirm them. The one who made those promises to the fathers is the God who fashioned the perceptible heaven and earth, the God whom Moses also proclaims in his account of the world's creation. And from what Paul says [?] in many other places, he is shown to be the Father of our Savior, whose promises the Savior, as his true Son, showed by his own act, and not through another, to be inviolable and true. How, then, does the shamelessness of the apostasy not hide itself in shame? But why should I cite Paul, great as he is in the fervor [?] of his [?] and in the wisdom of his grace, when one may hear the common Master himself, who insists: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it." And: "Amen, amen, I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke of a letter, will pass away until all these things take place." I came to fulfill the law. It takes evil mouths to say that I came to undo my Father's laws. I will leave nothing of it unfulfilled. There is nothing of evil inspiration in it; nothing in it will end in falsehood; all of it is full of truth [?]. I am the confirmation of the prophets' words. For they were servants and ministers of me and of my Father, and they clearly foresaw and foretold my coming and everything about my coming. Therefore nothing of what they foretold and the law contains, whether small or great, will pass away without being sealed by the fulfillment of the truth.

For if I am a servant of the circumcision to confirm the promises the Father made to the fathers, how could one iota, that is, the least thing spoken in the law and the prophets, ever pass away or fail to come to pass? 8. But turn with me now to another question: are the words in the law oracles of God? Paul says: "What is the value of circumcision?" And then: "Much in every way. First of all, they were entrusted with the oracles of God. What then, if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true, though every human being is a liar." He will not allow God's faithfulness to be nullified, but would rather have every human being proved a liar, so that God, who gave circumcision, may be acknowledged as true. If, then, the things entrusted to Israel are oracles of God, and Israel's unfaithfulness does not nullify God's faithfulness, and we must rather regard as liars those who do not believe God, and regard the one who gave Israel its laws as wholly true, how is the Old Testament not the legislation of the good God? Surely Paul does not call the Evil One, who was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, the fountain of truth! Surely he does not prefer that all people be carried off into falsehood so that the architect and maker of falsehood may be proclaimed the source of truth! And if the righteousness of God has been revealed, attested by the law and the prophets, how could the law and the prophets not be considered filled with the inspiration and truth that come from the good God? But look further at how dreadful and despicable this warring against God is. God redeemed the world from slavery to the Enemy through his blood. But the blood and the flesh — I shudder, and leave it to the thoughts and tongues of these enemies of God to state their own view — how could he have snatched our race from slavery to the Enemy by means of such a creation? Our enemy would deserve much gratitude, glory and honor if he had himself supplied the material by which we were to be freed from his tyranny. And he would be guilty of great folly and deserve ridicule if he had been induced to fashion the very things by which he would be stripped of his power over both our bodies and our souls. What else follows from the apostasy? That the Savior accomplished nothing great, that he did not achieve the whole work of our salvation from his own resources, but allowed the Enemy the greater share. O mind subject to [?] Satan! Taking from him something of which he himself was not the maker, and himself suffering in it, he delivers [?], which ought not to be (for the apostasy makes it the work of the Evil One), and transforms it into incorruption, and [causes] evil to remain immortal [?]…
9. And how could he be the enemy of our race who, through his own creation, contributed so great a share to our common salvation?

And how did he do anything evil at all in fashioning the body? The Savior not only saves the body and later makes it incorruptible, but through it he also benefits the souls that go with it, bringing the bodies united to them into a like immortality. So the zeal of those who split the one principle into two is darkness and chaos, blindness of reasoning, madness and deep drunkenness. They cut the one Lord Jesus Christ, the creator of all things, into two principles, setting one over intelligible things and the other over visible things. But how do those who say that our body belongs to the Evil One not sink in shame before the Depth and the Silence and the birth-pangs of their creator [?]? For Paul plainly cries out against them: "The body is not for fornication" (which is the work of the Evil One) "but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body." How can the Enemy's creation belong to the Lord at all? And why would one need to say that the body must not be given over to fornication, if in itself it is evil, the creation of an evil principle, wholly alien to the will and the creation of God? If, by its nature and laws, the body were evil, as the apostasy would have it, it could never belong to the Lord, and whether or not it gave itself to fornication would make no difference. Whether it fornicated or not, it would no less remain evil and the creation of an evil principle. Consider this as well. If the body is a creation of the Evil One, how can the man who so brilliantly outgenerals the Evil One and champions the truth call it holy? "The unmarried woman," he says, "is concerned about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in both body and spirit." If the body is holy, how is it evil? How is it the work of an evil creation? Evil deeds debase the creation of the good God and claim it for the Evil One and subject it to him. But when the body is kept within the laws of its creator, it has the strength to drive the Evil One away rather than to be enslaved by him. 10. That it is impossible, for those whose free will remains unenslaved to the passions of the Enemy, either to say or to think that there are two principles, and opposed ones at that, I believe the argument has shown sufficiently. Let us now examine the other part of the apostasy. Through what has been said, I think, it too has already given an account that is neither negligible nor brief. Nevertheless, let the remaining accounts now also be demanded of it, through the same sacred scripture. Paul, who daily offers himself as a sacrifice to God, cries out in a piercing voice: "Do I say these things on human authority… VARIANT READINGS AND NOTES. (35) "Before the Depth and the Silence" [?]…

[?]… Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the law say the same?" This is equivalent to saying: Do we support what has been said by human reasoning, or does not what is put forward belong to a divine legislation that is above human beings? And who it was that observed these things, he himself makes plain: "For it is written in the law of Moses," he says, "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." After saying this he adds: "Is it for oxen that God is concerned?" And to show for whom he is concerned instead, he continues: "Does he not speak entirely for our sake? It was written for our sake." So the doctrine that runs through the Old Testament is common to both, and governs under grace as well. Then, pointing to the natural likeness of the Son to the Father, and to the fact that he is in no way different from him, by the likeness of what each legislated, he says: "Just as those who serve at the altar were commanded to share in what is offered on the altar, so too the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel." So highly does he exalt the law, as belonging to the Father, that he has the Son too issue his commandments in imitation of it [?] [as one proceeding from the Father … [?]]. And making still clearer the connection and kinship between the law and grace, he says: "I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink." Show me now, in this passage, what is not free of the Enemy's frenzy [?]. "For they drank," he says, "from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." Do you hear how Christ gave drink to his Father's people, and how the Father led Israel to worship the Son and turn to him? Through whom, if not plainly through Moses and the prophets? Where, then, is the Evil One here? Where is the work of the evil principle? Where are the laws of the opposing party? [?]… of the Mosaic people, who were nourished by spiritual food and drank spiritual drink from the rock that was with them and followed them, which was Christ? Then again this man, learned in the law, who regarded all the gains he once prided himself on as rubbish for the sake of Christ, says: "Nor let us put Christ to the test, as some of them did." Who were they, if not plainly the people of Israel? And what was their reward? "They were destroyed by the serpents." So in testing the God of the law they were also, through the Father, testing his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. It was their lawgiver whom the people of Israel put to the test; but the initiate and guide into the ineffable mysteries, knowing that the kingdom of the Father and the Son is undivided and unbreakable, insists that when God, the Father of the good Child, is tested, Christ too is tested. Note, as a further consequence, that Christ also sent destruction by serpents as a plague upon those who had put him to the test at once. And in inflicting it he did not

lose his benevolence. Elsewhere, again, Paul testifies that the prophets spoke at the command of the eternal God and truthfully proclaimed beforehand the mystery hidden before the ages, which escaped the notice of the powers of this world and of the World-Ruler himself. How then could the prophets or the law be of evil inspiration, when they proclaimed the mystery beforehand, and it escaped all the scheming of wickedness? And again, elsewhere, he testifies that it was the same God, not one God and then another, who spoke long ago in the prophets and later in the Son: "In many parts and in many ways," he says, "God spoke long ago to our fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in a Son." The same God, not one and then another. Therefore the one who bestowed the New Covenant on the world in the Son is the same one who also established the Old Covenant in the prophets, according to the man who is wise in divine things if anyone is. How then does error invent one lawgiver and God for the Old and another for the New? And the same initiate and guide into the ineffable mysteries sets his seal on this sacred Scripture: in the beginning the Lord founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of his hands. For he takes up the song of the ancestor of God [David] and weaves it into his own thoughts, and so confirms that it is divinely inspired. If so, how are the company of the apostasy not ashamed when they pretend to call the man who proclaims these things their teacher, falsely, yet still they call him so? For they even take his name for themselves, and in doing so they act against his law: "Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" and "'I belong to Paul,' 'I belong to Cephas.' Is Christ divided?" Yet even the name they boast of they insult by their transgression. They flee to that name to escape the shame into which the mere mention of the teacher of their apostasy throws them. But how are they not put to shame? Paul, through the voice of David, teaches that the true and good God is the maker of heaven and earth. They say that the maker of heaven is one, and the creator of the earth another. Nor did they hear him cry out that "it was fitting for him," that is, for the Father, "for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist." Paul thus proclaims him creator of all things alike, not of some things and not of others. And how is it clear that he says this about the Father? The continuation of the words shows it: "in bringing many sons to glory, to make the pioneer of their salvation perfect through sufferings." For who but the true God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ either brought many sons to glory or perfected their pioneer through

[?] But he, being a sublime and holy man, and knowing that our Lord Jesus Christ holds the might and the kingdom undivided with the Father, says of him elsewhere: "For from him and through him and to him are all things; to him be the glory forever. Amen." "All things," he says: not only the things of the mind, as the madmen claim, but all the visible [?] things as well are the work of his creating hand. And the kingdom over all these things, and the authority and the might and the providence, belong to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. But I ask you to carry your study on to other sayings of the apostle as well. They call the believers brothers, holy, and sharers in the heavenly calling, and they set Christ our true God beside your servant Moses, for they present both of them as faithful to God the Father. Paul says in these very words: "Consider the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus Christ, who was faithful to him who appointed him," that is, appointed him high priest. Then, explaining how he was faithful, he shows it by means of Moses: "as Moses also was," he says, "in all his house." Whose house? Surely the house of the one who made our Lord Jesus Christ high priest? Then, teaching also the difference beyond all comparison between the Master and the servant, he calls the one a servant, faithful in all the house of God, and the other the one who built the house. For God, who builds all things, is the one who also ordered the building of his earthly house. "For God," he says, "who built all things": Jesus the Christ is his true Son, and for this reason he is also Lord of the house, and not a servant as Moses was. A little later he proclaims the good news that we are called the house of God, "if we who have believed hold the boast of our hope and our confidence firm to the end." Then he puts forward the [?] sayings to confirm what he has said. In them he first cries out that the Holy Spirit spoke through him, and then that the same penalty is demanded of those who now turn a deaf ear to the Master's commandments as of those who long ago hardened their hearts in the provocation. Those whose punishment is equal do not differ in their sin either; and where the sin is alike, each of the two parties, having sinned against the same God,

is convicted of having gone astray. But that warm and fiery lover of the truth was not content even with what he had said. To join the law to grace, and to show that both belong in common to the Father and the Son, he shows that those who provoked Moses, and through him God, tested no other than the one whom the Holy Spirit proclaims. "For on the day of testing in the wilderness," he says, "when your fathers tested me" (me, and no other) "and tried me, and saw my works. Therefore they went astray, since they chose not to know my ways, and they did not [?] enter into my rest." Then: "Do not, then, as they provoked God and disbelieved and fell away from him, fall away yourselves from the living God. Do not harden your hearts as they did, nor imitate those with whom God was angry for forty years in the wilderness, whose bodies fell in it. For indeed it was through unbelief that they could not enter into the rest of God. Let us fear, then, that we may fall short in any of the commands or fall sick with unbelief. For those of us who have believed will enter into his rest." And who decreed this? Tightening his argument still further, and showing that the same God, both in the Old Covenant and in grace, creates and saves and punishes and fulfils what he has promised, he adds with splendid boldness: "As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest." So the same one who back then did not bring in those who disbelieved now likewise banishes the unbelievers from the rest. Whoever examines these sacred sayings before us will observe countless other things there, and will find the same God steering the people of Israel through Moses and the people of grace through Jesus Christ. That same God, both long ago and now, brings some into the place of rest and casts others out. The lover of contemplation sees that both the old rest, which was the promised land, and the later rest, which is the heavenly kingdom, belong to the same God, and that the same God both inflicts punishment and awards salvation, and much else besides. But if, as their [?] reasoning would have it, the things of old belonged to the Evil One, then those who offended him should have been judged worthy of honours and crowns and have entered into the rest. They should not have left their bodies in the wilderness, nor paid such penalties as are laid up for those who sin against the true God.

12. But again, how does the same teacher of the world say that Aaron was called high priest by God, just as Christ was? "For no one takes the honour for himself," he says, "but only when he is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but it was he who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you." But if the one who called Christ high priest is the same who also

[Variant readings and notes: (54) Ἐπιθεωρήσει. Perhaps after this the word ἐκεῖ [?]]

anointed Aaron through Moses, and neither of them glorified himself as high priest, but the one who called them did, then how are the things of the New and the things of the Old not both the works and [?] of the same Good One? Will the apostasy, growing still more shameless, accuse even Christ, who is the Truth, of lying? For he says: "The ruler of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me." But the apostasy, which says that the body he wore was a fabrication of the Evil One, bitterly pours falsehood over the Truth. As Master and Lord and Creator of all, when he came to the passion he willingly accepted for the saving of the world, he declared to his disciples that he was Lord of both the donkey and the colt. For these too are creatures under his lordship and mastery, just as the world and what is in it are. So he says: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, Their Lord has need of them, and he will send them at once." Christ calls himself Lord as the creator of the donkey and the colt; but the apostasy will not tolerate this, and snatches them from his authority to place them among the creatures of the Enemy. Yet if nothing else, the other sayings of the divine Paul should have shamed these shameless people. These sayings declare that there is no other God greater than the one who swore to Abraham, that he does not change in his promises, and that it is impossible for him to lie (so completely is the dignity of truth one with his very being), and that he is the one who grants the hope of us Christians. For he says: "For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying," and so on; and he tells how Abraham, having waited patiently, obtained the promise; and that "the same God, wishing to show the heirs of the promise" (and we are those heirs) "even more clearly that his purpose cannot change, guaranteed it with an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong encouragement." Who might? "We who have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us." Have you noticed how he says that there is no God greater than the one who gave the oath to Abraham? How he proclaims him the fountain of all truth? How we who have believed in Christ draw from that source the encouragement and strength to lay hold of the hope set before us? Where, then, are the Good One and the Evil One, and the mutilation of the Old Testament? And again, who is it who accomplished the new covenant, with the house of Judah as well? If you do not wish to say it yourself, hear Paul, who initiates us into the mysteries, saying it. For he takes up as his own the prophetic

predictions: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will accomplish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah" (turn your mind to this, O man) "not like the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt." "Which I made," he says, and not, as you say, which the Evil One made with their fathers. Then: "They did not continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them." Who is speaking? The Lord, he says, not the Evil One. For he goes on: "This is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord." I will make it, not another; I will make the new covenant, as I also made the old. Do you see how from beginning to end Paul praises the same Lawgiver of both the Old and the New Covenant? How could the things of the former covenant be holy, and the Holy of Holies, if they came from an evil legislation? For he says: "The first tabernacle had regulations for worship and an earthly sanctuary. For a tabernacle was prepared, the first one, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the presence; this is called the Holy Place. And after the first tabernacle was the holy [?], the Holy of Holies, in which there was a golden jar holding the manna, and Aaron's rod lay there, and the tablets of the covenant." And how did the cherubim of glory overshadow these things, if they were the commands of the treacherous and evil principle? Again, how does the same herald of grace cry out that the ages were framed by the word of God, and that by the same God what is seen came into being from things that do not appear? For if God made the things that are seen by a word, as he also made the ages, does the apostasy invent one creator of what is seen and another of what is known by the mind? How much could one say, and with how many proofs could one refute how the apostasy fights against God and contradicts itself? How does the good God bear witness that Abel was righteous, and accept his substance [?], and how does Paul proclaim that his gift was offered in faith, if Abel was the work of an evil fashioning? "By faith," he says, "Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain, through which he was attested to be righteous, God himself bearing witness to his gifts." And how was the taking up of Enoch also a matter of faith, and how did he please God? And how must the one who comes to God believe

[Variant readings and notes: (50) After the first tabernacle, the holy. Otherwise thus [?]: after the second curtain, the tabernacle called… (51) From things that do not appear. Our author for μή [?]]

in the God who works these things, first that he is the one who truly exists, and then that he becomes a rewarder, if he was evil and himself the doer of evil works? And why must I speak one by one of those who were distinguished in the Old Testament, all of whose faith in God he attests: Noah, I mean, and Abraham, and Isaac? He attests not only that they were faithful throughout their whole lives, but also that they departed this present life in faith, and regarded themselves as strangers and sojourners in this perishable world, and that God was not ashamed to regard them as his own and to be called their God. Which God? The one who prepared the heavenly city for them. For how did he prepare the heavenly kingdom for them, unless they were known throughout their lives as his servants and the keepers of his commands, and kept their faith in him whole? For them the heavenly city was the prize, pure and free of doubt [?].

14. And do not pass over Abraham's marvellous sacrifice either, the sacrifice in which no victim was slain. God sought it and accepted his intention. Abraham readily obeyed, and not only obeyed but believed that God is able even to raise the dead. That is why it is reckoned to him as righteousness, and why he receives the dignity of fatherhood not only over the generation of that time but over those who came after, as it is written: "I have made you the father of many nations, in the presence of the God in whom he believed." And notice carefully which God he means, for Paul goes on to teach: "who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were." And again: "He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God." Do you see who it was who spoke in the law and the prophets? It was no other than the one who bestowed grace on us, but the very same. For he goes on: "It was not written for his sake alone, but also for ours, to whom it will be reckoned, who believe in him who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead." So he who made Abraham the father of many nations, who swore an oath to him, who never fails in his promises, who calls the things that are not as though they were, who gives life to the dead, is the very one who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, even if the ruinous mind of the apostasy divides them into two dominions and two gods. And consider also, I ask you, the rest who were plainly shown to have lived in the Old Testament: Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, and Moses himself. Paul praises them and extols their faith, and about Moses he adds that he also endured the reproach of Christ. He says in these very words that Moses "considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt," and he gives the reason: "for he was looking to the reward," which clearly God was able [?]

to grant him. But why need I list these men? The sublime man has already done it for us, saying: "Time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, did what was right, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, and were made strong out of weakness." Then, after going through their sacred [?] and marvellous deeds and sufferings, and their life of endurance in the desert, he adds: "of whom the world was not worthy." And not only that, but he rouses us to imitate them, and sets them before us as a kind of encouragement to take up virtue, saying: "Since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us also lay aside everything, and the sin that so easily entangles us, and run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith," who is our Lord Jesus Christ. So he became the pioneer of the faith in which our fathers remained noble and steadfast, and the perfecter of the salvation both of us and of them. And even if there were nothing else to turn them from their error and draw them over to piety by force, it would still be right for them to learn the truth quickly from what is about to be said. For Paul says: "What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means." And again: "For I know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh." And: "I delight in the law according to the inner man." And again: "So then I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh." For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. That is, the soul, made in the image of God and joined to the body fashioned by the same hand, longs to be carried up to its archetype. But the flesh, which means the desires of the flesh (for such is the custom both under the former grace and under the grace that came after it, since we were given grace upon grace: to call such passions by this name)... These desires of the flesh, then, do not readily follow the will of the soul, but fight hard against it in many things, with the Evil One as their ally, unless someone keeps careful watch, draws down help from above through prayer, and sets up a trophy of victory over them.

[?] Let [the argument] return. For he joins to what he said before: "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good." And it is clear that it is not one commandment that is

[Variant readings and notes: (57) Grace upon grace. The passage is from John 1[:16].]

holy, another that is just, and another that is good, but it is the commandment of the law itself and of the same God, who is just and holy and good. He from whom holiness, justice and goodness pour forth is himself their provider and giver. But as their cause, he himself is these things before all the things he has given others a share in. He is them not by sharing in them, [?] through his overflowing goodness, and what they share in is a participation shaped by the good [?]. And elsewhere the same herald of the truth cries out again that the just requirement of the law is fulfilled in those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. That is, it is fulfilled in those in whom evil deeds, the seeds sown by the Enemy, and sins have no strength, but who walk according to the Spirit, that is, in whom a way of life according to virtue and with God's help is achieved. But if the just requirement of the law is fulfilled not in those ruled by passion and sin but in those who are spiritual and work together with God, how do they not shudder to call it an evil legislation? And elsewhere again he could not hold back the fire of his faith and his eagerness for all to be saved, and the goal to which his fierce love drove him, that is, to bring all to Christ. He cries with a loud voice: "I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, to whom belong the covenants and the giving of the law and the promises and the worship." And he shows most clearly where these things come from and on whose providence they depend: "who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen." So the laws and the worship and the promises, through which the fathers pleased God, and from whom Christ sprang according to his human nature, belong to the God who is over all. And elsewhere he praises the law of Moses as the unfailing word of God: "For the word of God has not failed," he says. And when he discusses Jacob and Esau, how the elder will serve the younger, he all but muzzles the servants of error of old as well. For he says: "Is there injustice with God? By no means. For he says to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion." And so that no one might think he accomplishes all his good deeds by his own toil and sweat without help from above, he continues: "So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills." He shows that the same God is the fountain of mercy for those who act [?] toward him, and that he exposes and casts down the arrogance and harshness of those who are puffed up with pride. He praises the same God, who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, as loving and good, and teaches that all should obey him and that no one should rise up against his secret governance through their own reasonings. So he adds: "But who are you, O man, to answer back to
