Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople

…to God? Then, plainly proclaiming him to be the potter — and not only the potter, but also a judge with full authority, master of allotting to each whatever his judgment brought — he teaches that he brings wrath upon the vessels prepared for destruction, but lavishes the riches of his glory on those worthy of mercy. He announces that we too are sharers in this, since we who have believed in our Lord Jesus Christ were prepared and called beforehand to the enjoyment of good things. Elsewhere again, recording the irrevocable grace of the true God, and that the people of Israel was his, as were the giving of the law and the commandments, and that not all of them fell from the adoption [?] because of the transgression of some, he proclaimed: "Has God rejected his people, whom he foreknew?" And he shows clearly which God he means, and where the proof lies that he did not reject his people: "For I too," he says, "am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin." So the one who did not reject Paul but called him to election is the very one who made Israel his people. He did not reject them, but brought them to perfection through faith in Christ.

14. Again, he proclaims both the Old and the New to be of the one God. He shows that the New came forth from the Old as from a root, and that each shares in holiness, when he says: "If the firstfruits are holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches"; and: "It is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you"; and: "If God did not spare the natural branches" (for the bodies of those who tempted him fell in the wilderness, and many other sufferings overtook the guilty), "perhaps he will not spare you either." It is not one God for them and another for you, but the same. And again: "See, then, the kindness and the severity" — of whom? Of Christ — "severity toward those who fell, but kindness toward you." What could the firstfruits and the lump, the root and the branches, the natural branches and the grafted ones mean, if not their interconnection and kinship, and that they belong to the same lawgiver? The words themselves declare this most clearly. And again he says of the Israelites who had not yet run to faith in Christ: "As regards the gospel they are enemies for our sake, but as regards election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers." Then, to show that they are beloved, he brings forward the irrevocability of God's gifts and of his calling: "For the gifts and the calling of God," he says, "are irrevocable." And: "Whatever was written beforehand was written for our instruction." Why? "So that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures" — that is, the Old — "we might have hope." Then he proclaims the true God as the God of endurance and encouragement. The Enemy could not be a God of encouragement and endurance, however much more the servants of the Evil One might rave. He says: "May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in harmony with one another, in accordance with Christ

Jesus, so that with one accord and with one voice you may glorify the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Not one God and then another, but the one who foretold the coming of the Son, gave us the Scriptures and called us to faith in his Son: the God of encouragement and endurance, the giver of concord, for whose glory Christ received us, having become a servant of the circumcision. Elsewhere again he says: "Was anyone called when already circumcised? Let him not undo his circumcision. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing" — then pay attention — "but keeping the commandments of God." Not of gods. Of these commandments, one ordered circumcision and the other did not, and he declared both to be of the same God, not of different gods. So there is one true God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He gave circumcision through Abraham at the appointed times, for the fulfilment of a mystery, and through his Son he has received those in uncircumcision.

15. Elsewhere he says: "This perishable thing" (and what is that but our body?) "must put on imperishability," he says, "and this mortal thing must put on immortality." If the body were the creature of the Evil One, how would it befit a good God to refashion it from perishable to imperishable and from mortal to immortal? For if the evil body, the creature of the Evil One, is transformed by the good God from mortality to immortality and from perishability to imperishability, then the written word will not prove true that "Death has been swallowed up in victory," nor that at the end of all the ages the Enemy will be cast out of whatever he ruled in any way, as of things devoted to the works of the Evil One. Worse, the reverse will happen: he will then hold power undisputed and without end, since his mortal and perishable creature will have been raised to immortality and imperishability. But see here too the wealth of Paul's wisdom, into which he was apparently initiated when he was caught up to the third heaven. Note how he draws a distinction between the New and the Old. Then, foreseeing the apostasy and cutting off all its idle talk, he immediately adds what follows. For he says: "So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation — be renewed — the old has passed away; behold, all things have become new." But see the energy, the wisdom and the skill of the man: "All things," he says — that is, both the New and the Old — "are from God, who reconciled us to himself through our Lord Jesus Christ." Therefore, of things both past and present, the good Father of our Saviour Jesus Christ [?] … changed, and to be referred to "body" [?] … For otherwise "says" governs the phrase "to put on imperishability."

was himself the giver, the provider and the creator. How could the body be the creature of the Enemy, when the same Spirit-bearing orator takes Isaiah's prophecy as his own and says: "For you are the temple of the living God; as God said, 'I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people'"? Paul cries out that we are the temple of Christ, and he puts forward Isaiah as his witness. It was no other God who spoke in Isaiah but the Son of God himself, whose temple the divine Paul [?] calls us. Where, then, is the creature of the Evil One? Where is the double, opposed principle?

16. Further, unveiling the light of truth, he charges us to be pure and separated from the unclean, so that we would be as sons and daughters. He also names the one who promised these things: he is the Lord Almighty. He weaves in, too, to whom the promises were made: they come to us through the fathers. For he adds: "Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God." So these things have been promised to us, and the promise began with the fathers. The God whose people they were is the God whose people we are too. As the pure under the Old were a temple of God, so the pure under the New are a temple of the same God. Again, this same herald of truth often proclaims the creator of all things. He announces both the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and his true Son no less, even in the passages where he praises the grace given to him and the power of the mystery entrusted to him. For having said, "To me, the very least of all, this grace was given: to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light for all what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God," he at once adds: "who created all things through Jesus Christ." So the Father is creator of all things, and the Son is creator of all things. For just as their nature is shared and without difference, so too are their authority and kingship, the creation of all things visible and invisible, and the bringing of things from non-being into being and existence. And a little later: "For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named." "Every family," he says: not this one but not that one, nor only every heavenly one. Whether you speak of a heavenly family or an earthly one, or of any part of them, the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is the creator of them all. For from him every family in heaven and on earth is named, as this beholder and teacher of mysteries beyond words clearly proclaims. And elsewhere, setting forth the same theology, he says: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all." For he knows that, undivided and indivisible, just as [?]

the nature and the will are, so too are the creative work and the sovereignty of the Father and of the Son. So he cries out the same things about the Saviour with a bold voice: "For in him," he says, "all things were created." Pay attention: "all things, those in the heavens and those on earth." And so that madness may not slip other nonsense into the sacred words, he goes straight on to explain what the things in the heavens and on earth are: the visible and the invisible. All of these, he says, were created in him, through him and for him. How then does the frenzy of the apostates make one maker of visible things and another of invisible ones? If all things were created through Christ and for Christ, and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together, where is the Enemy's creation? It is the Good One himself who brings things into being. Bringing them into being, he holds them together, and holding them together, he provides for their continuance. By what other activity will they give the Enemy authority over God's creatures? Only through themselves, in that they carry out the Enemy's wishes and do not shudder to fight against God. For these people open a blasphemous mouth wide against the common Master and Maker. They rise up against his lordship as creator and bow themselves down to monstrous passions. By fighting against God and by doing lawless things, they have shown themselves to be truly creatures and slaves of the Enemy. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved. When we let ourselves be dragged down willingly into the passions, we thereby fall away from the Creator's providence and from our kinship with the true Maker. We bring in the Evil One as master over ourselves, and the Adversary persuades us to sharpen our tongues against our benefactor and Maker. In the same way, if we escape the darkness of the passions and are willing to acknowledge that both soul and body are God's creatures, we at once drive the Enemy out of his tyranny over us. Then, with cleansed eyes, we see that he has neither strength nor lordship over us, but is trampled underfoot and laughed to scorn by us, he and all his power. "For you shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk," it says, "and trample the lion and the dragon." But as long as we wallow in pleasures that destroy the soul and follow the desires the Enemy pushes us toward, none of us can ever be freed from his subjection and tyranny. Nor can we be brought to our true God and Maker and illumined by the light of devotion to him, so long as we cut up with tongue and life the nature and kingdom of our good and one God and the dignity of his creation, and parcel them out into warring portions. For by splitting the one principle and

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople

tearing ourselves away from it, and by rejecting the true Maker and Master, we let the Enemy gain great dominion over us. Then, with great authority, he persuades those he has already caught bowing to his impulses to confess him as maker and master too. What could be more wretched than this? To abandon the Creator and go over to the Enemy; to flee the Saviour and run to the destroyer; to disdain the one who grants the kingdom of heaven and eagerly follow the one who drags us to the punishment prepared for him; and so, deceived, to be condemned along with the deceiver to the gehenna of unending fire.

17. But you who share our nature and our creation, even if you have fallen away from the gift, come to your senses now, late as it is. Turn your hearts to our common Master and Creator, to our benefactor and provider, to him who formed the body and breathed in the soul. Turn to him who for our sake took flesh, became man and was crucified, and who inaugurated the resurrection through his own body. Acknowledge his good Father, who through the Son and through his Holy Spirit brought all things into being out of nothing: things visible and invisible, the powers, the authorities, and the Enemy himself. God forbid that he imparted wickedness to him, for how could evil be imparted by the Good? Rather, he granted him the enjoyment of goodness, and the Enemy turned it into wickedness, just as those who now obey him do. For they too received a great good, the freedom of their own reasoning, by which they also bear the image of their Maker. They perverted it, corrupting its use to the utmost evil. The very faculty they received to praise the Creator, they used to sing the praises of the Enemy. By using it rightly they could have become heirs of the kingdom of heaven, but by misusing it they are hastening to enter the gehenna of fire prepared for the devil. Come to your senses, then; rise up, keep watch, so that the Enemy's power may be stripped away from you. Do not make yourselves the fulfilment of the apostolic prophecies, or rather the prophecies of the Spirit. For the Spirit says expressly: "In later times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose own consciences are seared, who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods which God created to be received." Foods which God created, it says, not the Enemy. And received by whom? So that no excuse for error may be left to you, he immediately adds: "by those who believe [?]

and know the truth." So everyone who believes and knows the truth knows, together with all the faithful, that all things, foods included, are creatures of the good God. But whoever ascribes any of them to another is the one of whom the Holy Spirit spoke: he has given heed to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, and is an apostate from the true faith of us Christians. Of such people the interpreter of the Spirit prophesies elsewhere too: "In the last days," he says, "difficult times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, blasphemers, disobedient to their parents." After listing the other passions that follow, he ends the prophecy: "having the outward form of godliness but denying its power. And just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these people also oppose the truth." Here he ranks the truth with Moses, and those who opposed the truth with Jannes and Jambres. If Moses and the truth stand in the same rank, and Jannes and Jambres stand with those who oppose the truth, how can the prophecy not have foretold these things against these people? For those who rave against Moses oppose the truth, and side with Jannes and Jambres and join them in blasphemy. The same lie that once incited the old apostates to raise a revolt against Moses has made the new ones bold enough to stir up tyranny against the writings of Moses and against the one who gave them as law. [?] The difference is to their discredit. For with the old apostates the evil stopped at the plotting: punishment struck before the deed, and so drew back from the attempt those who would have carried it out had it not overtaken them. But these new ones have plotted their impiety even while God's love for humanity waited for their repentance instead of taking vengeance. They are despisers, who make their earlier evil worse with a second one, and they never stop arming their tongues against the Creator of all. Through the insults they pour on the divine servant, they also insult the Master's laws which they received. Through their drunken outrages against those laws, they hurl those licentious and godless words at the lawgiver himself, the Creator of all. Such is the new and recent tyranny of the apostasy against the Creator of all. Or rather, it is a beast born of that old apostasy, like some many-shaped and monstrous brood of a viper. It has devoured the belly of the one who bore it, and it spits out even more of the venom of blasphemy against the Creator. But of these things later.

Variant readings and notes. [?] … the consideration of the matter, so as not to proceed from the lesser things to the greatest [?]. Photius. [?]

[?] Our discourse has now run quickly through the sacred sayings that plainly declared and proclaimed the good Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and his beloved Son himself, to be maker and creator of the universe, of everything found among things perceived by the senses and things perceived by the mind. It still seems right to me to go on and show more clearly who is the first teacher of this war against God, bold in purpose and using these very words. I will also show that those who did not want the King of the universe to reign over them will expressly pay its penalty. Along with the other things of sense, they tear even their own bodies away from the Maker and attach them to the Enemy. The proof of this comes from no other source than the same divinely inspired and sacred Scriptures. Hear, then, the evangelist Luke, for there is nothing like hearing him. He saw the temptation by which the one who has tripped us up from the beginning attempted, in our form, to tempt even our common Maker. He recounts it in the sacred history, and after the first temptation he goes on to the second: "And the devil," he says, "led him up to a high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world. And the devil said to him." Pay attention, O man: see where this God-fighting voice first came from, and what the loathsome firstfruit of the apostasy is. Who first dared to call earthly things the work and kingdom of the Enemy? The sower of tares, who was a murderer from the beginning. He was the first to stiffen his neck against God, and because of his boasting and arrogant mind he fell like lightning from heaven. "And the devil said to him, 'To you I will give this authority.'" See what teacher the council of wickedness enthrones, what initiator and guide! O my wretched nature, what authority I gave the Enemy against myself! The Gospels proclaim so clearly where this great evil of apostasy broke out and came from, and who began it. Yet those who have gone astray, as if they had shut their ears or lost the use of them altogether, refuse to see whose disciples they are making themselves, and whose words they are taking up and adopting as their own. "And the devil said to him: 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.'" The audacity of the lie astounds you, God-loving audience, and the sheer size of the arrogance leaves you in extraordinary amazement. What astounds me more is the zeal of the evil teacher's evil disciples, and the ways they have striven to outdo their teacher. For he, though bold, shameless, lying and brazen in everything, nevertheless claims with his tall tale to have received the kingdom on earth from another who gave it

Variant readings and notes. (73) Περιδιδούς ("recounting"): I think one should read παραδιδούς ("handing down").

[?]… For “it has been delivered to me,” he says. But he did not claim, “I brought these things into existence out of nothing.” His noble disciples, however, are more impious than their teacher. He arrogantly said that he held the kingdom of earthly things because he had received it. They alter that teaching and, outdoing it in impiety, it seems, proclaim him the creator and fashioner of earthly things. And although they dare to think and say this, they have not shuddered, and they have not wished to see into what an abyss of destruction they are sinking. But do not pass over what follows either. For he says, “If you, then, will worship before me, it shall all be yours.” So whoever believes that earthly things belong to the devil, and thinks that he receives what is in them from him, is the one who worships the devil. Whoever confesses that he receives from him what was the wage of worship could not deny the worship. And who would these people be, if not those who confess that they have their body from him, and that it is a work of his creation and of his kingdom? And not the body only, but also bread and wine and water and all the other things by which the human compound is sustained and held together, and by which people make their way through this life of the senses. For the visible creation pours forth some of these things and yields others through cultivation. They have learned from him the doctrine that visible things are creations of the devil and of his kingdom, and yet they show by their deeds that they have these things from him and live by them. Such people, however much they contrive to cheat the eyes and ears of onlookers, are plainly and beyond doubt the ones who have offered him worship. One can also find in them another madness that surpasses their teacher's. He assailed the Master with three temptations in a short time, and after being rebuked as many times, he gave up such tempting and that boastful and godless arrogance. But they have been rebuked by the same words of the Master, not three times only but ten thousand times, or rather times beyond number. (The words that rebuked the teacher and silenced him are the same words that condemned his disciples to silence.) And for all the years since their teacher's boastful, God-fighting scheme fell to them, they have been rebuked by the divine words, yet they add still more to their shamelessness and behave insolently toward the Creator. In life and in word they split his kingdom and hand it over to the Enemy, because they truly do not want the common Master to reign over them. 19. But let us see, if you will, what reward they receive for advocating for the Enemy, worshipping him and proclaiming him king, and what prize awaits those who did not want the King of the universe to reign over them. The sacred parables liken our Lord Jesus Christ, or rather he likens himself, to a nobleman, for what is nobler than divinity? To pass over the rest, they liken the human race to his citizens, since they are his creatures, since he himself dwelt as a citizen on earth, and since, by taking our flesh, he consented to become and be called our fellow-dweller and fellow-citizen. Yet he bears in himself the nobility of divinity and received from the Father a kingdom that is equal and cannot be taken away. Since he knows all things, he was not unaware of the

uprising that some of the citizens plotted against him. And they denied his kingdom and did not want him to reign over them. He is the lover of mankind, the good Child of the Father, the fount of compassion, the God of mercy, the heart of pity that is never emptied. Yet he did not tolerate such outrageous conduct from his ungrateful citizens. For what they dared was not just one of the ordinary human sins. Their madness was directed against the Fashioner, against the Creator, against the Benefactor, against the Provider, and their zeal was on behalf of the enemy who began all evil, the murderer from the beginning, the Adversary. They meant to take the kingdom away from the one and give it to the other. What, then, does he do? What penalty does the just judge exact from the rebels? Better to hear the sentence itself: “These enemies of mine,” he says, “who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.” With their eyes they disregarded the Maker and looked to the supplanter. Therefore they are required to pay the due penalty before the all-seeing, all-surveying eye of justice. “And slaughter them before me,” so that the one they refused to acknowledge as king they may acknowledge even against their will, through the reckoning demanded of them, as both king and just. “And since they made the body that I fashioned for them the work of another's hand, slaughter them. Through that body they outraged me, dividing it from my kingdom and throwing it to the Enemy. So let them be cut in two through it and pay the penalty owed for rebellion.” “Slaughter them before me.” Consider how inescapable and bitter the punishment is. Who gave the sentence? Whose is the decision? To be slaughtered by the Enemy brings some grief, but it still offers much ground for consolation. It leaves the Master as avenger, and the hope of resurrection and of the joy it brings lets one regard the slaughter as a prelude to gladness. But when the Master himself commands the slaughter, he from whom comes vengeance, from whom comes mercy, from whom comes the exultation and gladness after the resurrection, from whom comes life and salvation, what words could convey the bitterness and unbearableness of that blow, or the sharp pains for which there is no comfort? To whom will one flee for refuge? What relief can there be for a suffering that admits no end, while the punishment goes on forever? So consider these things, and having considered them, fear the blow. See the dreadful and terrifying pain in others before you come to know it yourselves, and turn away from the same madness before you meet the same punishment. For fear and remorse in the midst of suffering bring no gain. While there is time for repentance, (75) “They denied”: [?] particle.

let us show our repentance. While the door of pardon stands open, let us not be slow to enter through it. While the threats are still suspended, let us show that we have turned back. For once the signal has been given and life is undone, there is no longer any way of salvation, and no hope is left of escaping what was threatened. The Gospel words have pilloried the teacher of the rebellion clearly and without any subtlety, and they have shown very plainly and conspicuously what penalty the just judge exacts from his disciples, who do not want the Lord to reign over them. After all this, what defense will those find who still cherish the rebellion? What remnant of pardon have they left themselves? What eye will shed a tear of pity for them? They have learned from the Gospels that their teacher is the devil, and that the disciples before them were slaughtered before the Master for not wanting him to reign over them. The venerable Gospels of our Saviour teach this loudly, and the same sacred oracles have cried out that those who split the kingdom of God are worshippers of the devil and insulters of the Creator. So if none of these things turns them away from the rebellion, what remains is the unending fire and the outer darkness that has been prepared for their teacher. That will turn them away from their war against God, against their will and with no benefit to them. [?] on the readiness of the discussion and the discourse.

By the same author, against the newly sprung error of the Manichaeans, to Arsenius, [?] monk, priest and abbot of the holy [?]. 1. Since, most beloved of holy men, the offshoots of Mani consented to hold discussions [?], they put their own way of thinking to shame. Long ago they held conversations with Nicephorus, who was not yet known by that name. He did not yet embrace the faith that has conquered the world. He was still wallowing in the remnants of the apostasy and bore a name taken from it, for he was called Berzelis. Since, then, you sought those discussions, which had been taken down

in writing, and since the plundering of my books has inflicted on them too the loss of exile, the little treatise is no longer at hand. Yet you are pressed above all by the need for its contents, namely the arguments by which, through the words of the Gospels and the apostles, it cuts out the growth of the Manichaean offshoot by the roots. (More than the others, these arguments bring the inescapable sickle of excision down upon them.) To put it summarily, these arguments show the following. Grace speaks in harmony with the Mosaic account of creation, and with all the other things by which a people newly established in the knowledge of God was trained and directed. Indeed, the one who brought the bodily and visible creation into existence out of nothing by a word is the same one who produced the intellectual and invisible creation with a like wealth of wisdom. The human body too belongs to the same benevolent and beneficent providence, just as the soul is its masterpiece. And those who excelled under the polity of the Law served the true and good God and stood in battle array against wickedness. These things, then, so far as we are able and the heaviness of the times permits, we have set down for publication and sent to your holiness, for in these, I think, your request is also contained. If you find them as you hoped, that will be the effect of your prayer and of the request you made in faith. But if the unexpected defeats your hopes, put it down to the constant illnesses that never stop troubling this poor body of ours, and to the harshness of the times. If at some point divine providence overlooks our sins, disposes our affairs more kindly and softens the human, groundless anger into gentleness, the work you originally requested may come into your hands. Do not be surprised, as you read it, if most of what is in it is included here as well. Be surprised, on the contrary, if anything has been left out. For forgetfulness has often prevailed even over things one knew better and things that were necessary, especially when present circumstances join forces with it. At the same time, do not overlook this either: we are not producing a different work. In our straitened circumstances we are providing, for ourselves and our friends, a consolation for what has been lost and a remedy for forgetfulness. 16 [?]. The opening of our battle against our adversaries is the Master's own works and words. There is no better general for us to follow, no surer way to strike the enemy, and no more fearful or wretched way for them to fall. See, then,

how from the very first engagement the King of all, our Saviour and general, tears up the enemies' palisade from its very foundations and overturns it. He throws their thinking into confusion and scatters the boldness of the rebels. What plan does he devise? What art does he set in motion? Nothing contrived, and nothing that proceeds through struggles and labours. He merely utters a sound, and everything the enemy has vanishes. “For every kingdom,” he says, “divided against itself is laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.” You see how the mere sound of the royal trumpet wrecked and laid waste the enemies' entrenchment. But why do I say entrenchment? It destroyed the city too, and the very palace of the rebellion, which they fashioned and fortified with their most impious and misguided notions. A kingdom divided against itself does not stand but quickly collapses upon itself and vanishes. The rule and kingdom that created all things, however, endures forever, and not even the rebellion itself would dare to deny this. For time, which brings innovation to all things, has never yet shown anyone raving to such a pitch of madness. If, then, the rule of the Good is beyond all dissolution, as is evident to all, it is even more evident that they have chosen the madness of insulting the kingdom of the common and good Master. With their audacities they tear apart its wholeness and set up an evil principle and fix it alongside, but the kingdom they raise against it they fashion and dissolve at one and the same time. For the kingdom of the Good is kept undivided, since division is a road to dissolution. The indissoluble rejects division, and before this attempt the Master declared that what is divided will be dissolved. And creation, from the moment it was brought forth and through so many ages, has been granted to prevail over dissolution, at least as regards its wholeness. It is plain to see that earthly things are bound up and held together with heavenly ones, and that intellectual and intelligible things are not separated, through uninterrupted providence, from bodily things discerned by the senses, but are joined to them in a most evident union. Moreover, man himself, a rational living being, is composed of visible and invisible parts fitted together. The creation and kingdom of the good God, then, does not admit [?] division. But in the kingdom they fabricate, they tear off with their tongue some portion of the whole creation, promote it with words of rebellion and set the Enemy up to reign in it. How could such a kingdom attain stability of itself? How could it stand, when it received its very origin from division and dissolution, and came forth and flowed off from cutting and severance, which bring even what is whole to ruin, even if it were not the fabrication of a blasphemous tongue? And how could it not be otherwise than the rule of the Good,

which is held together by its indissolubility, and as it advances endures all the more and changes, rising toward what is better [?]? The kingdom that the madness of the blasphemers newly invents has dreamed up its existence only on their blasphemous lips. It will sink into oblivion faster than it came forth, and will depart leaving its lovers nothing but laughter and mockery. In this way it exacts a penalty from them for their fabricated and baseless proclamation, by which they vainly, or rather impiously and godlessly, attached to it the name of kingdom, though it would not even be granted the rank of a handmaid. This is how the almighty, commanding rule that holds sway over all others knows how to overthrow the [?] of the enemies. This is how it strips the shield-bearers and bodyguards and pillories and makes an example of those whose contest it was. And by a single word it displays its invincible might. The rebels, then, see these things overturned, unable to hold out even against the sound of the royal trumpet: neither these things nor the kingdom they fashioned for themselves in their eagerness for innovation. Since everything has come to desolation for them, they ought no longer to keep up the quarrel, nor turn back to the tyrant once the tyranny has vanished. They ought to recognize the common Master and run to his kingdom. Through genuine conversion and fervent repentance, they ought to confess that they are the work of his hand, his creature and handiwork, steered and governed by his providence and love for mankind. And they ought to hate the Enemy and turn away from him completely, leaving him no authority, not even a way in, in anything they do in life. 3. But perhaps the deep darkness of rebellion that has overpowered them has so dimmed their minds that, even with the tyranny already dissolved and vanished, they still do not come to their senses and renounce it, but brashly choose to be ranked under it rather than under the kingdom of the Good. Come, then, let us show how the King of all punishes those who deny his kingdom. He does not stop at overthrowing their rule, destroying it and despoiling them. After much long-suffering and forbearance, he sends slaughter upon those who are incurable. Perhaps, seeing this brought upon them, they may gain some sense of their audacity. Then they may no longer think or say that they do not want him to reign over them, or that they do not want the Creator and King of the universe to rule over their bodies or over the rest of visible creation. For see how severely and vehemently the one who is by nature a lover of mankind brings the punishing sentence against them: “These enemies of mine,” he says, “who did not want me to (87) “Of the kingdom”: I think we should read “of the queen” [basilidos], which [?]

reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.” What do you say? Do you shudder at the sentence and flee the slaughter? Will you stop dividing the kingdom of the good God? Do you look toward conversion, so as to confess the Master's rule as whole and to ascribe to it lordship over both bodies and soul? Or will you keep up the quarrel until you suffer what is most wretched to suffer, a fate so harsh that no word can express it? For he does not only kill, nor only take away the present life. After killing, he sends both soul and body to be punished in an unending and unceasing Gehenna of fire. But I shall set many more things before you, taken from the same benevolent and almighty tongue. You may choose arrows that wound and destroy so impious a mind in many ways and many places, or saving remedies and cures for the disease, if indeed a longing for health has come over you in place of lying there wounded. And I will join you in the struggle for deliverance from the disease. 4. John proclaimed Christ when he did not yet share in grace but was still being tutored by the Law. He proclaimed him and spoke of him as God, testifying to all that he takes away the sin of the world. With a free voice he taught that he is the Son of God, who baptizes with fire and with the Holy Spirit, that is, who recasts and renews our fallen nature by the fiery and burning power of the Spirit. He also proclaimed the Father and spoke of him as God, as one who has unhindered power to raise up children for Abraham from stones. He proclaimed the Spirit too. He saw the Spirit come forth from heaven, come upon the only-begotten Son of God and remain on him as consubstantial with him. And, what is still more theological, he confesses the Spirit as partner in the work through which the salvation of the world was announced. He ascribes the salvation of humankind to them in common, since the Son takes away the sin of the world, while the world is cleansed and scoured by the all-holy Spirit. For he cried out plainly that the world, which receives freedom from sin and is counted worthy of salvation, enjoys so great a benefit by being baptized with the all-holy Spirit and then with fire. From this one may learn the fire-bearing, effective and purifying power of the Spirit. When the work of several is common and undivided, and that work is the renewal and refashioning of the world, how can they not share the same nature, the same power, the same love for mankind and providence? Thus, consuming the refuse in us from the very [?], melting away the filth of sin, and cooling toward [?]

[?] …from the very outset speaking of the Trinity in the language of theology, and announcing at the threshold of the preaching that awesome and venerable teaching of theology which the Saviour handed down more plainly to his disciples after the resurrection, would it seem to you that he was inspired from some other source to say and proclaim these things? Or that the law is out of harmony with grace? Or that God, who raises up children to Abraham from stones, was not the same who made plain to all that the Saviour of the world is his own beloved Son? But if the heralds of grace within the law, and God the lawgiver who ordained the whole Old Testament, proclaimed the good God and Redeemer of the world to be his own Son, and that at the very moment he was being baptized in the water, how are not all the things in the law and all the things in grace works and ordinances of one and the same providence, creation and goodness? 5. Consider also the praises with which the Saviour crowns John. He judges him superior to riches, set above all earthly glory, firm in his judgment concerning the faith, and in short unshakable in his resolve toward everything good. Having proclaimed him with these praises, see how he lifts the man still higher: he declares that no one among those born of women is his equal, but that he holds precedence over all. Then, having exalted him so far in virtue, he calls him a prophet, and more than a prophet. A prophet, to show that the name and office of the prophets belong to such works and dignities, which are gifts of goodness. More than a prophet, because, having received the same grace as they to foresee what was to come, he gained besides the privilege of seeing the one who was prophesied, and of being found worthy to baptize with water the one who baptizes the world with fire and the Holy Spirit and cleanses it of sins. Does grace, then, fight against the law? Or is there not great harmony and close connection between them? If John belonged to another principle, how could the lawgiver of grace have borne him such testimony, testimony that can be found for few, and those the elect among the people of grace who have achieved such things? And how could he, the good Son of a good Father and the fountain of goodness, have endured to bow his spotless head beneath the hand and voice of the law, which the apostates of the Adversary dare to call the Adversary's work and command, and to undergo baptism in water (O tongue that pours out the venom of asps!), if water were not the creation of the Good One? 6. But why do I not speak of what is greater still? It is something that the speaker can hardly utter without shuddering; it strikes most forcefully and cuts most deeply against those among whom error dances; and, so far as words can say, it is most necessary to say and most worthy of reverence. The good Son of the Good One was born from virginal loins for the salvation of the world; fashioning for himself our flesh from the spotless blood, he became man. And this, by those of old

among the impious, was struck out; but by those who sprang from them, who somehow love to deny it in deed, it is not deprived of honour in words. For one can see them speaking with great solemnity, both when they insist that they honour the Gospel Scriptures, and when they falsely claim the Apostle Paul, the God-bearer, as the author and teacher of their own way of thinking. Now our Lord Jesus Christ took flesh. The Son of Thunder cried aloud: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us"; and another of the evangelists records that the birth of Jesus Christ was from the Holy Spirit, and that the Virgin bore her firstborn Son and called his name Jesus. And the one who belongs to the same choir and company as these not only announces his incomprehensible birth, but also describes in detail the ineffable manner of his conception that preceded it; how the Virgin, when she had borne her firstborn Son, wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in the manger; and how the host of angels sang that a Saviour, Christ the Lord, had been born to the world in the city of David. Besides this (and it muzzles and shames still more those who make the mystery a mere phantom and reduce grace to nonsense, and after them their offshoot, against whom this discourse has been set in motion), striking them down and overthrowing them, he teaches that our Saviour, once born, underwent the circumcision of the flesh according to the law, and at the same time he records that he received the name Jesus, in this too fulfilling the commandments of Moses. Since, then, the embodiment, the incarnation and the becoming-man of the Word is so entirely manifest (up to this point our discourse has flowed along smoothly, with pleasure and grace; from here on dizziness and fear beset it. Still, I must say, even in anguish, what the refutation of error will not let me pass over), which will it be, you who dare what should not be dared: will you assign this very body of the Lord to the evil principle, or will you shrink from the enormity of that impiety? If trembling grips you too and fear has seized you, you will certainly remove it from the evil fashioning and principle, or rather from your own blasphemy, and you will show great zeal in ridding yourself of this audacity. But if you have hardened yourself to set your opinion against the wrath of God, against the judgment and condemnation of your own thoughts, and against shame before men, tell me: how was the Evil joined to the Good? How did the good God consent to accomplish the salvation of the world through the Evil? And, more astonishing and more dreadful still, how does it sit together on the Father's throne? For this is what the

initiate and guide into the ineffable mysteries taught. Either, then, you will adopt the denial of all these things: that the Word was not made flesh, did not come forth into the world by being born, did not save our race, did not seat the body he assumed together with himself on the Father's throne; or, if you do not deny these things, it remains for you to deny the goodness of God, outraging it and turning it into evil by that union, and indeed also to turn that evil into goodness, since not even [?] is left to you. And if you are set on fighting God at all costs, the choice of the former impieties would be lighter for you than that of the latter. For there was once a time when those who did not know the former things, and did not honour them because they had not yet come, were not made to pay for even one impiety. But to drag the goodness of God down to evil, or to dignify evil with a share in goodness: there is no age that does not exact an inexorable punishment from those who choose this. 7. While audacity and impiety surround their lovers on every side with such great evils, these people, far from recovering from their error, as though afraid of growing weary of fighting God, subject the nature of the Good One to a second profanation as well. For they hang the older of his covenants, and those who lived nobly under it, upon the authority and service of the evil principle. Since David and Abraham, from whom Christ came according to the flesh, belonged to that same company, it is clear that they brand the Master of all with a double profanation: first, in declaring that he took a body of evil creation; second, in that he took it not from some other race, but from those whose very life was the worship according to the law which they insult. Yet if it is the work of evil, how could it be necessary for the Good to assume it? What extreme of absurdity is left for one entangled in a twofold charge? To save his own creature, which had slipped into sin, by assuming it, was the work of the highest providence and goodness. But to take upon himself what is alien, and alien on two counts, set against him by nature, how does that not turn the dignity of his providence and goodness into its opposite? So there is nothing, absolutely nothing, more insane than those who say that the body, or the legislation of Moses, belongs to the Evil One; nothing more foul, nothing more godless. Besides, if bodies belong to the opposing fashioning and not to the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the one Godhead and authority, how could the good God drive out the diseases of bodies that are alien and wicked, being works of the Wicked One, and bring in wondrous cures in their place? That would be nothing but to strengthen the work of the one whose tyranny he came to overthrow, and to increase the power of the one who launched the rebellion from the beginning. Moreover, if the growths of the earth do not belong to the principle of goodness,

how did he himself partake of such bread, leavened from alien seed, and [?] wine [?], when he was perfectly able to prepare food for himself out of nothing? He even multiplied these loaves and fed thousands, taking the creation of the Evil One as the material for his miracle and making the Adversary a partner in his supernatural kindness, as if he could not have fed himself, and those who devoted themselves to his words and were formed by them, from some other material brought into being by his own power. And if those who lived under the law and kept it were not servants of the beneficent Godhead, how is it that, when his disciples were accused for nothing by the Pharisees, who strain out gnats but swallow camels, because in their hunger they plucked and ate ears of grain on the Sabbath to relieve the need of their bodies, he showed them to be above the charge and acquitted them? He put forward David as their advocate and support, and the priests who divide the meat and chop the wood on the Sabbath, and that in the sacred service itself, where the law ought most of all to be kept, while the work goes on. 8. What clearer or stronger proof could there be that the Evil One is master of nothing on earth than those words of his by which he claimed creation for himself? Approaching to tempt the Creator and Master of all, who was hidden and unrecognized, and showing him all the kingdoms of the earth and their glory, he said: "All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me." Now if he is a liar and has never stood in the truth (for this is what the Truth in person taught us), and if there is no one at all among those who confess Christ who would dare to strike out such a saying, how is it not plainer than anything that the maker of falsehood rules none of the creatures of the earth, nor is he their maker? He is maker only of those wills and actions which he himself sows, and of those people whose thoughts he has reshaped so that they inscribe him as their creator and maker; not because he brought their soul or body out of nothing, but because they were led astray into inscribing him as their lord. So the very thing that some of those in error seize upon to establish their impiety, that the Evil One rules earthly things, has been turned against them to prove that he has no share in ruling them. For it was he, a liar and the author of lies, who declared that he had rule over earthly things. And if bodies belong to the Evil One, how will the disciples be the salt of the earth? How will they be the light of the world? They will salt and enlighten only by halves, or rather not even by halves. For these halves again belong to the human compound, and in no way to the whole man [?]. The creature of the Evil One is incapable of being salted so as not to sink into some rot of wickedness, since it is by nature wholly such rot.

It is also unfit to receive the flashing rays of light; all the more since the error further implies that those appointed to accomplish these things have no power to do so, being subject to the same charges. When the Saviour himself cries out clearly, "I did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfil them," how is the shameless mind of the impious not afraid to say that the law and the prophets came forth from an evil principle and served it all their lives? For if our Saviour is the one who fulfils the law and the prophets, then (may the blasphemy that follows fall back on their own heads) one of two things must hold: either they transform the evil principle into the nature of the good, or else, leaving it within its own bounds of wickedness, they condemn him to have become its willing servant, he who out of his great goodness came to overthrow the tyranny of the passions among men. And the saying, "Truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke, will pass from the law until all has come to pass": what greater confirmation could it leave anyone? How does it not trumpet the overthrow of error and stop the unbarred mouths of the impious, even if they still contentiously mutter under their breath that the law and the prophets belong to the Evil One? 9. When you hear the evangelist tracing the ineffable coming of Jesus Christ the Son of God, and his deeds that surpass reason, from their very beginning back to the prophets, how are you not seized with shame and repentance for having been carried away into insulting those whom the sacred Oracles record as the heralds and revealers of so great a mystery of love for mankind, and whose prophecies are the foundations of the Gospel? For "The beginning," it says, "of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in the prophets: Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you." Who sent someone to prepare the way of the good Son and God, if not the good Father, who through his servants under the law foretold for many ages the self-emptying of the Son that would go even to flesh and blood? And at the end of the ages he sent his messenger John, saying: "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." And the water into which the loving Jesus went down and fulfilled all righteousness: how would he have endured to touch it at all, let alone be baptized wholly in it,

and to impart to it cleansing power and sanctifying grace, if it was not his own creation but the creation of the opposing one? He granted that this grace should well up not only while he was present in the body; he also graced those being saved in all the ages that followed to find through it, by the working of the all-holy Spirit, refashioning and rebirth, so that the gift of grace accompanies it undying. Again, John, who was found worthy of the manifestation of the good God and was proclaimed by Truth itself more than a prophet and greater than those born of women, how could he have undertaken to champion a commandment of the law, and that when he had been sent as the forerunner of grace? Yet he not only took up the struggle eagerly on behalf of the law, which was already passing away, so well did he know it to be a gift of God, but went so far as to place his own life second to its defence. When he rebuked Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife," where did he get the grounds for his rebuke, or which legislation was he defending when he brought the reproof to the king? Do you not see how far the forerunner of grace, who was found worthy to baptize the lawgiver of grace, was from insulting the commandments of the law? If the precepts of Moses did not come from the same divine and beneficent inspiration, how could this same servant of grace refuse to tolerate even their neglect, and be instead their fervent zealot and ardent avenger? All the more since the Saviour cried aloud: "No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon." And indeed, if the law and grace belong to two opposing lords, and not to the one goodness and sole rule, how was he, than whom no one among men is greater, found serving two lords, as their godless prattle would have it? The same holds for the assembly of the prophets before him. As for the fact that the Saviour himself, having become man, fulfilled the Father's will, and that he did not come to abolish the law or the prophets but to fulfil them, the godlessness here is so extreme that I could not bring myself to set it out more plainly. 10. Nevertheless, I will now state, second after that, the unspeakable thing, so far as is possible and so far as I can avoid wholly gratifying the enemies. John, serving both the discernment of the law and grace, and indeed the company of the prophets before him, pillory the impious with inescapable proofs: they traduce the Truth in person as falsehood, and they split the commandments between warring lawgivers by slandering the former ones; and even if they have not yet dared to do it bare-headed, they are caught no less (for what that is not wicked could come from falsehood?) making sport of grace as well. For if the good Master is the lawgiver of grace, and one of his teachings is that no one can serve two masters,

and the men mentioned above served in both portions, while the apostasy sets another Lord over the things of Moses, how, in insulting the law, even if behind intervening curtains, do they not insult grace along with it? For in this way (though it is unbearable to say even in refuting impiety, it is nonetheless more tolerable) they would be declaring it a covenant of falsehood. But what might someone object? "Why, then, do we who belong to grace not now live according to the law?" For your sake, no answer is required. For if some difficulty still perplexes you in your impiety, and I should choose not to resolve it, will you be any less impious? Will you profit from your outrage against the goodness that cannot be outraged, or get off more lightly? And yet the very difficulty that is raised refutes the apostasy no less; so does the might of truth flash out on every side, even through its opposites. For if the law is brought under suspicion of not agreeing with goodness because it is not practised by those under grace, how great a share in goodness is it not proclaimed to have by the fact that the good God came not to abolish the law or the prophets but to fulfil them? Against the apostates nothing more needs to be added. But for the sake of the devout, who are not unworthy to be initiated into the things of grace and to initiate others, it is easy and clear to say that the reason we do not live by the ancient laws is that Christ came and fulfilled all things. He gave grace in place of the grace that came through Moses, and in place of the holy things in the sanctuary, which were antitypes, he gave the very things they prefigured, the Holy of Holies: of the one Paul cried out, and of the other John, each speaking as a theologian. So it is rather now that anyone who lived by those laws would be convicted of daring to deny that Christ, the fulfiller of the law, has fulfilled all things. But we must return to the point from which the current of the discourse, following its natural sequence, carried us aside. The lawgiver of grace commands us to revere heaven and earth and Jerusalem, and even the very hairs of our head, so much so that we are not to make them the subject of an oath. He proclaims heaven the throne of God and the earth his footstool, and again Jerusalem the city of the same God, the great King. If, then, these belong to the creation of the good Father, as the Son, who knows all that is the Father's, has affirmed, how are the apostates, who attach their creation to the evil principle, not caught raving, even before their outrage against the creatures, against our Lord Jesus Christ himself and against his Father? VARIANT READINGS AND NOTES. (96) "They would be declaring." The manuscript punctuated thus: "declaring it a covenant. Well then." But more correctly [?]

11. But look at their impiety going deeper still, and at its daring and madness. When the Saviour was initiating us into the mystical prayer and handing it down to us, he himself commanded us to ask his Father for "our daily bread." They, however, refer the bread to the destructive principle, just as they refer everything on earth to it, and they tell monstrous tales about it nourishing the bodies brought forth from that principle. So they shamelessly rise up against the Lord's own commandment, calling bodies evil and food evil. Yet the Master expressly instructs us to ask the good Father for this food. How could they ever confess the true commandment? How could they even accept [?] it in the form of a myth? For to beg to be delivered from the Evil One while seeking from the Good to receive the Evil One as an indweller comes to the same thing, if food is indeed the Evil One's crop. And at the end of the prayer, as though refuting this very impiety in advance, he who came for the salvation of our race decreed that the plea for deliverance from the Evil One should be addressed to the same one to whom the request for food is addressed. In this way he showed that the one who delivers us from the Evil One is himself the one who also provides our bodily food. After these petitions the only-begotten Son of the Father who grants these things taught that the kingdom and the power and the glory are and will abide forever. Do you see to what depth the apostasy sinks? And do you see how the word of truth, living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, is let loose against it? Someone may say that the daily bread is not simply the bread supplied as food for the body, but the bread that is changed into the body of Christ and sanctifies the soul together with the body. Under that interpretation the impiety is exposed no less, if not more, and the word brings down on it a merciless cutting-off. 12. One cannot serve two masters. Yet the impiety would have it that our human compound is a creature of the Evil One, and so is subject to him even against its will and serves him as a thing moulded serves the one who moulded it. If so, no one could serve God purely and wholly. For them the divine proclamations are turned into nonsense, and so (what an absurd mind!) are the awesome coming and incarnation and everything the Master willingly underwent and accepted for our salvation. But you, regarding the food of human

bodies, have become wicked and ungrateful toward your benefactor, and you lay it down as dogma that this food is the crop of wickedness. The Saviour and Creator of all, however, shows that his heavenly Father and God, whose kingdom he bids us seek before all bodily things, supplies and provides not only human food but also the food of the birds. How could all right reason fail to vote that a penalty for the utmost madness should be paid by those who exchange the Lord's saving oracles for their own barking? These oracles expressly proclaim that our Father in heaven knows what we need. We were taught to lift our prayer to him, crying out, "Our Father who art in heaven." The oracles also proclaim that when we seek his kingdom and his righteousness he provides not only food but everything else by which the body is cared for. This includes not only what necessarily serves human need but also what ranks second or even last, and he is the cause of the natural clothing and growth of these things as well. "Consider," he says, "the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin." And not only these, but simply the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. For he says: "If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?" And how great and splendid are these natural garments with which the good Master clothed the grass! They push into second place the royal robe, the highest achievement of human ingenuity, flashing with purple. "For I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of these." Why, then, does the good God clothe the grass with its covering, while for the covering that the human soul puts on, I mean the body, you seek another creator and not the same one? And how do you not show yourself liable to a punishment far harsher than that of the grass thrown into the oven? The Saviour promises that to those who seek God's righteousness and kingdom through their works, he himself, whose kingdom it is, will supply food and clothing and everything else that holds the body together. But you hand these gifts of his generosity and goodness over to a stranger. How could he record himself as the provider of things he did not bring forth, things that are the works of another principle? And, more absurd still, would he supply and pay back the creations of the Evil One to the athletes of virtue who long for his kingdom, as a reward for their God-loving zeal and their countless contests? 13. That the law agrees with grace, however, is confirmed by each through the other. Grace is confirmed by the law because the law prefigured and foretold it

and sketched it in advance, as it were, revealing and pointing to it in its shadows. The law is confirmed by grace because through grace its predictions and sketches came to fulfilment in deeds, and grace unveils and proclaims the truth that lay hidden in the law under its veils. If grace and what came before grace had not kept their harmony with one another, how could everything declared by the law and the prophets have been seen being fulfilled before the eyes of all? And how could our Saviour, after cleansing the lepers by a word, send them to the priests under the law, commanding them to go and show themselves to them as the law ordered? Stronger still, he commanded them to offer the gift as Moses prescribed. And if the old is at war with the new, how does the Saviour himself gather from east and west those who fulfilled the Lord's commandments and lived under grace, and bring them into the kingdom of heaven and set them beside Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, who pleased God according to the law? This is the same as saying that he makes those of both covenants his joint heirs, sharing together in the promised and eternal goods. 14. Can anything be found more insane than the voice that speaks such things, or more godless than the mind that conceives them? They split grace and the law entirely into opposing camps. They say that those who excelled in each way of life did not serve the same good God, but were torn apart by opposing principles and advanced against one another in warring worship. Again, the one who brought in grace cites the commandments of Moses, one of which lays down: "Honour your father and your mother." Indeed, he goes further and demands that they be upheld, and he declares these to be commandments of God. By quoting it he lays bare and exposes the deceit hidden in the heart and the hypocrisy of the Jews: although this commandment stood among the divine ordinances, they put their own commandments ahead of the one God had given. Yet how much lighter a fault it would be to cling to human precepts than to those the author of evil set up [?]! He directs a severe rebuke at those who took offence without good reason, declaring that nothing that has to do with food and drink makes a person common or profane. And see how the divine verdict is pronounced not only against them but just as much against you yourselves. Against them, it rebukes the insult they offered to foods that in themselves bring no harm. Against you, it refutes and cuts off in advance the blasphemy that carried you away into saying and thinking that these foods belong to wickedness. For if (Note 4: πληρωτάς — so I read in place of πληρω[?] ... ὑμῶν [?].)

the seeds and shoots that grow from the earth, and whatever has been allotted an irrational nature, belong to the creation of the author of evil, how could they fail to profane and defile those who partake of them and are nourished by them? How could they fail to fill them with a double, or rather a manifold and unceasing, wickedness? On the one hand they would increase, hold fast and sustain the wickedness that has lurked in human bodies from birth. On the other hand they would foster the vice innate in those bodies and draw it on. But if the Mosaic laws were not the work of beneficent providence, how could the Lord of the kingdom of heaven have loved the scribe who agreed with them and accepted the first and second commandments of the law? How could he have welcomed him with praise, both because he wisely gave these commandments first place and because he was seen honouring and embracing them? And what is greater for their praise, and shows that the commandments given through Moses came forth from goodness: he declared that the man who had lived by them and knew their worth was not far from the kingdom of heaven. Then there are Zechariah and Elizabeth, who ordered their life by the law. One can see how the sacred account proclaims them righteous, and not merely righteous: their righteousness is openly declared to be before God. This teaches that their righteousness did not come from human opinion; by divine judgment they clothed themselves with it as an adornment. And what were they doing to have this grace adorning them? "Walking blameless," it says, "in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord." When the sacred oracles record that those who practise the Mosaic commandments are righteous and blameless by divine judgment, and you dare to insult them as servants of wickedness, how are you not, among your other falsehoods, also belying the very name of Christ that you bear? How are you not rising up against grace itself no less than against the law, if not more, and moving your blasphemous lips, while pretending with your tongue to worship grace and to hold it in reverence? Consider Gabriel's being sent from God; the sanctification of the virgin womb that knew no seed; David's being proclaimed father of God, the good Creator of all things; the King of all being entrusted with David's royal throne forever; and, in short, the good Son of the good Father taking flesh and being called man. (Here too I must pass over the matter under the law of silence, for an exact refutation brings with it a blasphemy that the ears cannot bear.) How do these things not overthrow all the daring and madness of the apostates who belong to the worse portion? Why need I state the more awesome consequence? Even unspoken, it makes itself understood above all, especially since it has been stated before. These men have been carried away into such drunkenness and hardness of mind that they disparage and condemn those devoted to the worship of the law. Even if piety had put forward nothing else against impiety, this awesome fact alone would have been enough: I mean the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, his taking flesh from the seed of David, and his

Against the Manichaeans, Book IV. coming forth into flesh from virginal blood, compacted by the overshadowing of the all-holy Spirit, and his becoming wholly man. If you wish, add the succession to David's kingdom, which fell to the King of all as an inheritance from his forefather, and whatever else the mystery contains. These things would have been enough, even without any further argument or addition, for two purposes. First, they could bring about some conversion and return to sobriety from their God-fighting opinion in those who have not entirely betrayed the gift of mind that the Fashioner bestowed with his right hand when he formed it. Second, in those who have completely quenched that gift through the things by which they fight God and have betrayed it to the enemy, they could check their boldness and drive them into silence out of sheer helplessness, even against their will. For what is more brilliant than this for refuting such impiety? What is more powerful for binding their jaws with bit and bridle and for displaying the multitude of scourges to which they have made themselves liable by going far from the truth and refusing any longer to draw near to God? It is not easy to bring forward everything that exposes their madness. Even so, it is perhaps neither superfluous nor useless to go on through the pertinent points. For the fullness of God's Church will take pride, if in nothing else, at least in the wealth and abundance of its proofs against the apostasy. 15. The hymn of the angels at the birth joined heaven and earth into one harmony and concord, and so it referred the whole sensible creation to one maker, bringing up together with its extremes everything that lies between them. It also announced the good news that the city of David had found the beginning of everlasting joy, since an inexpressible peace and divine good pleasure had gained the freedom to dwell throughout the whole earth. But these men have driven God's peace and good pleasure away from themselves by the absurdities with which they have filled their souls. It is fitting, then, that they have also fallen into the impiety of refusing to confess that their own Maker, who sent the angels to sing and accepted their hymn, is the same Maker of heaven and earth. These things, I think, fall within the first signs of the mystery. Consider now what comes next. There is Simeon, who lived under the law; the Holy Spirit that was upon him and the revelation given through him; and the old man's presence in the temple of the law, which itself did not happen without the all-holy Spirit. There is our Saviour, the fountain of goodness, submitting to the law; and not only submitting, but being escorted in arms that cherished the worship of the law. There is the temple itself. And there is Simeon again, who had reached the goal of his hopes and had seen the greater part of the revelation and what remained of it. He blessed God, who had revealed to him that he would see the ineffable, and who did not disappoint his hope but counted him worthy to behold with his own eyes the salvation of all the nations and the glory of Israel, which is our Saviour Jesus Christ himself. Do not let these words pass your ears carelessly. It was the Holy Spirit that was in the old man, sir, and not the Evil One. Through that Spirit also came the revelation (Note 6: Χρηματισμός — so I have written in place of χρηματισμόν, which) to a man

who lived by the law. According to the law the Saviour is brought up into the temple, and according to the law he is carried in arms. The man is not hostile to God [?] or given over to the worse principle. He is borne by God on two counts: the Holy Spirit was upon him, and he carried Christ in his hands. And he cries out that the salvation of all the nations and also the glory of Israel are not two different persons, but one and the same, our Lord Jesus Christ, the mediator and creator. For everything belonging to the old covenant and to grace belongs to his Father. Even if these points rank below the ones already given, they do not take second place when it comes to striking the God-fighters with refutations. For where do they leave any opening at all for blasphemy against the law, or against those under the law, or against the temple of the law? But why did I speak of blasphemy? What honour and glory do they fail to bestow, as far as these can be shared by those who share in grace, are bound up with it and agree with it? Then there is the prophetess Anna, whose life was prayer and [?]. To put it all in a word, there is the worship of the law. If that worship too did not come from the beneficent hand and providence, and if she did not draw from that source the inspiration for the life she lived and gloried in, how could she have given thanks to the Lord and spoken of the good God, saying that this child would be redemption for those in Jerusalem who were waiting for him? Did those who expected Christ to come for their salvation serve the evil principle while directing their hopes toward the good one? Who in command of his reason would not loathe such reasoning and judge it the height of error? [?] supposing him to be with them, with some of their relatives, since the search showed them (Note 7: εἷκεν: I think we should read εἷλκεν, from ἕλκω. So, shortly afterwards in §16, our author writes: "but how did they draw their inspiration from an evil working?")

that he was not with them, they quickly turn back, continuing the same search, to the temple. There they find him doing what it was fitting for the salvation of the world and the glory of Israel to do, just as the word had foretold. Then his Mother says to him: "Child, why have you treated us like this? Your father and I have been searching for you in anguish." Pay attention. Or rather, there is no need to gather one's thoughts, since everything is so clear and plain to see. For the fountain of truth and goodness answers them: "Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" What could be clearer than this, or more able to stop the mouths of the impious? It is as though he said: "He is truly my Father, to whom the temple is consecrated, and all that is the Father's is mine. So there was no need to search elsewhere, when you could find me among the things of my Father." The Truth testifies with a clear voice that the temple of the law and the doctrines of the law, which were being taught and discussed there, belong to his Father. But the servants of falsehood do not shudder to contradict him. They dare two extremes at once. They thrust the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ away from his own legislation and lordship. And these thrice-accursed men also take it upon themselves to set aside the testimony of the Son, whom they too do not refuse to call Saviour and Truth, even if only with the tips of their lips. Thus the abuse heaped on the law also heaps abuse on the very lawgiver of grace. Or rather, from the beginning the apostates conceived [?] the blasphemy against those who established both covenants. These men, bold in everything else, then shrank from coming to the deadly birth all at once for fear of their hearers. Yet instead of handing over to destruction the serpent's seed they had conceived, they only put off the birth for a short time, and then by a roundabout route and a contrivance they give birth through their tongue to the venom they had conceived just the same. For they pour out the venom against the legislation, and from their drunken outrage against the legislations they run back again and assault those who laid down the laws, no less fiercely, if not more. By holding back the all-out attack out of fear, they are convicted of knowing full well how great their audacity is. By not desisting even though they recognize it, they make their offence wholly unpardonable. 17. One can see the disciples of the truth, and our Lord Jesus Christ himself, mentioning Nazareth not casually or just once, but again and again, and calling it his homeland. They show no caution either toward those people or toward the earthly creation itself. And yet how much did [?] require him to acknowledge it as the beginning of his birth? But if this were the work of the destructive hand, would he, the good Child of the good [?], have endured to call this his homeland? (Luke 2:48. Ibid. 49.
