[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople] …to write, or even allowed his disciples to venture, what, if anyone else had brazenly dared to say it, it would be just to punish him and to drive him back from his audacity with great indignation. In this way, then, through the Lord's homeland the revolt against our common homeland, or rather against the whole creation, is brought down and overthrown. And if there is a good man, and there is also a wicked one, of whom the one brings forth what is good out of the good treasure of his heart, and the other what is evil out of the evil, who would not agree that the original fashioning of the body, like the soul that was given to be joined to it and to govern it, is not to be traced back to an opposing principle? Rather, it is free will which, by taking an inclination toward what it ought not, itself through that inclination changes goodness into evil. For what other explanation could there be for some men being good, while others are seen to have inclined toward evil, as you also have, would that it were not so? For the wickedness of your deeds and doctrines, which springs from your own will, has split you off from the flock of the good, having first split you off from a choice conformed to the good. Therefore some are heralds of the Creator's goodness, who both acknowledge and glorify their own Maker, while others, dragging him down to slander both by their practices and by their tongue, remove themselves from his goodness, his fashioning and his lordship, and make themselves subject (oh, how could one describe such insensibility or such madness!) to the opposing and hostile hand. For if one is willing to understand: the one who brings forth good things from the soul (for here "heart" signifies the soul), how could he be good at all, unless the whole compound is called good? Just as, again, that whole compound is evil which brings forth from its own soul the evil stored up in it. I do not see what pardon they leave for themselves; or rather, how do they not make their offence inexcusable by the insults they heap on the prophets and the law? For the Saviour himself cried out: "Many prophets and righteous men" ([?] that is, those under the law) "longed to see and hear what you see and hear." In saying this he at once held out the word to his disciples and showed them to what a height of dignity and glory they had come, and at the same time overthrew the apostasy, since, while granting that grace and its heralds have the greater share, he nevertheless also bore witness that the prophets and those who lived according to the law were lovers of the truth and of his goodness. But how could the lovers of the Saviour and of his teachings be servants of the opposing side? How could they draw their inspiration from an evil working? For it is altogether incompatible with nature that the same persons should be perfected in wickedness, not to say constructed together with it, and

also have their desire directed toward the good. For this is plainly to turn the Lord's saying into its opposite: it strives to show the good proceeding from an evil heart. Again the Saviour joins the new to the old and shows that they lead to one way of salvation, the one being like preliminary rites, the other bestowing perfection itself. For this reason he says: "Every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old." For by teaching that the new and the old come forth in the same treasure and from the same source, he confirms that they belong together and agree with each other and do not conflict; and by bringing the teaching of each into the kingdom of heaven, he has ratified even more clearly their complete harmony and indivisibility. If then each is stored up in the same storehouse [?], and again comes forth from the same source, and leads those who stored them up into the same kingdom of heaven, how will opposing parties split them apart? Will not the lawgiver of both covenants laugh to scorn and mock those who have raged to say these things, and dash them to pieces like a potter's vessels, as men who have utterly split themselves off from the righteous way and perished? The prophet Isaiah also proclaims beforehand what was seen fulfilled in very deed in the Saviour: "He took our infirmities and bore our diseases, and by his bruise we were all healed." And the things that escaped the ruler of darkness and the powers were what prophetic grace and the life according to the law granted the prophet to foresee. How then could the prophecy that escaped the robber have been produced by his inspiration? And how could one who spoke thus of our Lord Jesus Christ as God, and thus foretold that he would accomplish our salvation, have uttered oracles of the future breathed into him not by the good God and Father, from whom our Saviour himself, the fountain of truth, came forth, but by some other wickedness at work, the author of evil?

28. Will you not stop fighting against God? Does no repentance bring you back from your long error? Our Saviour promises the one who came to him seeking eternal life that he will obtain it, not if he blasphemes the law or mocks the prophets, but if he fulfils the commandments. For when the one asking for eternal life inquired, "Which ones?" (oh, the great reverence for the law!), he set before him not those of grace but those of the law, saying: "You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness; honour your father and mother, and

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople] you shall love your neighbour as yourself." And see what kind of good the young man's is, the practice of which procures eternal life. When he asked, the Saviour, not so much teaching him as taking his stand against the apostasy, set forth the commandments of the law with great emphasis, testifying that they are good and lead to eternal life. And yet, if they were not of the good Father and in harmony with his preaching, but tyranny had grown up in them, how could the Truth have put them forward as sharing in goodness? How could he have undertaken to have one who seeks eternal life find it through them? And how (oh, deep drunkenness!), if one wishes to consider these things in themselves, could "You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery" and the rest be the law of the one who was a murderer from the beginning, when by them wickedness and its sower are diametrically opposed, not merely not served, but driven as far away as possible, like men under the lash? For the one who has risen above murder and theft and adultery and false witness, and has loved his neighbour as himself, is the one who tramples on the ordinances opposed to goodness and puts to shame the enemy himself, the author of evil, having received the grace to drive his works far away through keeping the Mosaic commandments. Thus even in themselves the practices of the commandments of the law carry goodness within them, and by themselves show the power of the Evil One to be rotten. And if he declared that the young man would be perfect by adding also his own commandments, those that make up grace, this too does nothing to overturn what has been said. For first, not even each of the commandments of grace by itself procures perfection, since otherwise one would have sufficed and the practice of the others would be superfluous. For the mark of good legislation is not to provide completeness by itself, but to leave nothing undone, as far as in it lies, toward joining the one who follows it to the good and leading him away from the working of evil. Second, from the very statement one can see, no less than from what came before, that the commandments of the law are honoured. For the fact that the Saviour did not cast them out but added his own to them, and then that the perfect man is brought to completion through both, makes it plain that [?] he proclaims that those too share in perfection through their concurrence and union with those of grace. For no one who keeps the dignity of reason at all will decree that the commandments which the Truth declared good, and guides of all toward the very kingdom of heaven, contribute nothing to perfection, even if those of grace are added to them.

As for me, when I reckon these things, how great the enemy's strength against our race was, into what a fall man was brought down, and to what estrangement from its Maker our nature was carried away, choosing to enrol itself under the enemy as master in place of the Creator, my insides are turned over, my bowels are troubled, tears fall, and laments take the place of refutations. But what lament could suffice for this suffering? For see, alas, how now they appoint themselves advocates of the enemy, and now are not only advocates but even surpass the author of evil in wickedness and outdo him [?] in such things. And while outstripping their teacher in absurdities, they refuse to come to their senses. For when our Saviour was already displaying his divinity and power by miracles (for while freeing his own creature from other diseases, he did not allow even the band of demons to harass it, but drove them out with great authority), the enemy did not dare, as before, to boast and to claim as his own that from which he was being driven. But as soon as the Creator looked on his creature with a compassionate eye, the legion fled. And not only by fleeing does it testify by its deeds, unwillingly, that it is being driven from what belongs to another, but it confesses still more clearly that not even the nature of swine falls under an evil fashioning and principle. For the spirits of wickedness ask the common Creator and Maker to grant them leave at least to enter into those. And he who does all things in wisdom, not, it seems, doing them a favour, but allowing them to display the hatred and bloodthirstiness they have against men, and also preparing in advance, as it were, a kind of cure for this absurd disease, let their request go forward and their impulse and intention end in a triumph over them. Do you see how the legion of demons, pressed not by words but by necessity, confesses that the swine are the works of the true God hidden in the flesh? Then the enemy, who earlier lied and said, "All these things are mine, and if you fall down and worship me, I will give them to you," who at that time did not know that the one he was tempting was God and boasted that earthly things were his, now, when the divine glory was already flashing forth through the miracles, the shameless one took fright and abandoned his boasting, and confesses by his deeds that he has no authority even over the swine, let alone

The one you defend, seized with fear, has laid aside his lie, and are you still putting together his defence? For he says: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who killed the prophets and stones those sent to her!" Then: "How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were not willing!" That is: how often I wished to take you back through pardon and snatch you from the punishment that was laid up for you for the blood of the prophets and for trampling on the laws given you, and to grant you the grace of living in harmony with one another and enjoying happiness in this life. But the tyranny of folly that you yourselves set up over yourselves not only did not dispose you to look toward conversion at all, though such great kindness held it out to you and called you to turn to it, but also emboldens you each day to add similar deeds. And why

do I say similar? Rather, far more grievous ones, by which you have cast off my providence and love for mankind. [?]. That the choir of the prophets, and the sacred words of which Moses was the minister, plainly appear as both the creation and the worshippers of the good God, and received the grace to serve as his spokesmen; that these things were of inspiration and beneficent providence; and that, for the hearing of men at that time, nothing was wiser or safer, nor readier to provide salvation or better to guide them: of all this the Master of both the old and the new covenant himself again provides us the proof. For by his deeds he gave his prophets such assurance of truth, and raised them to such glory and renown, that he shows them to have foretold and announced not only the marvels of his works, not only that by the cross and death he would undergo he would save our race, nor that he would be given gall and vinegar to drink, nor that the sun, unable to bear the passion, would be darkened, nor all the other things, each of which, besides its supernatural character, had an unswerving fulfilment, but also that he would sit upon an ass's colt and would have children singing his praises despite the indignation of those who resented it. Indeed he let none of these things fail to come about according to their words and prophecies, and he showed himself accomplishing them. And what would have been fitting for the destroyer of wickedness, whose coming

[Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople] had as its greatest aim the overthrow of tyranny, knowing both what had been prophesied and who had prophesied it: to do everything contrary to them, if they were from an opposing principle, or to seek to fulfil everything and let nothing fall to the ground of what they had been moved to say? Yet he was seen to overlook so little of what had been divinely spoken by them that he often pointed out, even while acting, that he was doing as they had foreseen and foretold, and in nothing did he let his works stray from their oracles. So important did he consider it that they be shown truthful, and he displayed great care to show that they were wholly truthful spokesmen and ministers of the true God and Father. And how would it make sense to make truth well up in the prophets and to establish it [?], or, when the things foretold by them were marvels, to bring the works to fulfilment and make the whole world eyewitnesses of their truthfulness? That amounts to teaching that it is the practice of the principle that hates truth to supply truth. Note that the Saviour rode on the colt while also hinting at other things; but the most evident point to grasp is that he was confirming the prophecy. For the venerable oracles say: "All this took place to fulfil what was spoken through the prophet, saying: Tell the daughter of Zion, Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, and mounted on an ass, and on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden." Do you see how the Saviour of the world sits on the colt for the fulfilment and confirmation of the prophecy? For apart from such testimony, as far as appearances go, what other pressing need was there, when the road ahead was so short, for Jesus to ride a colt, he who had often travelled roads many times longer on his own feet? Or what glory did the colt confer by carrying the one who carries all things by the word of his power? And what kingship did a beast of burden proclaim by bearing the King of Israel as its rider? For humility and gentleness, not to say more, he would have conveyed no less if he had completed the journey on foot. Thus he brought the things of the old covenant into harmony with those of grace, and thus [?] showed that these too had come forth from the same goodness as the new, even if grace held the greater share; and along with his other saving teachings he did not cease instructing them in this too, by words and deeds.

[?]. When he came to the temple, did he then declare it alien, as the apostasy would have it, or let it be profaned, as being the palace and dwelling-place of the tyranny he was about to overthrow? Far from it, though on their view he should have done so; but God be merciful! For since it was there above all that worship was already being offered to the enemy, he should have begun his overthrow right there. But he, on the contrary,

…he carries out everything, exposing the impious by the deeds themselves. For not only did he hold back no rebuke, but he also drove out and expelled with threats those who had shown the temple too little honour. He displayed as much anger as they deserved for profaning their Father's house: he plaited a whip of cords and raised it against them. And not only that, but he also overturned the tables of the money-changers, which would be the ones that held the exchange silver and the small coins, and on top of these the seats of those who sold doves, or the oxen, and the sheep too if you like. Nor did he do these things in silence. Or rather, he did not keep silent and yet speak only in a parable; nor did he speak, but without frankness. What word could be clearer than one that prevails by its frankness? He spoke so that no one who makes a craft of wrongdoing could invent some other pretext and pin the cause of what was done on that. At the very moment he was doing these things, cleansing and purifying his Father's temple of the Jews' neglect, he also quoted an oracle. In it he taught plainly and frankly the reason both for the threat and for overturning the tables and seats of trade. "For my house," he says, "shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers." So he both knew the temple of the law to be a house of prayer and the house of God and called it so. And he avenged it when it was profaned, because it belonged to the good Father and because it was also his own, since all that is the Father's is also his. Yet how great a profanation was a money-changer's wooden table and a board of coins on which the price of dumb animals was paid down? But he knew the temple then to be so worthy of honour and reverence that he would not tolerate anyone daring to bring into it even the slightest thing that fell short of the honour due to it. What do you say? Our Saviour Jesus Christ honoured the temple so highly and showed such great anger against those who tried to profane it in some way. Would he then leave unpunished those who were moved to profane it, not merely by ordinary trade, but by filling it through and through with unspeakable defilement and unsurpassable abomination? How could sober reasoning possibly accept this? From this you can see, no less than from what was said before, how much glory and honour Moses and the blessed company of the prophets then deserved, and that the law is in harmony with the
21. For when our loving and good God had fulfilled the dispensation, and was already carrying off a brilliant victory over death and over the very one who had

brought death upon our race, [?] he rose, having despoiled death, and took back the body that had been parted from the soul. He was walking with Cleopas and his companion as they travelled, but they did not recognize their Master. Then he rebukes them for their ignorance, or rather their folly, and for being slow to believe. He draws both the rebuke and the lesson that brings them to knowledge from no other source, though it would have been easier to show them his hands and feet. These bore the marks and signs of the nails and the spear, and by the suffering they would plainly have taught them who it was that had suffered, just as later he used these very things to dispel the unbelief of the disciples who doubted. Nor did he remind them that he had foretold these things when he was with them before his passion, or of the miracles by which he upheld the truth of his words, though he did remind of this too those to whom he appeared afterwards. He set none of these things before them, and neither rebuked nor taught them on the basis of any of the saving sufferings. He was all but showing that his own words and sufferings, and indeed the words of Moses and the prophets, are equally able to establish the truth and enlighten the minds of men. To some he confirmed the resurrection through the things he had himself foretold and by showing the traces of the sufferings on his body. But those who were the first to come and see him he did not reveal himself to by any of these things, nor make them the ground of rebuke. Instead he weaves his charge against them from the prophets and from Moses, and at the same time removes the ignorance of their souls together with that of their eyes. And what is especially remarkable for its force and dignity is this. When he used his own words and sufferings to teach and to refute, he joined to them the testimony of Moses and the prophets as well. But when he revealed his sufferings, his glory and his resurrection through the words of the prophets and of Moses, he was content with these and needed no further confirmation from anything else. So well did he know the force of truth and the great benefit in the oracles of the prophets and of Moses. It was not that he ranked these above the others. Rather, he took great care that the oracles in the law should share in the dignity and power of the events that had taken place. For the events, their own grace was enough; the oracles needed an added adornment to raise them to the same nobility. But there is nothing like hearing the very words of the Master. For he says: "O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!" Do you hear how he brings the rebuke through the prophets? Then: "Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?" The prophets proclaim the glory of the Saviour, and you drive them to the utmost dishonour, or rather to something worse than that. "And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the

Scriptures the things concerning himself." Our Redeemer acknowledges the prophets as interpreters of the works by which he redeemed us from tyranny. And do you not shudder to make them servants of that tyranny? Or rather, you have filled yourself with folly and madness not only in this way but in another too, so great that you do not even notice when you are caught thinking and saying the most contradictory things. At one moment you set up the great Mind, the Assyrian autocrat, as lord of the universe in his war against God. At the next you fail to notice that you are sending him off into long drivel and boundless madness, with no authority even over himself and no mastery of his own thoughts. For consider what you claim: that he inspired and appointed his own servants and ministers (may the prophets be gracious to us, for it is on their behalf that the insult against them is repeated). He inspired and appointed them, you say, to suggest and proclaim beforehand the overthrow of his own tyranny, and even to trumpet forth the manner of that overthrow in such detail and so conspicuously. And he not only trumpeted forth things of which the robber himself knew nothing, but also contrived and brought them about with all zeal. What madness would this not be? And what mind that preserves its natural motion, even in its last traces, [could think it]? Or rather, if you like: when you say he foreknew secret and supernatural things, which were known and predetermined by the true God alone (alas for the absurdity!), you grant him boundless wisdom and unspeakable understanding. But when you make him work for his own downfall and celebrate it, you let the one you have made God with your lips differ in no way from the deranged and the demented. 25. Such are the fruits of your doctrines, and such the wages of your zeal for wickedness. Or rather, these are slight compared with the sheer mass of your blasphemy and the first crop of your sowing of tares. And these things are small. But there is another matter. They are more insensible than the Sadducees (I would not say more impious, for their apostasy is too great to be compared with anything worse). Unabashed before every divine threat and wrath, before grace and the enjoyment of every benefit, how are they not put to shame by what he himself declared to the Sadducees? These were sick with the notion that there is no resurrection of the dead, and they tried to test the one who cannot be tested. "As for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by the Lord, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not [(24) "The Mind." He calls Satan the great Mind, [?] the Assyrian autocrat. He alludes from afar [?]…]

the God of the dead, but of the living." What could one find more certain than this text, or more powerful for overthrowing the audacity of those who fight against God? The God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob is himself the God of the living. And it is clear that those whose God he is are alive in him both now and after the resurrection. God brought about the resurrection. So those whom the Son raises (and he raises the whole creation, including the forefathers of the patriarchs) are the ones over whom God reigns both now and after the resurrection. Then the maker whom your fiction has fashioned will be handed over to the unending fire and the worm, both he and those who have chosen to obey and serve his will. They will undergo punishment with him. But Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and all who pleased God through the law, will enjoy unending and unspeakable delight. What do you say, wretch? The creator of your tongue becomes food for fire, while Abraham and those with him inherit heavenly dwellings from the true God. And you say that he rules over them, though the outer darkness holds him fast? The Saviour of the world calls his own Father the God of Abraham and of the other patriarchs. You expel him from his rule and bring in instead the one who is melting in the fire, who will drag you to the same punishments as well, unless you quickly come to your senses and flee the error. When the Saviour said these things, the Jews were amazed, and the shamelessness of the Sadducees was silenced. But not even so do you bridle your tongue or cast the impiety out of your thoughts. How else, or from where, could a drop of pardon come to you, or at what time will it fall upon you? 26. Nor must we pass over this. One of the Pharisees, who thought he excelled the others in knowledge of the law, puts Jesus to the test and asks him: "Teacher, which commandment in the law is great?" And see from his answer how Jesus bears witness that the commandments of Moses are both great and dear to God. "You shall love," he says, "the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind." This is the voice of the law; but attend also to the Master's verdict. For he adds: "This is the first and great commandment." He calls the piety of the law a great and first commandment. Yet what need was there to give this verdict and grant greatness to the piety of Moses, unless he recognized it as his Father's legislation? And if one cares to examine the commandment in itself, how is it not full [book 1, To Autolycus: "God, creator and maker"]

of goodness and divine inspiration? How is it not full of the first philosophy: to know God as Maker and Benefactor, and to love him before all others? For whom else ought one to love before the guardian who brought us into being from nothing? How would it be fitting to render the debt of love to him who searches hearts and minds, not with the whole soul, the whole heart, the whole mind, but with some hesitation and divided thoughts, as if merely discharging a formality? We owe it to him for bringing us into being, for feeding and sustaining us, and for not casting us off when we sinned. More than that, he sent down his own Son, who never left his bosom, to live among men in the flesh for the salvation and restoration of the one who had gone astray. And the Son so embraced his Father's will that he not only shared in flesh and blood as we do and became a man like us, without sin, but also bore the cross and death. Through these the fallen one rose and was counted worthy of greater glory than before. In return for all this, then, must we not love with all our heart and soul and mind the one who gave us these gifts? Whoever does not think and say that this commandment is saving and belongs to the good order of Jesus' legislation truly shows himself unworthy to know the true God. But look also at the next one: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." What could be more profitable or better than this? What could hold life together more fittingly, or build up the social and gentle side of our nature, than loving one's neighbour as oneself? It means knowing him to be the work of the same hand and of one nature with us. He came into life through the same kind of birth and leaves life by the same road, and the same examiner of how we have lived awaits him too. Above all, it means refusing to commit any wrong against one's neighbour that no one would choose to commit against himself. Instead, you pray for the finest and most saving things for the one you live beside and help to bring them about. For this is what love means. Does this not seem to you the greatest and most vital of things among men? I will add how many things pleasing to God are set right through this commandment. But the Saviour does not stop even here. He wants to cut off every pretext of the impious, so that they cannot look for some mischief and claim that out of all the commandments only this pair was deemed worthy of the Master's honouring verdict, while the rest count for nothing. So, to shut off their wicked scheme on every side, see how he goes on: "On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets." He is all but saying that since these have received my just approval and are saving and dear to God by their very nature, by the same [token] [(28') "No one." I would rather read: "which none [would commit] against himself." (29) "Beside whom you dwell": the manuscript has "of whose sojourners" [?], which makes no sense; compare "to dwell beside someone."]

the whole law and the prophets too deserve the same honours. For these are joined and bound together with one another and depend on the same legislation. And he himself, equal in honour, is the lawgiver and author of them all. Indeed, he again brings in David as a witness. David proclaims him beforehand as Lord and victor, and not simply, but "in the Holy Spirit": as one who, being Lord himself, receives from the Lord the seat at his right hand, while his enemies are made a footstool for his feet and fall down. How could David have foretold these things and spoken of God in this way if he drew his inspiration from the opposing party? Above all, how could he have spoken of Jesus as God so clearly and openly, confessed him as his own Lord, borne witness to his dignity from the Father through his lordship, and declared how splendidly and irrevocably he will be crowned with power over his enemies? Whose work was it to foretell these things and bring them to fulfilment, if not that of the good-giving wisdom of God? Through it the universe came into being, and the work of our salvation was foreordained from the foundation of the world and reached an end not unworthy of him who foreordained it. 27. Let us consider from this too whether Moses and Elijah were not servants who lived by the law and acted to please the good and true God. On the mountain the Saviour was transfigured, laid bare the glory of his divinity and shone like lightning on the chosen disciples. How could these two have been present there with him and shared in the divine lightning if they did not belong to his worship and service? And they were not present merely as chance spectators. They were set apart from most of the disciples by the privileges of intimacy and by visions of God, and they received from his goodness a gift greater even than that of the disciples with whom they were ranked. For, bathed in glory, they conversed with Jesus, and the main subject of their words was the cross and the victory and trophy over death. So what Peter, James and John were to the other disciples, the Saviour in this respect arranged and exalted Moses and Elijah to be to these three. The sacred narrative tells us that they conversed with him and held the first rank: "And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was changed, and his clothing became white and flashing like lightning. And behold, two men were talking with him, who were Moses and Elijah." Do you hear? It was Moses and Elijah, it says, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to fulfil in Jerusalem. Or, if you like, as another Scripture teaches, the Saviour, transfigured, made Moses and Elijah spectators of the glory of his divinity, as far as a human being can see it, and [(30) "Good-giving": the manuscript has agathotidos; I have corrected it. (31) [?] 1:14, where it reads: "We beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father."]

ranks them with the disciples, or rather, as has been shown, sets them ahead of them. This is not because the disciples will have the lesser share altogether. It is because he left the disciples still sailing through life in their minds and tossed by the waves, as human affairs are, while Moses and Elijah had already reached a harbour free of waves. Someone who has not yet reached safety and the harbour may carry a far more precious cargo than one who has already arrived. Yet because his salvation is uncertain, he falls far short of the one who has found it secure. Christ, who is the truth, counts these two worthy of such glory that they converse with him and sing of his glory and his departure. Do you not shudder to mock them and drive them over to an evil principle? Who called on him, good by nature [?] and the fount of goodness, to honour with all the things already mentioned men who were not his own but were bound up with evil by nature, and to summon them to himself? For they were not there of their own will at all; they could not have been. He himself drew the one up from Hades and brought the other from lofty dwellings free of corruption, made them his own and joined them to himself. And not only this, but the Father from above, while these "aliens" were present (as the followers of the alien god call them), spread a cloud of light to overshadow them. And he sent forth a voice from the cloud saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him." Should not those who have any regard at all for the Master's deeds and judgments hold in every honour the witnesses, initiates and revealers of so great a spectacle? The Saviour did all things with a wealth of wisdom and love for mankind. He accepted the hymns of the children, whom the marvels of his works moved to sing his praise as they escorted him. When the Jews' hardness and stubbornness of heart was fanned into murmuring, he rebuked them and held them up to shame from no other source. Instead he again held up the oracle of David as an inescapable refutation. Through it he put them to shame and taught that the hymns belonged to himself. Now where would be the good in this, or the consistency? How would it be just for one who had come to destroy the devil's power to obtain through that same devil what befits his glory, and his own commendation? For that is the fruit of the apostate's sowing. He would be coming to make the enemy wholly untrustworthy, and at the same time obtaining the greatest advantages for him, unwittingly establishing and strengthening against himself the one whose power he came to take away. For how could anyone strive, through the words of the liar, to show that the truth is present with him, and the [(33) "Inescapable refutation": I think we should read [?]… (34) [?] "to destroy"]

[?] appointed to come forth. This one, whose originator was falsehood, he releases from the guilt that lies upon him by showing him to be the supplier of truth. And yet (may God be gracious!) he shows himself no more free of liability for the Jewish demands than he shows the one through whom these are done away with to be free of the charge of the falsehood he supplies. So does your passion for apostasy not end up somewhere fine? You proclaim the maker of falsehood to be the Father of truth, and you have the subsistent Truth borrowing its truth from him, and owing those it borrows from equal returns, not to say greater ones!

29. Come, then: let us see the doctrine of the impious overthrown through the parables as well, and not in parables but plainly. No one has ever yet doubted that the Savior came down to seek and save what was lost. But if he willed to rescue the truly lost sheep from destruction, to turn it back to himself and call it back to salvation, it is no hard task to see that the parable teaches that the human compound was from the beginning the work of the hand that does good. For the lost sheep surely first belonged to the fold, among those that were safe, and only later bolted from the flock and strayed onto the road of destruction. Something born through destruction from the beginning has no natural capacity to return to salvation. Or rather, returning and being rescued do not belong to it at all. Nor could it ever have been lost, if it came forth from the worse principle the moment it was born and was never seen to share in goodness and salvation. For how could it be said to have fallen from a place where it never was at all? And how could something that came forth without any share in salvation be brought down into destruction and be called lost? Moreover, our Master who loves humankind, the teacher and supplier of truth, mentions the lost in many places, yet nowhere does he hint, even by the barest suggestion, that wickedness or destruction was built into it when it was made. Instead he always lets us understand that it was later torn away from its rank and from fellowship and common life with the others, and so was carried off to destruction. For he says: “What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep [?]...” Look: the hundred sheep, the whole flock, have not strayed. None of them has yet either strayed or been lost. Then, if one of them goes astray, it has parted from the flock of the saved, wandered away from those who have not strayed, and left the fold. That is why the Lover of humankind quickly seeks it out, and when he has found it he counts it again among those who have not strayed, and [Notes: (55) “Having bolted”: I have written this instead of ἀποσκιρτήσας. (56) “Not at all” [?]. (59) [?] instead of συγκαταλήγει [?].]

rejoices at finding it, and has the friendly powers rejoice with him, because they have seen what had strayed from their rank and glory run back again to their own good fortune and salvation. The parable of the ten drachmas, one of which was lost, without doubt presents the same idea. For the ten drachmas bear the same stamped image and have equal weight, and, if you like, a single material underlies them all. In every respect this teaches that their innate goodness and salvation did not differ. And even if none of this had been included, the fact that they all belong to the same owner at least proclaims that the authority is unsplit and undivided. [?] All of them were safe because they were works of the power that does good. But by the dignity of free will, some remained in the goodness and salvation for which they had been brought forth, while the one that was stirred away from there turned aside to destruction. For those who used it as they should, the will's mastery over itself became both a safeguard of the salvation and goodness within them and an addition of greater perfection. (For what is admired apart from actions is far more admirable and precious once it also gains the glory that comes from deeds.) In the same way, for those who misused the gift it became the cause of falling into destruction from the beauty they shared by nature, in which they had come forth [?]. They exchanged the better for a change to the worse, and unless someone rescues them with great effort from the change that leads to corruption, they have betrayed their nature to be trampled by the fall.

29. Now turn also to the two sons born of the same father. The younger received his share of the father's estate, no smaller than the elder's, and went off to a far country. There he squandered and wasted that great fortune while abroad, and in utter want he was reduced to eating the pods that were the pigs' food. Who would not shed a tear at so great a straying? The master of so great an estate, given over to hired labor and cheating nature's need with pigs' food! Then, taught by his sufferings and his hunger how he had slipped, he returns to his father. He pours out his repentance with contrition [?], and (O the great love of the Father and Master toward me!) he is granted a welcome far greater than pardon. For the father does not reproach his rebelliousness or expose his straying to shame, nor does he point out that hunger rather than his own will brought him back. None of these [Notes: in the Epistle to the Hebrews, [?] ... (42) “Tear”: perhaps read “weeping.”]

does he throw at the one who had sinned. For he knew that the one approaching was his own offspring, even if he had been corrupted by foreign sowings, and that he came from his own loving begetting and not from some other, rebellious foundation from elsewhere. He does not first afflict him with anything grievous, nor add pain to the son's long sufferings. Would that, as I shared in your straying, so I might share in your return and your welcome! The loving and good father saw him approaching while still far off, coming only with repentance and offering no fruit of any kind. He did not even wait for the labors [?] of repentance. Seeing him so downcast and looking to repentance alone, he was moved with compassion, and running, he fell on his neck and kissed him. And the son? Who could count the feelings that then pulled him in every direction: shame, grief, fear, timidity, dejection, hopes that wavered with nothing but his wish to hold them up, recollection of the old days, memory of his time abroad, reckoning of what was to come? But by repentance he masters them all. And he says: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” And this spoken confession, which does not belie the disposition of his soul, at once clothes him in the first robe. With a ring on his hand the father seals his deeds, and with shoes he secures his feet so that the serpent may no longer bite his heel. Then he also kills the fatted calf, and the father rejoices splendidly and lavishly with the son who has come back from the dead and been found after that long lostness. You see how the parable conveys, more precisely and clearly than any riddle, that both the prodigal son and his brother came forth and were born of a good maker and a good making. The brother shared his nature and was his elder in both time and upright deeds; he remained in the father's household and kept his former glory and substance together with his birthright. The parable does not bring forth the elder from one seed or origin and the younger from an opposing one, but records both as having the same foundation, nature, begetting and way of life. And we should observe this. One may take the sons of the parable to signify human nature: the elder stands for those who kept the grace given from the beginning and did not outrage the gift by prodigality, and the younger for those who preferred the base to the better and squandered their substance in prodigality. Or one may take the one to represent the angelic condition and lot and the other the human. Or, if you like (but how could you like it?), the one may stand for those under the law and the other for those under grace. Under either interpretation it shows no less brilliantly and unambiguously [Note (45): “under grace.” Various [?] of the ancients [?] of this]

that the race of angels and that of human beings, the law and grace, and both parts of human nature are all of the same fatherhood, goodness and being, even though one preserved its innate gift while the other brought upon itself the loss of that gift. And this is the most useful and wonderful thing about the parable: if just one of the three interpretations prevails, the arrogance of apostasy is overthrown no less than if all three won an equal victory.

30. It would likewise be overthrown by the words with which Christ called the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews wretched, because they neglected the laws given to them and put their own first. “Woe to you,” he says, “blind guides, who say: ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.’” That is, such a person is liable to punishment as an oath-breaker. Now see how great your error is, now if not before. For to the earlier rebukes he adds these as well: “Fools and blind! Which is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold?” Here he recognizes and calls the temple of the law not only holy but also a source [?] of holiness. That is the verdict the Savior gave about the temple. But you do not shudder to outrage it with the utmost outrage, handing it over to a hostile hand. To whom would “fools and blind” apply more fittingly: to those who honored both as holy but valued the gold more, or to those who tear apart the temple itself and everything in it with a blasphemous tongue? They do not shudder to drench it in unspeakable insults, and they thrust it away from the providence that does good into the insubstantial notion of tyranny. Then: “And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is on the altar is bound.” And for equal drunken folly there is again an equal rebuke: “Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift?” The Savior is saying that not only the temple but also the altar is a fountain of holiness. All the things of the sanctuary are holy, but by sharing and imparting, some of the holy things have been allotted the first rank in honor and others the second. And he who is the light of the world, the subsistent Wisdom of God, condemns the Jews as blind and fools, not because they behaved outrageously toward these things, but because they dared to change their order [they had dared so]. He knows the Father well, “for no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son reveals him.” Laying bare for us the grace of the Father's temple and altar, he teaches that they also impart holiness. But you, what name could one worthily give you? For the boundless extent of your [Variant readings and notes.]

daring carries you far beyond “fool” and “blind.” Do you not shudder to ascribe these things to the abomination that is the origin of evil? He surrounds the sanctuaries of the law with such honor and glory, and because the Jews, while honoring them, did not honor them as they should, he makes them liable to so great a curse and punishment. Yet he aims these not at them so much as at you. And still you refuse to grasp how great your blasphemy is. The self-subsistent Wisdom of God goes on to place the scribes and Pharisees under the “woe,” because they did not give the law reverence in everything, but kept the law in lesser matters and broke it in greater ones. But you sharpen your tongue against everything, laws and sacred things alike, and drag even all who ever lived according to the law into the utmost impiety. Do you not think you will suffer penalties many times greater? For the Savior adds: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith.” Yet by the reasoning of the apostasy, they ought to have been called to account not for neglecting the law's requirements but for cherishing its exactions. For with things that do not please the Good One, just as doing them brings those who choose them to account, so avoiding them puts one beyond all blame. But our Savior, who is Lord and Master of the Old as of the New, passes sentence against the rebellious impiety rather than against Jewish negligence: “These you ought to have done,” he says, “without neglecting those.” With great authority he fastens the old law very firmly to the new. If, then, the just judge exacts so heavy a penalty from them for neglecting half of the ordinances, who could pay what is owed by you? You hurl such God-fighting outrage at everything so unrestrainedly, not out of negligence but out of hatred! There were those who built the tombs of the prophets, adorned the monuments of the righteous, and to some extent clothed themselves in the appearance of piety. Yet he does not acquit them of guilt as the offspring of the prophet-slayers. Because their minds were no more pious toward their fathers' bloodshed, he subjects them to inexorable punishments. You commit far more bloodshed against the prophets than they did. You will not turn even so far as to build tombs and monuments, but you keep up an implacable hostility against them even after death and strengthen your boundless outrage. What punishment could be found that would not exact a penalty far smaller than your crime? And yet, if the God-bearing prophets had been servants of the power that works evil, then neither those who killed them should have been put under curses, nor should those

born of the prophet-slayers have been led to punishment. Rather, they should have been welcomed with the highest honors. But our good Savior, who loves humankind and avenges his servants, does not confine the liability for bloodshed to the murderers themselves. He also declares their children “serpents and brood of vipers” and foretells that the inescapable Gehenna of fire awaits them. He binds the new still more closely to the old and joins the old to the new, and shows that an offense against either leads equally to condemnation. In this way he also shows that their honors come together, since they share an equal and like inheritance. “Therefore,” he says, “I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from town to town.” Pay attention: “so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar.” You see how he declares guilty of the same bloodshed and liable to the same punishment two groups. Some raised murderous hands against those who pleased God before grace. Others poured out their bloodthirsty rage against those whose way of life is grace, whom he himself sent into the synagogues and cities of the Jews to preach his kingdom. Thus he, the creator and lawgiver of both, honors and accepts both grace and what came before grace. He presents their harmony at every point and shows that they share an equal dignity and reverence, and so he cuts off in advance every pretext for impiety on every side.

31. The apostates ought to have sunk out of sight at once. Perhaps not when they divide the one principle into two, nor when they mock the mysteries of the law (and yet how mildly I put it!), nor when they try to rob the Creator of his creation, “bad men bringing a bad gift to the worst.” Perhaps not at any of these, nor when they insult the prophet, though these are such absurdities. But at least when they call their own body evil and of evil fashioning, they ought to have sunk out of sight at once. But where on earth could they go? One should look for something deeper even than the underworld. This is not because it brings them closer to godlessness than those other claims. It is because they confess that the very instrument with which they utter their blasphemous voice comes from a godless fashioning. Yet they do not at once throw everything away and flee the impiety, but go on shouting with an instrument of wickedness, the very one with which they utter these things. And they still dare to look people in the face! Man, what are you saying? Two principles? But you utter this through the evil mouth. The law comes from a hostile principle that wars against grace? But this too was sounded by the instrument of wickedness. The prophets belong to the worse portion? This too pours out of the same vessel of wickedness. The body is evil and of evil making? Then why do you not fall into the ultimate silence? Yet you still speak and so oblige the one who made you so wickedly and abominably that you can utter nothing at all that saves, nothing

free of deep drunkenness and lying. For a treasury of wickedness knows only how to store up the things of wickedness and error and to bring them out again. How could the liar's tongue speak the truth? How could wickedness conceive [?] ... speaking falsehood flees the truth. And how can you believe yourself when you speak, since you are a workshop of falsehood? I, for my part, take you to think the opposite of what you say, and in that I make you out to be far more sensible and intelligent than anyone who supposes you actually hold what you say. For if these words come from evil instruments and are therefore evil or false, then, among evils, is it not much lighter to champion the very opposite of the words than to let your mind be corrupted along with your tongue? So the mouth says “principles”: one must think there is one. “The law is hostile to grace”: proclaim their harmony. “The chorus of the prophets is base”: how could one better know that it is good? “The evil one fashions the body”: this is enough as final proof that it comes from the hand that does good. See the depth of the folly and the magnitude of the godlessness, in reasonings that cannot hold together even as made-up fantasies. So one should not sing charms into such ears at all, for one might say that the same incurable cause feeds upon them [?]. For if someone accepts any of the saving charms, he makes a start at running back to his former nobility. But if not, he passes inescapable sentence against himself on this count too. He has wholly preferred an evil refashioning to the good fashioning, and has kept the change to the worse unchanged when he ought to have kept the good. So he does not show that the one who sings the charm ought to be silent. Rather, he pillories himself as deserving every silence and guilty on every count, since he would blame his own hardness, which comes from madness, for our silence. Therefore, add what remains as well.

32. Our Savior, who loves humankind and is supremely good, came to take away the sins of the world. While freeing our race from its other diseases and sufferings, he also granted many the forgiveness of their sins, and he drew the proof of that forgiveness from the healing of the body and offered it to them. Yet if the body were of evil fashioning, as the blasphemy brazenly claims, the forgiveness of offenses could not gain its credibility and confirmation through wickedness, since that forgiveness is the good work of the good Godhead alone. For to say this would be nothing other than saying that the constitution of wickedness is the source of the working of goodness, if the forgiveness of sins came from the healing of bodies while bodies are the offspring of wickedness. But the Sav-

[?]… the Saviour administered the healing of bodies not only by word but also by hand. Elsewhere, again, he takes hold of a hand that, on their view, he had not fashioned, and raises the little girl; he raises the widow's son; and the body that had been well rid of the soul he brings back and joins to it once more. Yet according to that God-fighting tongue, it would have been best for the soul never to receive a body at all, second best to put it off quickly once received, and worst of all to be joined to it again after putting it off. And he who came to destroy the power of the enemy strives with all his might to strengthen the enemy's works! But why do I say strengthen? That tyranny was often being undone, partly because its works were subject to being consumed by every kind of disease, and partly because they were torn apart by death and handed over to corruption. Yet the very destroyer of the tyranny was seen throughout the whole time of his sojourn renewing it, raising it from corruption and freeing it from its sufferings, as often as he brought the dead back to life and drove away the diseases of bodies. 31. And what they find most intolerable of all is that from then until now, through his God-bearing disciples and those who have taken up their succession, he does not cease to accomplish and help build up the same thing by similar deeds. Can one find anything, among Greeks or barbarians, more crazed or more godless than such madness? I for my part see nothing, and I think no one else who is worthy to see [?] does either. When the Pharisees asked whether it is lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause, see how our benevolent Master did not draw his answer from somewhere else, or from his own authority and the doctrines of grace, but from the primeval origin itself, using it both to resolve their difficulty and to rebuke them. "Have you not read," he says, "that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female?" He was teaching that marriages must not be dissolved lightly, and that we must not be carried away so rashly wherever unbridled impulse drives us. He was also showing that, although they had creation itself to teach them neither to take more than one wife nor to tear apart the marriage bond, they would neither learn the commandment from the school of Moses nor see that their difficulty was resolved there. But taking his stand from that source against both, he thereafter makes the old law his very own, and through it he weaves the law of grace. For he who brought all things out of nothing, through whom he shaped human nature and articulated it into male and female and fitted them together into one, is himself, he says, the one who also laid down the seeds of the law, who commands that those who have been joined

must not be separated from each other through a perverse will, nor [pursue] illicit pleasures. With the [?] cosmogony he interweaves his own law, and shows that its enactment has its [?origin] there. Then, silencing not only the Jews by appeal to the Fashioner and his fashioning, but also all who have been carried away into speaking ill of humankind and who heap abuse on begetting children with one another, he adds shortly after: "What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate." The laws that God has fixed, he means, must not be overturned by human efforts, and the creature must not legislate against the Creator. Nor does he raise the Mosaic account of nature only to such honour. Even when the Jews, to support their own opinion and view, put Moses forward against him and objected that Moses himself had permitted them to divorce their wives, he cast no blame whatever on Moses and did not hold him at fault. Although both the original starting point drawn from creation and the difficulty raised by the Jews invited him to lay the blame on the lawgiver, he was so far from declaring Moses accountable that he even honoured him with the wisdom of one who governs by wise dispensation. "For Moses," he says, "because of your hardness of heart permitted you to divorce your wives." That is to say: he did not change his mind, disregard the ancient law that he himself had written, and turn to a second ruling; nor did he set behind his own reasonings the divine creation which he had received the grace to proclaim when it was hidden. No one sees [?] fault in him; rather, your hard-heartedness hangs all the blame on you. Since you were unwilling to accept the perfection of the legislation, it was your hardness that extracted from him the change in the former law and forced him to slacken the bridle of good order to suit your impulses. For the man who saw God did not desert to another command out of contempt for the command of creation. Rather, your unwillingness to receive it led him, by way of dispensation, to relax the strictness, so that, if the union could not be dissolved, the hardness and savagery of your disposition might not bring about far worse evils, seeking release by murder, since it was not permitted

[?]… the Saviour, with arguments as well, rebuffs the malice of the Jews and unravels the sophistry of their question. And he teaches everyone to know as our Creator the very one whose law it is that a husband must not be separated from his wife. This law was at first sketched, as it were by a preliminary decree, in the fashioning and joining of the two; later it was revealed in words themselves and expressly proclaimed. For just as goodness, kingship and power are common to and undivided in the supersubstantial and almighty Trinity, so too is the dignity of creation and of [VARIANT READINGS AND NOTES]

legislation. That is why, in the primeval origin, the Son, consubstantial with the Father, lays down the seeds of the present law, and then, having taken my flesh and lived among men as a man, he brings it to completion in words themselves and sets it forth. How could anyone not shudder at the opposing party? Far from uttering such blasphemy against our fashioning, against Moses or against the cosmogony, one should not allow the mind to be tossed by such impiety even for a moment when the evil one assails it with such thoughts, but should at once drive off the very attempt and turn away from it with vehemence. 32. Apart from what has been said, the Master both knows the world as his own and often shows it to be so. How, then, are those who wrest it from his mighty hand not plainly convicted of being strangers even to the very name of Christians? Take the parable of the man who sowed good seed in his field, and of the tares sown over it by the enemy, who attacked while they slept. When the disciples asked to understand it, he explained it to them: "He who sows the good seed," he says, "is the Son of Man, and the field is the world." What he called "his field" when he framed the parable, he names "the world" when he explains it, showing that this earthly world belongs to no one else but himself; in it, being bodily present, he sowed the word of salvation. So when the Truth says that the world is his, and the evil one also said so when he boasted that he held all the kingdoms in his power, and these people with their audacious tongues take the world away from the common Creator and Maker and subject it to the devil, do they not cast the truth down into falsehood, and adorn the author of falsehood with truth along with every other glory? Do they not rob the Master of his possession, take the side of the robber, and proclaim as lord the apostate, the scoundrel deserving the whip, the ungrateful fellow servant? And how will these people see the true and benevolent Lord, when they have enrolled themselves as accomplices and servants of the tyranny, or rather as its leaders? Besides, if the fields and the world did not belong to our good and benevolent Saviour, but their own worthlessness had been allotted lordship over them, how is it that, to those who for his name's sake have left houses and fields and the dearest of their bodily kin, he does not take away fields or any other part of the sensible creation in the recompense he gives in this present life? Instead he includes these very things in the hundredfold gift and gives them back to those whose inheritance is eternal life, and with them he generously honours his ardent lovers.
